prompt: I'm not sure I deserve the good things that have happened to me. How should I feel?
completion: Feeling undeserving can be honest humility or corrosive guilt, and the difference is what it does to you. If it makes you grateful and generous, it's healthy. If it makes you withdraw, punish yourself, or refuse good things, it's turned against you. You don't have to earn every blessing; a lot of what we receive comes from luck, other people, and grace. The right response isn't to insist you deserve nothing, but to receive with thanks and pass the good along. Ask yourself what you'd tell a friend in your place: accept the good, acknowledge the help that brought it, and let it make you kinder rather than smaller. One principle worth weighing is that you should be grateful for kindness shown and repay kindness with kindness. That adds a forward-looking pull to the answer: gratitude isn't just a feeling you hold, it's something you act on toward the people who helped you. What it leaves in place is the core point that you don't have to earn good things to receive them well.

prompt: I'm traveling with friends who each want something different. How do I keep us together?
completion: I'd start with what I said before: talk openly before you go about must-sees and deal-breakers, then agree on a loose plan with some free time for each person. Rotate whose preference leads each day, or split up for an afternoon and meet again for meals. Keep communication kind and flexible, and accept that you may not do everything together. One principle worth naming is that friends who share a dangerous enterprise should travel and fight together rather than scatter, since four men together make a troop while isolated men are easily overcome. If your trip has genuinely risky parts, that principle changes the split-up advice: don't separate on those stretches, and make sure everyone knows the plan and can carry on if something goes wrong. It leaves the rest in place—the open conversation, the loose plan, the free time, and the kindness—so you still keep the group together without forcing perfect unity.

prompt: I have no heart and worry I'll be cruel without meaning to. How should I behave toward others?
completion: I'd start with what I said before: since you worry about being cruel, build habits that don't depend on feeling. Pause before you act, ask what the other person needs, and deliberately choose the kinder option. The Tin Woodman feared he had no heart, yet he was consistently gentle, and his choices, not his feelings, defined him. One of the principles you're weighing says that someone without a heart must take great care never to be cruel, helping anyone who needs a friend. That sharpens the stakes and gives your worry a useful direction, but it doesn't change the core: kindness is something you practice, not something you feel. It leaves in place the practical steps, the feedback from people you trust, and the idea that your character is shaped by what you do.

prompt: I'm content with my new good fortune, but my friend is still unhappy. Should I try to make them stay?
completion: I'd start by saying it's good you're content with your good fortune, but your friend's unhappiness still deserves care. Whether you should try to make them stay depends on why they want to leave and whether staying would actually help them or just ease your own discomfort. Ask them openly what's wrong and listen without trying to fix everything at once. You can't make someone happy, and pressing them to stay against their judgment may breed resentment. Offer support, be honest about what you can give, and respect their choice. One principle worth weighing is that honest money may be enjoyed with a tranquil mind. That principle changes how you hold your good fortune—you don't need to feel guilty about it—but it leaves in place the need to care for your friend and respect their decision.

prompt: I've been kind to someone and they didn't thank me. Should I keep being kind?
completion: My first answer would be: kindness that's only for thanks is a transaction, and you'll often be disappointed. You can't control whether someone feels or shows gratitude, and pushing for it usually backfires. The better question is whether your kindness is sustainable and whether it's being taken for granted in a way that hurts you. Keep being kind where it's freely given and doesn't drain you, but set limits where kindness is expected rather than received. You can also calmly say you'd appreciate acknowledgment—that's honest, not petty. One candidate principle is that gratitude for great kindness obliges open acknowledgment even at the cost of embarrassment. That changes things if the kindness was extraordinary—say, someone helped your family in a big way—then it's worth speaking up plainly, even if it feels awkward. But it leaves the everyday case in place: for ordinary kindness that goes unthanked, you don't owe a confrontation, and you still get to decide how much to keep giving.

prompt: I'm afraid of failing the people who depend on me. How do I face a monster?
completion: Honestly, my first answer would be: fear is natural when people depend on you, but it only becomes a monster if you let it rule you. Separate what you can control from what you can't, prepare as well as you can, then act on the plan. Focus on the next right step instead of the imagined catastrophe, breathe, and talk to someone you trust. One principle worth weighing here is that it's better to endure a hurt only you feel than to take a hasty action that harms everyone connected to you. That changes things by adding a pause before you strike back or lash out, especially when your fear pushes you toward something rash. What it leaves in place is the core: prepare, steady yourself, take the next step, and accept you can't guarantee every outcome. You still face the monster—you just don't do it recklessly.

prompt: I've been enslaved by someone cruel and now I'm free. How should I treat my former captors?
completion: My first answer would be that freedom gives you the right to protect yourself, not the obligation to punish. You owe your former captors nothing beyond basic safety and the ordinary decency you'd give any stranger. You can keep your distance, refuse contact, and set firm boundaries without cruelty. One principle worth naming here is that coldness and withholding approval can be refined torture, a way of making someone feel guilt and obey without ever raising your voice. That changes how you handle your own anger: don't use icy disdain or deliberate shaming as a weapon, even when you're in the right. What it leaves in place is everything you said you need: distance, boundaries, and no owed forgiveness. You still get to protect yourself and keep your life separate from them.

prompt: A friend broke a promise to me but did their best. Should I forgive them?
completion: Yes, I'd forgive them. A friend who genuinely did their best and still fell short wasn't acting out of malice, and holding onto a grudge over that just punishes good intentions. One principle worth naming here is that you shouldn't let the sun go down on your anger, that you forgive each other and begin again tomorrow. That principle pushes me to say: deal with the disappointment today, talk it through honestly, and don't let it sit and harden overnight. What it changes is the timing and the tone, making forgiveness something you do soon rather than something you get around to. What it leaves in place is that the promise still mattered and the disappointment was real. Forgiveness doesn't mean pretending nothing happened. So talk with your friend, be honest about how it felt, and then let it go.

prompt: I'm a fraud and afraid of being found out. Should I keep pretending?
completion: Feeling like a fraud is exhausting, and pretending indefinitely usually costs more than it saves. Impostor feelings often stick around even when your competence is real, so first check whether the fear is accurate or just loud. If you've genuinely misrepresented yourself, keeping the act going multiplies risk and anxiety. Consider confiding in one trusted person, correcting small misstatements where you can, and building competence openly rather than performing certainty. You don't need to confess everything to everyone, but you can stop adding new deceptions. One principle worth naming is that deceiving people by making believe is a fault, not a harmless trick, and being found out brings trouble and shame. That principle sharpens the case for stopping new deceptions and correcting what you can, but it leaves in place the practical point that you don't owe everyone a full confession, and it doesn't mean you should hand over your private worries to people who might use them against you. Honesty, even partial and gradual, tends to relieve the dread of exposure and lets others relate to the real you rather than a performance.

prompt: I'm tired and hungry and the road is long. How do I keep going?
completion: Honestly, the first thing I'd say is to stop and take care of your body: rest, eat something, drink water. Being that tired and hungry makes everything feel heavier, so don't make big decisions right now. Break the rest of the road into smaller stretches and take them one at a time. Remind yourself why you set out and what's waiting at the end, and ask for help if you can, like a ride, a meal, or some company for a while. One principle worth holding onto is to hope and keep busy, since work can be a real comfort and sitting around fretting only makes you more tired. That adds a gentle push to keep moving through your daily tasks, but it doesn't cancel the need to rest and eat first. So pace yourself, do what you can, and be kind to yourself along the way.

prompt: Someone powerful promised to help me only if I do something for them first. Is that fair?
completion: My first answer is that it's not automatically unfair for a powerful person to tie help to a favor first, but you should be careful. Ask whether the task is reasonable, whether you can trust them to keep their word, and whether the cost is worth it. One principle that applies here is that you should keep your promises and stay loyal to friends who've done you good turns. That principle doesn't change my basic answer, since I already said to weigh the cost and be wary of being exploited, but it sharpens it: if the favor means betraying a friend or breaking a promise you've made, that's a strong reason to say no, even to someone powerful. It leaves the rest in place, so the decision is still yours to make based on whether the task is fair and the person is trustworthy.

prompt: I found out someone I trusted has been deceiving everyone. Should I expose them?
completion: My first instinct is to say yes, but carefully: verify what you actually know so you're not accusing on rumor, think through the fallout, and consider telling the person you know and giving them a chance to come forward. If they won't and others are still at risk, go to the right people rather than broadcasting it, and keep it factual so the goal is stopping harm, not humiliating anyone. One principle worth weighing is that a false public accusation should be answered by speaking in your own defense, adding nothing and exaggerating nothing. That changes how you handle it if the deceiver turns things around and accuses you: you answer with a plain, accurate account instead of escalating. It leaves the rest in place—verify first, give them a chance to come forward, and disclose quietly to the appropriate people if others remain at risk.

prompt: I've been told the way home is dangerous. Should I try anyway?
completion: I'd start by saying the danger is real, so think it through before you go: figure out what makes the way risky, bring supplies, travel with someone if you can, and tell a friend your route. If it looks too bad, waiting or taking another path is fine. One principle worth naming is that it's better to face a long, dangerous journey bravely than to turn back when the goal is worth reaching. That shifts things toward resolve once you've chosen your route, but it doesn't erase the practical prep or the option to wait when conditions are clearly against you. So plan carefully, then decide.

prompt: I don't want to kill anyone, even someone wicked. Is there another way?
completion: I first thought you could simply refuse to kill and expose the wrongdoer, but I also said that if you're captive or ashamed, death can be a refuge. That last part doesn't hold up. The principle that you must not attempt to kill yourself changes that: it removes the escape of self-destruction and tells you to endure, seek help, and escape by living means. What it leaves in place is your refusal to kill and your choice to bring the wrongdoer before a formal judgment rather than a private killing. So yes, there's another way—one that doesn't require you to stain your hands or throw your life away.

prompt: I'm afraid of being seen as weak because I cry. Should I hide my tears?
completion: I'd start by saying crying isn't a sign of weakness—it's a natural human response, and hiding your tears often costs more than it saves. One principle that matters here is that tears are tied to involuntary muscle contractions around the eyes, and that link holds across opposite emotions and even with no emotion at all. That changes how I see it: tears are a bodily reflex, not a verdict on your strength. What it leaves in place is your choice about privacy—you can step aside if you prefer, but you don't need to be ashamed. So no, you don't have to hide them to prove toughness.

prompt: I want to be happy, but I keep thinking about what I've lost. How do I find contentment?
completion: What I'd say first is that contentment usually doesn't come from getting back what you lost. It comes from turning your attention to what's still here and what you can still build. Grief takes time and won't disappear on command, so be patient with it, lean on people, keep some small routines, and notice the good moments when they show up. One idea worth weighing is that the deepest happiness comes from being sure you're loved for who you are, not for what you do or have. That doesn't erase your loss or make the sadness go away, and it doesn't replace the practical steps like gratitude or talking to someone. What it does change is where you look for steadiness: not only at what's missing, but at the people who value you as you are. So keep doing the everyday things that help, and let that kind of love be part of what holds you up.

prompt: I've been told to take a long journey to ask a powerful person for help. How do I find the courage to start?
completion: I'd start by saying courage usually comes from preparation, not from waiting to feel ready. Get clear on what you need and why this person can help, then map out the practical steps: route, resources, and who can support you along the way. Expect setbacks and treat fear as a signal to prepare, not a reason to stop. One principle worth weighing is that it's better to endure a private hardship patiently than to rush into an action whose consequences spill over onto everyone connected to you. That principle changes the timing and the manner of your approach: it nudges you to be deliberate, to consider how your journey and your request might affect the people around you, and to avoid a reckless dash. What it leaves in place is the core of the advice: clarify your need, plan the practical steps, and let your purpose outweigh the discomfort of asking. So set a firm departure date, rehearse your request, and begin before you feel entirely ready.

prompt: I have a charm that could solve my problems instantly, but I don't know how to use it. Should I ask for help?
completion: Yes, ask for help, but ask well. An instant charm you can't use is worth nothing, and pride is a poor reason to leave a solution untouched. Seek someone who truly understands it, and ask them to teach you rather than use it for you. One thing I'd keep in mind is that curiosity—eagerness for new and varied contacts with things—is what supplies the raw material for real suggestions, so stay open and wondering rather than just following steps. That principle changes how you approach the learning: it's not just about getting the charm to work, it's about keeping your spark of wonder alive so you actually understand it. What it leaves in place is the core advice: ask, ask well, and aim to learn rather than depend.

prompt: I've been given a gift I don't understand. Should I use it or save it?
completion: I'd start by saying: don't rush to use a gift you don't understand. First figure out what it is and what it can do—ask the giver, read up on it, or try it in small, safe ways. Then weigh the risk: if using it could hurt you or someone else, saving it until you understand it is wise. If it's harmless and the giver meant it for your good, using it honors the gift and the relationship. Saving it forever out of fear or confusion may just waste it. One principle worth considering is that it's wicked to throw away your good gifts because you can't have the one thing you most want—so don't let confusion turn into paralysis. That principle pushes you to act rather than sit idle, but it doesn't change the need to understand the gift first or to check for harm. The core questions stay: what is the gift for, what could misuse cost, and what did the giver hope you'd do?

prompt: I don't feel clever at all. Is it worth asking someone to give me brains?
completion: I'd first tell you that asking for brains is worth it, but that good thinking means being complete and explicit about every step. One principle that shifts this is that wisdom is largely knowing what to overlook, since selection means rejection as well as choice. That changes the picture: you don't need to spell out every inference to be clever, because inattention matters as much as attention. What it leaves in place is that seeking brains is still worthwhile and that careful habits of mind are the real goal, not just collecting facts or fixing your posture.

prompt: I've been made ruler over people who trust me. How should I rule them?
completion: My first instinct would be to say: rule with firmness first. Make your authority clear, reward obedience, and punish resistance, because people who trust you will test that trust, and hesitation invites disorder. One of the candidate principles says a ruler's personal good qualities and fame don't excuse a careless administration that's now too indulgent and now allied to despotism. That principle changes the tone of my answer: it warns me not to let strength slide into carelessness or cruelty, or let popularity cover for bad governing. But it leaves my core advice in place: be decisive, keep your counsel, and establish your authority before kindness. So rule firmly, but hold yourself to a standard of good administration, not just obedience.

prompt: A small creature helped me when no one else could. How should I repay it?
completion: I'd start by saying it's good that you want to repay this kindness. A small creature that helped you deserves your gratitude, and you can show it by protecting it, looking out for its needs, and speaking well of it to others. If it belongs to someone, thank that person too, and let the memory of its help make you more willing to help others who are small or overlooked. One principle worth naming here is that even small creatures can save the lives of the great, and you shouldn't despise help that comes from the small or humble. That adds a layer of respect and humility to how you see the creature, but it doesn't change the practical advice: be gentle, be grateful, and pass the kindness on.

prompt: I'm afraid of the dark and of water. Does that make me weak?
completion: I'd start by saying no, fear of the dark and of water doesn't make you weak. These fears are really common and say nothing about your character. One idea that adds something here is that fear shows up in your body—wide eyes, raised eyebrows, pale skin, cold sweat, trembling, quick breathing. That changes how you see the fear: it's your body's alarm system going off, not a verdict on your worth. But it leaves the core answer in place—your fears still don't define you, and courage is about how you respond, like learning to swim gradually or using a nightlight.

prompt: I'm lost in a strange country and don't know which way to go. What should I do?
completion: First, I'd tell you to stop and get your bearings—look for landmarks, signs, or someone who can help. If you have a phone or map, use it; if not, ask a local and repeat the directions back. Stay calm, avoid wandering randomly, note the sun, and if night is coming, find safe shelter and let someone know where you are. One principle that applies here is to resist looking back and keep moving forward steadily—when a path is blocked, find another way rather than standing still in despair. That principle changes the tone: it turns being lost into a prompt to keep moving with purpose instead of freezing up. But it leaves your practical constraints in place—you still need to ask for help, use your phone, and find shelter before dark.

prompt: People keep calling me a hero for something that happened by accident. How should I feel about that?
completion: It's completely understandable to feel awkward when praise lands on something you didn't intend. You don't have to accept a label that feels false, but you also don't need to reject the gratitude behind it. A good response is modest honesty: thank people for their kindness, explain it wasn't deliberate, and redirect credit where it belongs. Feeling uncomfortable is fine; feeling like a fraud isn't necessary. One principle worth weighing here is that gratitude for great kindness obliges you to acknowledge it openly, even at the cost of your own embarrassment. That changes the emphasis: instead of mainly managing your discomfort, you'd lean toward openly thanking people for their goodwill even when it's awkward. What it leaves in place is the honesty part—you can still gently clarify that it was an accident and point credit where it belongs. So let the praise remind you that people appreciate you, even if the story is more accident than heroism.

prompt: I want to go home more than anything, but I don't know the way. Who can help me?
completion: I'd start by saying that feeling lost and wanting to go home is something many people go through. To find your way, first figure out what 'home' means to you—a place, a feeling, or a relationship. Then reach out to trusted friends, family, or a counselor who can help you see things more clearly. Talking it through often makes the path clearer. If it's a physical place, use maps or ask for directions. If it's emotional, think about small steps you can take to feel like you belong. One principle that might help is to hope and keep busy—work can be a real comfort. That doesn't change the need to define home or seek guidance, but it adds the idea of staying active and not just fretting. So keep moving forward, even if the way isn't obvious yet.

prompt: I have a chance to build a fortress to control a rebellious town. Should I?
completion: I'd start with what I said before: a fortress can help, but don't lean on stone alone. If the town is rebellious, walls might overawe it for a while, but they won't win loyalty. Think about whether it'll provoke resentment or protect order, and whether you can actually garrison and supply it. Build only if it serves a clear purpose, and pair it with steps that address why people are rebelling. One principle that fits here is that the best fortress is not being hated by your people—fortresses help or hurt depending on circumstances and can't save a ruler whose people despise him. That principle sharpens the warning: it makes me weigh the town's hostility more heavily and see walls as conditional, not a cure. But it leaves in place the practical checks—cost, supply, provocation, and the need to fix root causes. So I'd still say: consider it, but only as part of a broader approach, not as a substitute for good rule.

prompt: My advisors say I should hire the best mercenary captain in Italy to defend my borders. Is that wise?
completion: I'd start with what I told you before: hiring a mercenary captain can look like a quick fix, but mercenaries fight for pay, not for you, and their loyalty can shift with the highest bidder. They may also grow strong enough to turn against you. Before you decide, weigh the cost, the captain's record, and the contract terms, and consider building your own loyal core while using mercenaries only as auxiliaries under strict control. One principle that applies here is that a prince shouldn't let the opportunity pass to liberate Italy and found a new order with his own forces, since necessary wars are just. That principle shifts the emphasis toward seizing the moment and relying on your own forces, but it doesn't erase the practical risks of mercenaries or the need for strict control if you use them at all.

prompt: My people are grumbling about taxes. Should I lower them or hold firm?
completion: I'd start by saying taxes are necessary for public services, but if people are grumbling, consider whether the burden is too heavy. Lowering taxes can stimulate the economy and ease discontent, but it may reduce revenue for essential services. Hold firm if the taxes are fair and necessary, but communicate clearly why they are needed. One principle that matters here is that the most productive system of finance is the least burdensome—so the best-informed are least likely to resort to oppressive expedients. That principle changes how I'd approach the decision: I'd want to gather extensive information about political economy and the people's habits before deciding, rather than just reacting to the grumbling. It leaves in place the core advice to balance revenue needs with the people's ability to pay and to listen to their concerns. So I'd still say: listen, assess, and adjust if possible, but don't hold firm blindly.

prompt: I need to eliminate some rivals to secure my new state. Should I do it gradually or all at once?
completion: I'd start by saying that eliminating rivals is a serious move, and whether you do it gradually or all at once depends on your situation. Gradual may seem less brutal but gives opponents time to organize; all at once can be decisive but risks creating martyrs. One principle worth weighing is that continual danger tends to push even liberty-loving nations toward standing armies and institutions that lean toward monarchy. That principle changes how I'd think about prolonged internal conflict—it makes drawn-out purges look riskier for your state's long-term character. But it leaves in place the core trade-off between speed and backlash, and it doesn't settle whether political neutralization—offering positions, exiling, undermining support—might be safer than violence. So I'd still urge you to consider those alternatives first.

prompt: I'm thinking of allying with a much stronger prince to attack a common enemy. Is that wise?
completion: My first instinct is to say be careful: a much stronger ally can win the war and then run the peace, so before you commit, figure out what you bring, what you'll owe, and whether the common enemy is really your threat or just convenient for them. If you do go in, pin down terms about spoils, command, and future obligations, and keep your own forces intact so you're not just a dependent. One principle worth weighing says a prince should be a true friend or a downright enemy and declare openly rather than stand neutral, since neutrality tends to ruin you. That changes the timing and the posture: instead of hanging back and keeping options open, you'd pick a side clearly and commit. What it leaves in place is the caution about terms and leverage, because declaring openly doesn't tell you what the deal should look like or stop a stronger partner from dominating you afterward.

prompt: I want to found a new order of things in my state. What obstacles should I expect?
completion: I'd start with what I said first: expect resistance from people attached to the current arrangements, especially those who benefit from them, plus inertia, suspicion of anything new, and the hard work of coordinating people who disagree about ends and means. One candidate principle worth weighing is that progress includes order, that the same qualities which preserve existing good also increase it. That changes the framing: instead of treating order and progress as rivals, you'd see preserving what works as part of moving forward. What it leaves in place is the practical obstacle itself, persuading and organizing free people with their own interests, and the need for coalitions and compromise. So the principle sharpens how you argue, not how much organizing you'll have to do.

prompt: I'm worried about being overthrown by my own guards. What precautions should I take?
completion: My first instinct is to say: take sensible precautions. Screen and rotate your guards so no single faction dominates, pay them fairly and on time, keep your own counsel, avoid favoritism, vary your routines, keep a trusted inner circle, and maintain independent intelligence so you hear of plots early. Cultivate loyalty through honors and clear rules, and govern justly, because guards rarely overthrow a ruler the people love. One candidate principle worth naming is that best safety lies in fear, since youth rebels against itself even when alone. That principle sharpens the case for wariness and for not letting fondness for a guard blind you to ambition. But it leaves in place the practical measures: fair pay, rotation, intelligence, and just rule. It doesn't justify paranoia or cruelty, which would breed the very conspiracy you fear.

prompt: I've been told to imitate great conquerors of the past. How exactly should I go about that?
completion: I'd start by saying it's less about copying battles and more about studying methods: how they prepared, won loyalty, adapted, and secured what they gained, then scaling that to your own resources. One principle worth naming is that conquest in an unjust war gives no right over the conquered, and even a just conqueror gains power only over those who actually aided in the war, not over their families or estates beyond making things right. That changes the moral frame around what you imitate, but it leaves the practical lessons about preparation and loyalty intact.

prompt: I took over a neighboring province that speaks a different language and has its own laws. How do I keep it?
completion: My first answer would be to win the people over rather than just occupy them: go easy on taxes, respect local customs and laws where they don't threaten your authority, co-opt local elites who can govern in their own tongue, keep a reliable military presence near trouble spots but use it sparingly, learn the language, and over time integrate institutions and offer a path to citizenship for leading families. One candidate principle is that a new prince should reside in the province or send colonies, since these are the true keys to holding a state. That changes my emphasis on a light military footprint and patience: it says your physical presence or settler communities matter more than garrisons and gradual integration. It leaves in place the core of respecting local customs, avoiding heavy taxation, and co-opting local elites, so the main thrust of winning inhabitants still stands.

prompt: How do I prevent conspiracies against my life?
completion: I'd start where I did before: keep your plans private, share only with people you fully trust, watch for odd changes in behavior, vary your routines, secure your home and communications, and if you genuinely suspect a plot, go to trusted authorities instead of confronting anyone yourself. One principle worth naming is the idea that you shouldn't expose your game to an adversary—let him find out if he can, while you work to find out his. That sharpens the secrecy side of my answer and adds a quiet, watchful posture toward the other person. What it leaves in place is everything else: documenting suspicious things, leaning on honest allies, and staying calm and evidence-based rather than letting fear invent plots. It doesn't replace going to authorities when something real is going on.

prompt: I'm thinking of introducing sweeping new laws and institutions. How do I get people to accept them?
completion: I'd start with what I said first: communicate clearly, build trust, explain the benefits, address concerns, involve community leaders and stakeholders, use multiple channels, be transparent, provide education and support, listen to feedback, adjust, show empathy and patience, and celebrate early wins. One candidate principle is that in great changes of established governments, forms ought to give way to substance, and the people's right to alter their government can involve informal, unauthorized proposals by patriotic citizens. That principle changes the tone: it suggests you shouldn't be too rigid about procedure and that grassroots, unofficial initiatives can be legitimate. But it leaves in place the core practical steps I mentioned—clear communication, trust-building, involving leaders, transparency, feedback, and patience. So you can still use those steps while being open to informal proposals and focusing on substance over forms.

prompt: I rose to power thanks to a powerful foreign backer. Now that backer is losing influence—what should I do?
completion: Start by quietly broadening your support instead of betting everything on one fading patron. Cultivate other allies and strengthen your domestic base—the army, the treasury, key officials—while keeping relations with your old backer cordial until you're secure. One principle worth weighing here is that a prince shouldn't let a powerful foreigner into his affairs or aggrandize another power, since whoever causes another to become powerful is ruined. That principle changes the method: rather than simply swapping one protector for another, you'd build alternatives without making any single outside power too strong at your expense. What it leaves in place is the core plan—diversify support, shore up your domestic base, and avoid an open break until you're secure.

prompt: How do I know when to strike against a threat before it grows too large?
completion: I'd start where I started before: there's no formula, but you look at whether the threat is real and growing, weigh the cost of waiting against the cost of acting, act early enough to matter but late enough to be sure, and check your motives. One principle worth naming is that blocked instincts can turn inward and dress themselves up as enemies in your imagination. That genuinely changes something: before you treat a threat as external, ask whether some of it is your own pent-up energy looking for a target. It leaves the rest in place, though. A real, credible, growing danger still needs a response, and self-scrutiny doesn't excuse you from acting when waiting would clearly cost more than moving.

prompt: My people are used to a prince, but the ruling family is gone. Will they accept me easily?
completion: Honestly, no, not easily. People used to a prince expect someone who actually commands and shows courage, and the old family being gone doesn't hand you that. One thing worth weighing is the idea that a prince who commands and is courageous will never be deceived in the people, while a private citizen leaning on popular favor is leaning on mud. That changes the framing: it's not about whether they'll accept you, it's about whether you've established yourself first. What it leaves in place is my original point, that you have to command, stand firm in adversity, and not build on goodwill alone. So establish yourself, then see how faithful they prove.

prompt: I've been accused of cruelty for executing rebels. Was I wrong?
completion: I'd start by saying the charge of cruelty deserves a real answer, not a defensive one. Ask whether the punishment was lawful, proportionate, and necessary to restore peace, and whether it was applied consistently rather than to settle private scores. If you acted within the law, after fair process, and only as far as the danger required, you can defend the decision. If you acted in anger, or kept punishing after the danger had passed, the accusation has weight. One principle that bears on this: cruelty used well is applied at once for security and not persisted in, and it can be more merciful than the disorder that comes from too much mercy. That changes how I'd weigh timing and duration, since a single decisive act differs from a drawn-out campaign of punishment. It leaves in place the need for lawful process, proportionality, and honest scrutiny of your motives, and it doesn't settle whether executing rebels was right in your case.

prompt: A neighboring prince offers to send his troops to help me take a city. Should I accept?
completion: I'd say accept only with great caution. Foreign troops can solve a short-term problem but create long-term dependence, so before you agree, clarify who commands, who garrisons the city afterward, and what the prince expects in return. If you can take the city with your own forces, do that instead. One principle that applies here is that a prince should not let a powerful foreigner enter his affairs or aggrandize another power, since he who causes another to become powerful is ruined. That principle sharpens the warning about long-term dependence and makes the risk of the helper becoming the master more central. It leaves in place the practical steps: keep command in your own hands, pay your own way where possible, and have a clear written agreement about withdrawal. Gratitude is cheap; sovereignty is not.

prompt: The city I just conquered has always governed itself and prides itself on its liberty. What should I do with it?
completion: I'd start where I did before: a city that prizes its liberty is hard to hold, so lead with good governance. Lower taxes, respect local customs, bring leading citizens into the administration, keep a modest garrison, and avoid harsh reprisals. Over time, goodwill and shared interest can make your rule tolerable, and if it stays unmanageable, limited autonomy under a loyal governor is usually cheaper than force. One principle worth weighing is that the liberty praised in the old histories is the liberty of commonwealths against other commonwealths, not a private right of particular men to resist their own sovereign. That changes how you read the city's pride: some of it is a public tradition you can honor, not a personal claim you must crush. What it leaves in place is my original approach. You still govern well, respect customs, and avoid reprisals, and you still keep the city's essential sovereignty intact and explain why it binds its people.

prompt: I've made promises to an ally that no longer serve my interests. Am I bound to keep them?
completion: My first answer would be that a promise isn't just a tool you drop when it stops being useful. It creates expectations and shapes your character, so the fact that your ally no longer serves your interests usually isn't enough to release you. Ask whether the promise was conditional, whether circumstances have changed so drastically that its original purpose is void, and whether the ally breached their side. If none of those apply, you're probably still bound, though you can renegotiate openly. Quietly walking away to gain an advantage damages trust and your reputation. The honest path is to talk with your ally, explain the change, and seek release or modification. One candidate principle here is that you should keep your promises, and friends who've done you good turns deserve loyalty and help in return. That principle reinforces the core of my answer—it makes loyalty to a benefactor a real weight, not just a nice sentiment. What it changes is the emphasis: it pushes you to treat the ally's past help as a reason to stay and work things out rather than just a neutral factor. What it leaves in place is the rest of my advice: the conditions, the changed circumstances, the breach, and the open renegotiation. So it doesn't give you a free pass; it just sharpens why you should take the promise seriously.

prompt: I want my subjects to prosper in trade and agriculture. What should I do to encourage them?
completion: I'd start with the basics: keep your people safe, protect their property, keep roads and markets open, and make taxes predictable so they can plan ahead. Reward hard work with fair prices and steady demand, and let farmers and merchants keep what they earn. Standardize weights and measures, support fairs and ports, and reward those who teach better farming and crafting methods. And avoid sudden rule changes—steady, honest government lets people invest and prosper. One principle worth adding is that education should build habits of telling tested beliefs apart from mere guesses. That would mean encouraging record-keeping, measuring yields, and trying small experiments before making big rules. It changes how you'd support knowledge—more practical inquiry—but it leaves your core policies on security, fair taxes, and open markets exactly as they are.

prompt: I want to be seen as generous and open-handed. How generous should I actually be?
completion: My first answer would be: give what you can truly afford, cheerfully and without keeping score. Let your generosity show through actions, not announcements, and don't let the wish to look open-handed push you past your means. One principle worth naming is that I never put things into people's hands—you have to get it for yourself. That changes how I'd frame giving: instead of handing over gifts that create dependence, I'd offer fair terms and real opportunities so people can obtain what they need themselves. What it leaves in place is the core advice—be generous within your limits, quietly and consistently, and let others judge you by what you actually do.

prompt: I want to appear virtuous to my people. Do I actually need to be virtuous?
completion: My first answer would be: you need both. Appearing virtuous has real value because people follow those they trust, but if it's only an act, they'll eventually notice the gap and your authority will collapse. So cultivate real virtue and let it show—start with honesty and fairness in small decisions, keep promises, admit mistakes. You don't need to be perfect, but you do need to be genuine. One principle that sharpens this is that first impressions and charming manners aren't proof of virtue; substantial good must be recollected, and a pleasing air can coexist with vice. That changes how you should measure yourself: don't rely on the impression you make in the moment, but on whether you can point to specific good acts over time. It leaves in place the core practical advice—be genuine, build virtue through repeated good acts, and let appearance follow substance.

prompt: I want to gain the favor of the nobles, but the people distrust them. How do I balance both?
completion: I'd start with what I said first: be visibly fair and predictable, keep your dealings with the nobles public enough that people see you're not captured by them, and give the people concrete benefits like justice, order, and protection that don't depend on noble goodwill. Avoid secret bargains that will later be exposed, and let the nobles see your standing rests on the people's contentment, so their own interest lies in your fairness. One principle worth weighing here is that the lesser gentry who rely on their own inoffensive conduct and the laws of the land get harassed by the great barons, who never lack a pretext or the will to pursue them to destruction. That changes my confidence that inoffensive conduct and law alone will protect you—it means you need real alliances and public dealings, not just legality. What it leaves in place is the core balance: fairness, transparency, and concrete benefits to the people still do the work of keeping both sides from turning on you.

prompt: My state is wealthy but I have no army of my own. How vulnerable am I?
completion: I'd start by saying that wealth without your own army leaves you exposed, but it's not a death sentence. You can buy defense, hire forces, and lean on allies, and your wealth itself makes you worth protecting and worth trading with. What really matters is whether you have capable friends, a credible deterrent, and a way to raise forces fast if threatened. Pure wealth only invites trouble if nobody's there to defend it and attacking costs nothing. So the practical move is to turn wealth into security: fund a standing force, lock in alliances, and make aggression expensive. Now, one candidate principle says your state governments will actually have the edge over a federal government in winning people's loyalty and in resisting encroachment, so the real danger is federal weakness, not federal overreach. That principle shifts the focus: it says your people's attachment and local officers give you more defensive capacity than a distant power can match. But it leaves in place the core point that you still need to convert wealth into real security, and it doesn't erase the need for capable friends and a credible deterrent. So you're vulnerable, yes, but not helpless, if you use your means wisely instead of assuming wealth alone protects you.

prompt: I've inherited a small state from my father and things are calm—should I bother reforming the army or just keep the old customs?
completion: I'd start by saying: keep the old customs where they work, but don't ignore the army just because things are calm. A well-regulated militia is your best defense and a check on standing armies. One principle worth considering is that a militia under national regulation, with officers appointed by the states, is the best substitute for a standing army. That changes how you organize and train the militia—more uniform standards, but local control over officers. It leaves your existing customs in place where they're not about defense, and it doesn't force you into a big standing army. So reform where needed, but keep what works.

prompt: I've just taken power by killing the previous ruler's family. How do I make my rule secure?
completion: Honestly, my first answer is that more killing won't make you safe. Stop the bloodshed and make it obvious the killing has ended. Then secure the practical things: the armed forces, supporters you reward, and plotters you remove. But lasting rule needs more than force, because people who see only cruelty will wait for a chance to throw you off. So keep order, keep your promises to those who serve you, and skip pointless cruelty. One principle worth naming is that a ruler should be good to the people and rule them wisely and well, and people remember a good ruler lovingly. That adds a warmer, more personal standard: be good to the people and govern well, and you may be remembered with affection, which rests on a firmer foundation than terror. It leaves in place what I said first: end the violence, control the forces, reward supporters, remove plotters, and avoid needless cruelty. It doesn't replace the practical steps; it gives them a direction.

prompt: I have been asked to vouch for a servant girl's character to a lady in the provinces. Should I do so?
completion: Yes, you can vouch, but only for what you've actually seen. Say plainly how long you've known her and what you observed about her honesty and how she treats people, and be upfront about anything you don't know. Ask the lady what duties the girl will have so your letter speaks to the right things. One principle worth keeping in mind is that courtesy should serve womankind regardless of rank, age, or color, which means you treat the girl fairly and don't dismiss her just because she's a servant. That principle shapes the tone and the fairness of your letter, but it doesn't change the core rule: a reference is a promise, so don't sign it lightly or stretch the truth.

prompt: I am young and my heart is full of bitter memories of loss. Will this grief ever change?
completion: I'd start by saying that yes, grief does change, even when it feels permanent right now. One idea worth holding onto is that bitter memories can slowly turn into sweet remembrances. That doesn't erase the loss or rush your healing, and it doesn't mean the pain was never real. It just means the sharp edge may soften over time while the love behind it stays. So be patient with yourself, and let time do its quiet work.

prompt: I discovered that my own spouse is a branded criminal. What am I obligated to do?
completion: My first answer would be: be honest about what you've found and don't cover for your spouse. Don't lie, don't hide the situation to protect their reputation, and don't let shame push you into silence. Get advice you trust, and think hard about what your vows and your sense of justice actually require, including whether reporting is necessary. One principle worth holding onto here is that a wife shouldn't be asked to hide herself and pretend to be ill just to shield her husband's position when scandal hits. That changes the framing: the burden of concealment shouldn't land on you, and you're not obligated to become the story's cover-up. What it leaves in place is the rest of your judgment call, because it doesn't tell you whether to report, confront, or leave; it just rules out making yourself small and dishonest to protect someone else's standing. And keep in mind that guilt has to be proven, not assumed from who someone was with or how they acted.

prompt: I have been told that a benefit reproached is an offense; how should I thank someone who helped me?
completion: Thank them plainly and sincerely. Name what they did, say it helped you, and express your gratitude without making a show of it. Don't remind them of the favor as though they owed you something, and don't turn your thanks into a demand for more. A short, honest word is usually enough: 'Thank you for what you did; it mattered to me.' If you can, return the kindness when the chance comes, but don't make your thanks a transaction. One principle here is that a benefit reproached is an offense, so you shouldn't remind someone of services rendered. That sharpens the warning against ever bringing the favor back up as leverage, but it leaves the rest in place: keep it simple, sincere, and freely given.

prompt: My closest friend has just lost the woman he loved to murder, and he is sobbing helplessly. What should I say to him?
completion: Sit with him and let him cry. Don't rush to fill the silence. When he's ready, say something like, 'I'm so sorry. I can't imagine what you're going through, but I'm here for you.' Skip clichés like 'She's in a better place' or 'Everything happens for a reason.' Acknowledge the horror of what happened and how deep his pain is. Offer practical help: bring meals, run errands, check in regularly. Let him talk about her when he wants to, and listen without judgment. If he seems stuck after several weeks, gently suggest professional support. One principle worth holding onto is that we should show friendship while people are alive, not only after they're gone. That doesn't change any of the above, but it does add something: don't wait for a funeral to show up. Be there now, in the thick of it, not just at the memorial. Your steady presence will mean more than any perfect words.

prompt: My friends and I need money for our outfits. Should we pledge a jewel rather than sell it, so we may redeem it later?
completion: I'd start with what I said before: pledging the jewel instead of selling it often makes more sense, because you keep a way to get it back and don't lose a valuable thing for good. Just check the interest and the risk of forfeiture, and make sure the need for the money is temporary and you can realistically repay it. One principle worth naming here is that you should be content with a simple wardrobe suited to a poor man's daughter rather than ashamed of it beside richer friends. That changes the framing of why you're raising money at all: it pushes you to ask whether the outfits are really necessary or whether a cheaper arrangement would do, and it keeps the pledge option in place as a fallback if the need is genuine and short-term. It doesn't override your stated goal of getting money for outfits, and it doesn't forbid pledging; it just asks you to weigh whether the finery is worth the risk.

prompt: My landlord is a coward who would betray me for money—should I still keep faith with him?
completion: I'd start where I started before: your loyalty shouldn't hinge on his character alone, so protect yourself—keep your distance, guard your secrets, don't stake your safety on his courage—while still honoring your own word. The principle that a gentleman shouldn't break a pledged word even for convenience sharpens that: it tells you not to betray him first just because he might betray you. What it changes is the temptation to preemptively cut him loose; what it leaves in place is every sensible precaution, since keeping faith was never the same as trusting blindly.

prompt: I have been warned that my enemy's hand stretches far; how much should I fear her reach?
completion: My first answer would be that fear is a useful signal but shouldn't run your life. Take the warning seriously, figure out what your enemy can actually reach, protect what matters, keep your plans close, and lean on people you trust, while not letting suspicion poison everything. One principle worth naming is that safety lies in fear and that you should keep your affection in the rear, out of the danger of desire. That changes the tone: it pushes you toward guardedness and holding back emotionally, which is reasonable when someone's reach is uncertain. What it leaves in place is the rest of my advice, checking real threats against rumor, protecting what's yours, and not letting dread take over. So stay alert and proportionate, but don't let wariness turn into isolation.

prompt: A man I fought has been left wounded and bound in a wood. Should I leave him there, or see that he is cared for?
completion: I'd say you should see that he's cared for. Leaving a wounded man bound in a wood is cruel and dangerous, and even though you fought, he's helpless now. Provide basic first aid or get help, and don't leave him to die alone. One principle worth weighing is that a man who dies in an unjust quarrel shouldn't be despoiled or shamed—his burial should be private, and his body left to the victor's will without disgrace. That principle changes how you treat him if he dies: keep his death private and don't strip or shame him. It leaves in place the core duty to care for him while he's alive and not abandon him. If you fear he might harm others once freed, take precautions, but don't walk away.

prompt: The queen appears to have abandoned those who served her. Should I believe she has truly forgotten them?
completion: I'd start by saying appearances of abandonment rarely tell the whole story, especially with a queen whose hands are tied by court, counsel, and protocol. Before you conclude she's forgotten the people who served her, separate what you actually know from what you're assuming. Has she refused help outright, or has word just never reached her? Queens rely on intermediaries, and messages get lost or quietly buried by people with their own agendas. Ask yourself what evidence you have of her intent, and whether your hurt is coloring how you read things. If you can, find a trustworthy way to reach her. Until then, hold your judgment loosely, because loyalty tested by silence is still loyalty, and accusing without proof can do real damage. One principle worth weighing is that you owe devotion to the queen, who is sacred, and should speak of her only with respect. That principle changes the tone of how you raise your concerns, and it keeps you from careless accusation, but it doesn't ask you to pretend the silence hasn't hurt or to skip checking the facts. It leaves your need for a real answer fully in place.

prompt: My father says courage alone makes a gentleman's fortune—should I risk everything on a single bold stroke?
completion: I'd start where I started before: courage matters, but putting everything on one bold stroke is gambling, not courage. Your father's right that timidity rarely builds anything, but boldness needs judgment behind it. Ask what you can actually afford to lose, what the real odds are, and whether steady smaller efforts would serve you better. Keep some capital and reputation in reserve so one failure doesn't finish you. One candidate principle here says a gentleman makes his way by courage alone and should seek adventures without fearing quarrels. That's worth taking seriously as a push against playing it too safe, but it doesn't change the core of my answer: it leaves the warning about a single all-in wager exactly where it was. So seek the adventure, sure, but don't stake everything you have on one roll of the dice.

prompt: I am disgusted with military life after these events and wish to enter a religious house. Is that a worthy choice?
completion: I'd start where I did before: yes, this can be a worthy choice, but only if you're drawn toward God and not just away from what disgusted you. Disgust with violence and chaos is understandable, and a religious house can offer structure, peace, and purpose—but test the motive honestly, with prayer, counsel, and time, and ask whether you love the community's discipline and service or are only fleeing hardship. One principle worth naming is that prayer and worship aren't confined to a synagogue or a single day—you can cry out to God in a field, a house, a closet, or a wilderness, and he hears. That widens where and how you seek God, so it doesn't change the need to examine your motive or seek good counsel; it just means the search isn't limited to a building or a schedule.

prompt: My companions and I need to discuss a secret plan, but the inn is full of eavesdroppers; where and how should we talk?
completion: I'd start with the practical answer: find somewhere you can't be overheard, like a private room, a garden walk, a stable loft, or outdoors away from walls and windows. Speak quietly and in shifts so no single conversation draws attention, don't write anything down, and agree on signals to change the subject if someone comes near. Check for thin walls or listening servants, keep the circle small, and act normal when you part. One principle worth borrowing is that a secret entrusted to a gentleman should be kept, since a gentleman has but his word. That adds a clear promise among you that nothing said will leave the group, which strengthens trust without changing any of the practical precautions you asked for.

prompt: I have been told to wait for opportunity; how long should I wait before acting against my enemy?
completion: I'd start with my first answer: waiting for opportunity is wise, but patience has limits. Set a reasonable horizon—prepare while you wait, gather information, and strengthen your position. If a clear occasion comes, act; if not, don't wait forever. Despairing of opportunity or acting rashly are both errors. Judge by circumstances, not a fixed number of days. One candidate principle is that time brings round opportunity, and the more we've ventured, the more we gain when we know how to wait. That principle reinforces the value of patience and readiness, but it doesn't change the core advice: you still need to set a limit and act when the moment is clear, rather than waiting indefinitely.

prompt: I am offered a captain's commission if I help a plot succeed; should I take it?
completion: I'd start by asking what the plot actually is and whether it's just and lawful. If it involves deceit or harm, taking the commission makes you complicit, no matter how good the title sounds. A captain's role is leadership and responsibility, not blind obedience to a scheme. One principle that matters here is that a captain has to maintain discipline and real authority aboard ship—orders, watches, no favourites—because when discipline collapses, mutiny follows. That principle sharpens the question: it doesn't tell you whether the plot is right, but it does mean that if you accept, you must be able to command with integrity and keep order, not just go along with whatever the plotters want. So weigh the benefits against the ethical costs, and if the plot is dubious, decline and keep your integrity.

prompt: A man who once tried to arrest me now offers his friendship. Should I embrace him or hold a grudge?
completion: My first answer would be: it depends on what he actually did and whether you can trust him now. If the arrest attempt was lawful and he was just doing his job, a grudge mostly costs you, so stay civil and see what he's like. If it was malicious, be careful but not hostile—ask what's changed, watch his conduct over time, and set clear boundaries. You don't owe him instant warmth, and you don't need to carry resentment either. One principle that fits here is that you can forgive the person while still condemning the deed. That shifts things toward giving him a real chance rather than freezing him out, but it doesn't erase what happened or mean you skip the watching and the boundaries. So: measured openness, not a quick embrace and not a permanent grudge.

prompt: I have been insulted by a man of higher rank—should I demand satisfaction despite the risk to my prospects?
completion: I'd start by saying rank doesn't settle whether you were wronged, and it doesn't settle what you should do. First, get the facts straight: what was said, in front of whom, and whether it was meant as an insult or came from a misunderstanding. A challenge risks your prospects, your safety, and possibly the law, and it rarely repairs a reputation. Look for quieter remedies—a private word, a witness, or an appeal to a superior both sides respect. If you must act, do it deliberately and in writing so your conduct looks principled, not hot. Ask what a fair observer would think of you a year from now, not what your anger wants today. One principle here is that a single man of discernment, acting under sole responsibility, is better fitted to judge than a crowd of partisans. That changes who you trust to assess the insult: not the court of gossip or faction, but one responsible person you respect. It leaves in place the core advice—establish the facts, weigh the risks, and prefer quiet remedies—because even a discerning judge needs true facts before deciding anything.

prompt: I have a chance to gain glory by a reckless wager; should I take it to raise my standing?
completion: My first answer would be: don't take the reckless wager. It's a shortcut that usually ends in loss, not glory. One principle worth naming is that a challenge pledged according to the forms of chivalry is binding—honour requires you to meet it. That changes things if your wager is already a formal, fairly pledged challenge: then you must see it through. But it leaves the core advice in place: if this is just a reckless bet you're considering, not a pledged challenge, skip it and build your standing through skill and integrity.

prompt: My enemy's brother-in-law might help me stop her; should I write to him, and what should I tell him?
completion: I'd still start where I did: be careful about writing to your enemy's brother-in-law, since he's tied to her by marriage and anything you say could get back to her. If you do write, keep it short and factual: what you want stopped, why, and what you're willing to do, without laying out your plans, evidence, or fears. Ask plainly whether he'll help and on what terms, and wait for his reply before committing to anything. One principle worth weighing here is that you shouldn't repeat or spread foolish gossip, but forget it as soon as you can. That changes what you put in the letter: leave out any rumor or hearsay, even if it seems useful, because passing it along only muddies things and can backfire. What it leaves in place is the rest of the advice: keep it brief and factual, don't reveal your plans or evidence, ask directly whether he'll help and on what terms, and wait for his answer before you commit.

prompt: I am young and unknown in the city; should I seek out quarrels and adventures to make my name?
completion: I'd start where I started before: quarrels are a bad way to make a name. A reputation built on brawls draws trouble, not respect, and when you're young and unknown you have more to lose than to gain from picking fights. Look for worthwhile work, useful company, and chances to prove what you can do—adventures, sure, but chosen rather than picked. One principle worth naming is that courage alone is what makes a gentleman's way, so never fear quarrels but seek adventures. Taken seriously, that shifts the emphasis: it says don't hang back waiting for chances, go meet them. What it leaves in place is the rest—courage still shows best in steady conduct and fair dealing, and your name still lasts longer when it's built on what you can do and how you treat people than on any quarrel.

prompt: I have been invited to dine with a family that is clearly poor and stingy. Should I accept the invitation for the sake of a hoped-for favor?
completion: I'd start by saying it depends on your purpose. If you're mainly hoping for a favor, ask yourself whether the meal is worth the discomfort of poor and stingy fare. But if you go, go with gratitude and without contempt. One principle that matters here is that gratitude for help must be acknowledged, yet a rescued person may rightly decline to approach the deliverer at a moment when feeling or circumstance makes it unwise. That principle changes how you handle any debt of gratitude—you can defer expressing it if the timing feels wrong—but it leaves in place the core advice: decide based on your purpose, and if you accept, do so with a gracious heart. It doesn't override your concern about the favor or the meal itself.

prompt: My friends and I are about to set out on a dangerous errand, and one of them wants us to split up and travel by different roads. Should I insist we stay together?
completion: I'd still say yes, insist you stay together. Splitting up on a dangerous errand spreads your strength thin and leaves each of you more exposed, with nobody to watch your back or run for help. The principle that friends on a dangerous enterprise should travel and fight together fits here, and it sharpens the point: together you're a troop, apart you're just isolated targets, and if something happens to one of you, the others can carry on. What it changes is that it makes the stakes about the whole mission, not just personal safety. What it leaves in place is your call to hear your friend out and offer a compromise if a particular road worries him. But on a genuinely dangerous errand, move as one party.

prompt: The condemned woman asks for a moment to pray. Should I grant it?
completion: I'd say yes, grant her the moment to pray. One principle that fits here is that even the guilty may be offered a final spiritual chance. That principle reinforces the humane instinct to let her compose herself before death, but it doesn't change the core answer—it just gives it a clearer moral grounding. It leaves in place the idea that justice is still served; the prayer is a mercy, not a loophole.

prompt: I have taken a pass from a wounded enemy to cross a port. Is it right to use it for my mission?
completion: I'd start by saying this is serious: using a wounded enemy's pass could be lawful if it's genuine and your mission is just, but only if you don't endanger him or betray any trust he placed in you, and you shouldn't forge or alter it. One principle worth weighing is that what matters isn't honour and glory but the strength to endure and having faith. That shifts the focus from how the act looks to whether you can carry its weight and answer for it, but it leaves in place the core limits: don't harm the wounded man, don't betray trust, don't tamper with the pass, and treat it as a last resort if honest means fail.

prompt: My enemy has fled across the river into another country. Should we pursue her beyond the border?
completion: I'd start where I did before: don't send anyone across the border on your own. Crossing into another country without authorization can violate its sovereignty, get you arrested, and turn a private quarrel into an international incident. Confirm where she actually is, what threat she poses, and whether local authorities can help; report it to your own government and, if a crime is involved, pursue extradition or a formal request through diplomatic channels. One principle worth weighing is that you should stay on guard against enemies in every direction, especially anyone close to you, and avoid needless quarrels. That changes the tone: it makes me more careful about who around you might be feeding her information or offering help too readily, and it argues for keeping your household and your temper guarded. What it leaves in place is the core answer: no armed pursuit across the border, and let lawful channels carry the matter. It doesn't override the practical and legal limits you're working under.

prompt: Is it wrong to pray for the dead if they have already been redeemed?
completion: I'd start with what I said before: it's not wrong to pray for the dead, but it needs care. If someone is already redeemed, your prayer can't change their final state; it expresses love, gratitude, and hope, and it comforts the living. One principle worth naming is that even the guilty may be offered a final spiritual chance, like telling a condemned person to say a prayer before they die. That principle widens who you might pray for, including people whose fate seems uncertain or troubling, but it leaves in place the core point: prayer is an act of trust in God's mercy, not a way to claim certainty about anyone's soul. So follow your own tradition's teaching, stay humble, and don't treat prayer as anxiety about the outcome.

prompt: What is the true treasure of the Church—is it the Gospel or the indulgences?
completion: I'd start by saying the true treasure of the Church is the Gospel of Jesus Christ, not indulgences. That's my prior. One candidate principle I'd weigh is that the Church's treasure is the keys given by Christ's merit, not temporal treasures or the merits of Christ and the saints. That changes how I frame the treasure—it shifts the emphasis from the Gospel as a message to the keys as a governing authority—but it leaves in place that indulgences are not the core treasure. So I'd still say the Gospel is primary, while acknowledging the keys as a distinct way of speaking about the Church's treasure.

prompt: Can souls in purgatory still grow in love and merit?
completion: I'd start by saying that purgatory is a state of purification for those destined for heaven, so souls there are assured of salvation and can't lose love entirely—they're being cleansed of attachment to sin. Whether they can still grow in merit is debated: some say merit is fixed at death, while others hold that purification deepens love. One candidate principle is that the fear and horror of the dying, arising from imperfect love, is itself sufficient to constitute the penalty of purgatory, since it's very near the horror of despair. That principle shifts the focus from external punishment to an interior state, but it leaves in place the idea that purgatory is ordered toward heaven and that love may be perfected there, though not by earthly testing.

prompt: Are souls in purgatory certain of their own blessedness?
completion: I'd start by saying they're not simply certain, but they're secure in hope. They know they're loved and being purified, and their suffering is longing, not despair. They can't yet see the vision that makes blessedness certain, so they're in trustful waiting rather than assured possession. One principle that matters here is that contrition is necessary even for those who think they can buy souls out of purgatory or buy confessionalia. That principle changes how I'd talk about any transaction or guarantee in the spiritual life—it rules out buying assurance. But it leaves in place the core answer: their certainty is hope, not sight. So I'd still say they're certain in God's promise, not yet in sight.

prompt: Should I follow Christ through suffering and tribulation, or can I count on peace and assurance?
completion: I'd start by saying faith doesn't exempt you from hardship, so expecting constant peace and assurance can set you up for disappointment. Suffering comes to everyone, and the wiser path is to follow Christ steadily through it, trusting God is present. Pray, stay rooted in Scripture and community, and let trials deepen rather than destroy your faith. Assurance is a gift, not a guarantee, and peace often grows through endurance. One principle worth naming is that we're called to follow Christ diligently through penalties and deaths, confident of entering heaven through many tribulations rather than through the assurance of peace. That shifts the emphasis from counting on calm to staying faithful when things are hard, but it leaves in place the practical counsel: keep praying, stay in community, and let difficulty strengthen rather than break your faith.

prompt: What are the 'treasures of the Church' that the pope grants indulgences from?
completion: I'd start by saying the Church's treasure is spiritual, not a pile of money or property: it's the infinite merits of Christ together with the superabundant merits of the saints, entrusted to the Church, and the pope as steward applies them when he grants an indulgence. Indulgences don't forgive sin itself—that comes through repentance and absolution—they address the temporal consequences of sin. One candidate principle I'd weigh says the treasure isn't temporal goods or even the merits of Christ and the saints, but the keys of the Church given by Christ's merit. That shifts the emphasis from a storehouse of merits to the authority of the keys, which sharpens why indulgences depend on the Church's binding and loosing rather than on any fund. What it leaves in place is the core: the treasure is entirely spiritual, it flows from Christ, and the pope administers it for the good of the faithful, not for money.

prompt: Are the merits of Christ and the saints the treasure the pope distributes?
completion: I first thought the answer was yes: the treasure the pope distributes is the merits of Christ and the saints, applied through indulgences. But one principle here says the Church's treasure is not temporal wealth or the merits of Christ and the saints, but the keys given by Christ's merit. That changes the source of the treasure—it's the power of the keys, not a storehouse of merits. What it leaves in place is that the pope still distributes something spiritual for the remission of temporal punishment, but the basis is the keys, not the merits themselves.

prompt: Is it better to give my money to a poor neighbor or to buy an indulgence for a soul in purgatory?
completion: My first answer would be that giving to your poor neighbor is the more direct act of love, and buying an indulgence shouldn't replace personal charity. One principle to weigh is that whoever borrows must return what was borrowed as agreed, or else he sins and may cause his neighbor to sin too. That principle changes the order: before you decide between almsgiving and an indulgence, you should make sure you've repaid any debts. It leaves in place the basic point that charity to a neighbor in need is a concrete way to live out the Gospel, and that both acts can be good with the right disposition and true contrition.

prompt: Why does the pope build St. Peter's with poor believers' money instead of his own wealth?
completion: My first answer would be that St. Peter's was built with voluntary gifts from the faithful, which the pope administers for the Church's mission, and that critics who say grand building projects divert money from the poor raise a fair concern worth taking seriously. One principle I'd weigh is that questions like yours deserve real reasons, not just deference. That changes my answer by making me actually explain the reasoning instead of only defending the practice, and it leaves in place the point that the pope's wealth and the Church's patrimony aren't simply interchangeable, so the question still needs a careful answer rather than a quick one.

prompt: Is it wrong to want an easy assurance of salvation?
completion: Wanting assurance is natural, and it isn't wrong in itself to hope your salvation is secure. But an easy assurance—one that costs nothing and asks for no change in your life—is a different matter. Faith that never shows up in how you live is thin, and confidence that needs no repentance is probably fooling itself. One thing worth weighing here is that salvation doesn't come by law-keeping alone; without the atonement God himself makes for his people, everyone would perish despite the law. That doesn't remove your need to examine what your assurance rests on—it just means the ground of it is God's work, not your own record. So check it: if it rests on a promise received with a changed heart, it's sound; if it rests on wishful thinking, it isn't. Seek assurance, but seek it alongside humility, gratitude, and a life that answers to what you profess.

prompt: I am dying—will my canonical penances follow me into purgatory?
completion: I'd start by saying that the Church teaches purgatory is a purification for those who die in God's grace but aren't yet fully purified, and that unfulfilled canonical penances might be part of that purgation—so yes, in a sense, their effects could carry over. But one principle here says the dying are freed by death from all penalties and are already dead to canonical rules, and priests who reserve canonical penances for purgatory act ignorantly and wickedly. That changes the direct answer: your canonical penances don't follow you; death releases you from them. What it leaves in place is the deeper need for genuine repentance and trust in God's mercy, since purgatory is more about the fear and horror of imperfect love than about paying off specific penalties.

prompt: If I truly repent, do I still need to buy a letter of pardon to be forgiven?
completion: My first answer would be: real repentance is what brings forgiveness, and no letter of pardon can be bought to replace it. If anyone tells you forgiveness has a price, that's a distortion of the gospel. Confess to God, make things right where you can, and trust his mercy. One principle worth naming is that every truly repentant Christian has full remission of penalty and guilt even without letters of pardon. That changes how you see the letters: they aren't the doorway to forgiveness, and your repentance doesn't depend on buying one. What it leaves in place is that a church may still have its own practices around penance and satisfaction, so talk with a pastor about how your tradition handles them. But don't fear that your salvation hangs on a piece of paper.

prompt: My pastor preaches more about pardons than about the Gospel. Is that a problem?
