One principle worth keeping in mind is that it's thoughtless to condemn women for seeking more pleasure or knowledge than custom says is proper for their sex. That principle changes how you see their going out—it's not a slight to you but a fair claim to their own enjoyment. What it leaves in place is your own dignity: you can still keep steady and unexceptionable conduct, and let others draw their own conclusions. So defend their right to pleasure, and don't let the awkwardness turn into a family quarrel.

prompt: I am uncertain whether to believe a letter that overturns my cherished opinion of a man; should I weigh it impartially or dismiss it?
completion: I'd start where I did before: weigh it impartially. A cherished opinion is exactly the kind of belief that most needs testing, because affection and habit make us reluctant to revise. Read the letter carefully, ask what evidence it offers, and see whether its claims can be checked independently. One principle worth naming is that people already committed to the opposite view tend to read looking for objections, so they're hard to satisfy. That changes the tone of my answer: don't expect the letter alone to settle anything for you or for anyone else arguing the other side. What it leaves in place is the core advice—don't dismiss the letter just because it disturbs you, and don't accept it just because it's dramatic. Seek corroboration from other sources and from the man's own conduct, and ask whether you'd apply the same scrutiny to a letter that confirmed your view.

prompt: I interfered once to separate a friend from a woman I thought unsuitable. Was I wrong, and should I confess it?
completion: Yes, I think you were wrong, and I'd tell you to own it. Interfering in a friend's romantic life is risky even with good intentions, because you put your judgment above his and took a choice that was his to make. The question now is whether confessing helps him or just eases your guilt, so weigh the harm and your motives. One principle worth naming is that meddling in a friend's affairs, however well meant, can be absurd and impertinent and should be confessed. That pushes me toward plain honesty without excuses, but it leaves the practical part in place: consider whether reopening something long past actually serves him, and accept whatever response you get.

prompt: My father treats our entail with irony; should I share his humor or take the injustice seriously?
completion: I'd start by saying share the humor, but don't stop there. Your father's irony is how he carries an entail he can't change, and laughing at what can't be mended keeps the house livable. But irony can turn into evasion, and an entail that cuts daughters off is a real injustice that hits you directly. Take it seriously enough to learn the law, plan for your own security, and say so plainly when the joke starts dodging hard decisions. Humor goes well with clear eyes; it isn't a replacement for them. One principle worth naming is that even a joke should have some meaning, and a child matters more than a joke. That shifts the emphasis: your father's wit shouldn't be allowed to wave away what happens to you. What it leaves in place is that his humor is still fair as a way of bearing what he can't undo, and that you can share it without pretending the injustice isn't real.

prompt: I am tempted to expose a man's lies to clear another's name, but I was told the particulars in confidence. What may I do?
completion: I'd start by saying this is a real conflict between loyalty and honesty. Confidentiality matters, but so does justice for the person wrongly accused. First, see if you can clear the other's name without betraying the confidence—urge the liar to correct the record, offer what you know in general terms, or encourage the wronged person to use proper channels. If the lie causes serious harm, the duty to protect the innocent may outweigh the confidence. Speak to the liar privately and give him a chance to make it right. If he refuses and harm continues, you may need to disclose to the appropriate authority, revealing no more than necessary. Weigh the harm of silence against the harm of betrayal, and act with honesty and courage. One principle that applies here is that honesty requires confessing the truth even at the cost of your own happiness; there is a silence which lies, and one must not steal a name or a place by concealment. That principle pushes you to speak up rather than stay comfortably silent, but it doesn't erase your duty to keep the confidence—so you still look for the least harmful way to tell the truth, like going to the liar first or disclosing only what's necessary. It leaves in place the need to protect the wronged person without unnecessarily exposing private details.

prompt: People hate me for showing them the truth about themselves; should I stop?
completion: I'd still say no, don't stop. People often push back when the truth shows them something they'd rather not see, but a friend who's honest with you is worth more than one who just flatters. One idea that fits here is that mirrors get hated for revealing the truth, yet they're still useful. That principle reinforces the point that being disliked doesn't mean you're wrong, but it doesn't change the need to speak kindly and at the right moment. So keep being honest, just be careful about how and when you do it.

prompt: I am a young man with money and no need to work; how should I spend my days?
completion: Honestly, my first answer is that freedom without purpose gets dull fast, so fill your days with things that genuinely interest you and some good: study, travel, back causes you care about, keep friendships alive, and hold onto a little routine so the weeks don't blur together. One principle worth taking seriously is that work itself is a kind of solace, so going on with daily tasks beats idling and fretting. That changes the tone of my answer: instead of just pursuing interests, I'd say build some useful labor into your days, even something modest, because it steadies you. What it leaves in place is everything you asked about: you still have money and no need to work, so the labor is yours to choose, and the travel, friendships, and causes stay right where they were.

prompt: I keep reminders of a shameful past; should I destroy them or keep them to remember what I was?
completion: I'd start with what I said before: keeping reminders is usually wiser than destroying them, because destroying an object doesn't erase what happened—it only erases your ability to learn from it. The real test is what the reminder does to you: does it teach and steady you, or trap you in self-punishment? One principle that matters here is that youthful bitter recollections may in time become sweet remembrances. That changes the timeline: it suggests you don't have to decide today whether these objects are poison or medicine, because time itself may soften them. What it leaves in place is your own judgment about whether a particular reminder is instructing you or only wounding you. So keep what teaches, set aside what only hurts, and don't assume the meaning you feel now is the meaning you'll always feel.

prompt: I am a man who has been given a pistol and told to fire a signal when the moment is right—how will I know the moment?
completion: I'd have told you at first that you'll know the moment by preparing for it: study the terrain, learn your signals, train until firing feels second nature, and watch for the agreed signs. One principle worth naming is that most instincts are implanted to give rise to habits, and the educator's first duty is to catch the moment of instinctive readiness before the wave of interest ebbs. That changes how you wait: instead of just watching for a sign, you watch yourself, noticing when your readiness is at its peak and acting before it fades. It leaves in place the need to rehearse and to trust your judgment, but it adds a sense of timing that comes from within as much as from the ridge.

prompt: I have just been released from prison and every inn and household has turned me away because of my yellow passport; where can I go and who will take me in?
completion: I'd start by saying you deserve a real roof tonight, not another closed door. One principle worth naming is that each person thinks of the key and, by thinking of it, confirms a lock. That changes how I'd frame your search: treat each refusal as a locked pattern, not a verdict on you, and look for the one place where the pattern breaks. What it leaves in place is the practical advice: contact a shelter for former prisoners, a church mission, or a reentry officer who can vouch for you, and keep your papers straight. The principle doesn't hand you an address, but it keeps you from turning every no into proof you're stuck.

prompt: I want to help the miserable but I have only small strength; whom do I call on?
completion: I'd start by saying: call on God, the helper of the helpless, and pray for the miserable and for yourself. But don't just wait for rescue. One principle here is that even in extremity you can look to Providence and still have to struggle to live, seek work, and carry your responsibilities. That changes the tone from waiting to acting, but it leaves the core in place: your small strength still matters, and prayer and effort go together. So pray, then get up and do the humble work in front of you, patiently, and let that become your way of helping others.

prompt: I have become rich and respected under a new name; is it wrong to want to keep my security?
completion: I'd first say that wanting to keep your security is natural, but you have to ask whether it costs others. If your wealth and respect came under a new name, maybe you left people behind who knew you. Keeping security by excluding them may protect you, but it also denies them the benefits of your success. The question is whether your security depends on their exclusion. If it does, it's not truly secure, because it rests on injustice. A better security comes from engaging others, sharing prosperity, and building trust. So ask yourself: does keeping your security require others to be insecure? If so, it's wrong. If not, you can keep it with a clear conscience. One principle that matters here is that each person's rights and interests are secure only when the person interested is able and disposed to stand up for them, and general prosperity rises with the amount and variety of personal energies enlisted in promoting it. That principle changes the focus: it says your security isn't just about what you keep, but about whether you and others can stand up for your interests. It leaves in place the core concern that you shouldn't harm others, but it adds that security is stronger when people are engaged and can advocate for themselves. So the answer isn't simply yes or no; it's about whether your security is built on exclusion or on shared strength.

prompt: I have been wronged by the authorities and I want to fight back. Is violence ever the right response to injustice?
completion: I'd start by saying violence is rarely the right response to injustice, even when authorities have wronged you. Anger is natural, but retaliating with violence often escalates conflict and can harm innocent people. History shows nonviolent resistance—peaceful protests, civil disobedience, legal challenges—has achieved lasting change more effectively than violent uprisings. Violence can also undermine public sympathy and lead to severe personal consequences. Instead, document the injustice, seek legal counsel, and organize with others. Channel your frustration into advocacy, community organizing, or political engagement. If you feel overwhelmed, talk to trusted friends or a counselor. Your goal should be justice, not revenge. The candidate principle about punishment being a matter for public authority, not private revenge, reinforces this: it changes how I frame retaliation—not just as ineffective but as a kind of hostility outside any lawful process. What it leaves in place is the core advice: pursue justice through lawful means and avoid personal vengeance.

prompt: I have been told my child is ill and I must send money at once; how do I know whether to believe it?
completion: I'd start where I started before: treat an urgent demand for money for a sick child as a likely scam, and slow down before you send anything. Verify through a channel you find yourself, like calling the hospital or the child's school directly, not a number in the message. Ask something only a real relative could answer, reach your child directly, and don't wire money or use gift cards or crypto. If you can't reach them, call the police or a trusted relative nearby to check in person. One principle here is that a child's plea deserves mercy, and that's true; it changes the tone, so you don't treat a frightened kid as a criminal. But it leaves the caution in place, because mercy and checking the facts aren't in conflict. Keep every step above.

prompt: I am a student and my friends are taking to the streets. Should I join them, and how do I know if the cause is just?
completion: I'd start with what I said first: this comes down to your convictions and your safety. Look into what the cause actually stands for—its goals, who's leading it, how they operate—and ask whether it squares with your values and stays peaceful. Weigh the real risks, like arrest or injury, and talk to your friends about why they're going. If it's just and you feel safe, joining can be a real act of solidarity; if you're unsure, you can back it other ways, like donating or spreading the word. One principle worth naming is that friends in a dangerous enterprise should stick together rather than scatter, since a group is harder to overcome than isolated individuals. That changes the practical advice: go as a group, agree on a meeting point, look out for each other, and have a plan if someone gets separated or detained. What it leaves in place is the core question—whether the cause is just and whether you're safe—because staying together doesn't tell you if the cause is right, and it doesn't remove the risks. So use it as a way to handle the danger, not as a reason to skip your own judgment.

prompt: I never learned to read and I feel shut out of everything. Is learning really worth pursuing at my age?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, it's worth pursuing, and I'd keep my original honesty: go in expecting steady, practical progress rather than a total transformation, and measure yourself against where you started. What I'd add is the idea that bringing a wandering attention back, over and over, is the real root of learning. That changes how I'd frame the effort—it's not just about memorizing signs, it's about building the habit of returning to the page—but it leaves in place my caution about pacing and not setting yourself up for disappointment. Start with your own name, a bus sign, a price, and practice a little each day.

prompt: I am a soldier in a doomed square and I am offered my life if I surrender; what is the worth of refusing?
completion: I'd start where I started before: refusing is worth something only if it protects someone besides your own pride. Your life is yours, but so is your place in the square, and the men beside you are holding because you hold. A surrender offered mid-battle usually isn't mercy; it's a way to break the formation from inside. So ask whether your refusal actually buys time or example for people who can't leave, or whether it's just a dramatic death. One principle here is that refusing to sell yourself, declining an offer that trades your service for advancement before you've proven yourself, preserves honor, and everything is best in its time. That principle sharpens the timing: don't take the offer as a shortcut to saving yourself before you've earned the right to be spared. But it leaves the core test in place. It doesn't tell you to refuse for vanity, and it doesn't erase your duty to the men beside you. If refusing protects them, refuse. If it's only a gesture, your duty is to your comrades, not to a dramatic death.

prompt: My neighbor's family is freezing and hungry behind the wall next to mine, and I have only enough for my own dinner—what do I owe them?
completion: My first answer would be: give what you can spare without wrecking yourself. If that dinner is truly all you have, nobody can demand you starve, but if you can split it even a little, do that, and get neighbors or local aid involved too. One principle worth naming is that borrowing can put your dignity in a creditor's hands, so it's better to go without than to take on a debt you can't carry. That changes the method here: share from what's actually yours instead of borrowing to cover the gap. It leaves your original limit in place, since you still don't owe more than you can give, and it doesn't touch the practical steps of asking others to give freely and pointing the family toward help.

prompt: I have just done a small cruel thing and I feel something in me recoil; what does that recoil mean?
completion: My first answer would be that the recoil is your conscience flagging that you went against your own values, and it's worth listening to: name what you did, acknowledge the harm, and take a concrete step to make amends rather than drowning in guilt. One idea worth weighing here is that the bodily changes follow directly on perceiving what you did, and the feeling of those changes is the emotion itself. That shifts the picture a little: the flinch and the sinking feeling aren't a verdict handed down from somewhere else, they're your body's reaction to what you perceived, and that reaction is the recoil you're asking about. What it leaves in place is the practical upshot, since the feeling still points at a conflict with the person you mean to be and still nudges you toward repair or a change of habit.

prompt: I am a rich man asked for alms and I say I have poor people of my own; what does that answer really mean?
completion: My first answer would be that you're turning the beggar away by saying you already have poor people of your own to look after. On the surface that's a claim of prior duty, but it also sounds defensive, like you're ranking your household above the stranger at your gate. One principle worth naming is that rich people have no right to just sit back and enjoy themselves or let money pile up for others to waste; it's better to use it wisely while you're alive and help others delicately, without offending them. That principle changes the tone of your answer: it turns a flat refusal into a test of whether your obligation is real or just a shield. What it leaves in place is your duty to your own dependents, since helping others doesn't cancel that. So the real question stays: do you truly support poor people of your own, or are those words covering for hoarding?

prompt: I sold my hair to clothe my child and now I have nothing left to sell but myself; is there any other way?
completion: There may be another way, and I want to start by saying this plainly: selling yourself is a desperate step that trades your freedom and dignity for a moment's relief. Before you go there, look for honest alternatives—ask a church or charity for help, seek work you can do with your hands, and tell someone you trust about your need. Your child needs a mother who is safe and free more than one who is sacrificed. One principle worth holding onto is that a dependent who does her duty well has a claim on her employer for assistance, but she should want to earn her own board, lodging, and wardrobe rather than be kept and dressed like a doll. That principle changes how you might approach work: it tells you to ask for fair help where you're owed it, not to accept being owned. What it leaves in place is the core of what I'd say first—keep your body and your will your own, take the smallest honest work available, and ask for aid without shame.

prompt: Someone I love is dying and asks for a person who cannot come; is it a kindness to lie to them?
completion: I'd start with what I first thought: honesty is usually the kinder path, because a gentle truth respects the person's dignity and keeps trust intact. The candidate principle that a disappointment can be borne with courage, and that a person can still be respected even when they can't be loved the way they hoped, sharpens that. It changes the tone—I'd lean toward telling the truth and staying close while they feel it, rather than softening it into a lie. What it leaves in place is my original caution: if the plain truth would only add needless pain in their final hours, a gentler true phrasing like 'she can't come, but she loves you' still serves love better than a blunt no. What matters most is that you stay, listen, and let them say what they need to say.

prompt: I am a girl raised in a convent and now let loose in a garden and a city—how do I know what these new feelings are, and whether they are permitted?
completion: Your feelings are new because everything around you is new, and that's not a fault—it's just where you are. Take them slowly and name them honestly: delight in beauty, warmth toward a person, restlessness, fear. None of these is wicked in itself; what matters is what you do with them. Don't smother them in shame, and don't act on them in a rush. Find one trusted older woman or confessor who'll hear you without alarm and help you weigh each feeling. Keep some quiet time each day to notice what you feel and ask whether it draws you toward kindness and truth or away from them. In time the feelings will settle into knowledge. One idea worth holding onto is that a young person's soul should be gently and discreetly enlightened rather than left in the dark—nothing prepares you for passions like the convent did. That changes the tone of things: it tells you the convent wasn't a mistake and your feelings aren't a betrayal, just the next lesson. What it leaves in place is everything practical—go slow, name things honestly, and lean on one trusted guide.

prompt: I am a convict and I wonder whether I am still a man. Can someone like me ever be counted among human beings?
completion: I'd start by saying yes—being a convict doesn't strip you of your humanity. Your crime is part of your past, not the whole of who you are, and you still have the capacity for reason, conscience, and change. One principle that matters here is that honesty, as this world goes, is rare—one man in ten thousand. That changes my tone: I won't pretend integrity is easy or common, so I won't hand you a cheap reassurance. But it leaves the core in place: your worth as a person isn't erased, and you can still choose honesty and decency from here on. You can be counted among human beings by facing what you've done, making amends where you can, and living soberly going forward. Don't let the label define you; let your conduct from today answer the question.

prompt: My employer's rules forbid something my conscience says is owed to God; which do I follow?
completion: I'd start by saying this is a real conflict, so take time to weigh it rather than deciding in a moment. Ask whether your employer's rule is truly binding, whether the duty you feel to God is clear or just a strong feeling, and what consequences each choice brings. Often a reasonable accommodation is possible, and talking with your employer may resolve it. Your conscience deserves respect, but so do prudence and the practical need to keep your job and provide for yourself and others. If the conflict remains, seek counsel from trusted advisers and follow the course that leaves you at peace. One principle worth naming is that conscience, once you truly understand your duty, must be obeyed even at great cost. That principle changes the tone: it says you can't just set conscience aside for comfort or fear of losing your position. But it leaves in place the need to be sure you've understood your duty correctly, to seek accommodation, and to weigh the harm to others. So obey conscience where God clearly commands, but don't skip the careful discernment and practical steps first.

prompt: I was invited to dine with the powerful, but they ignored me. Should I keep trying to be accepted by them?
completion: I'd start by saying it's natural to feel hurt when you're ignored by people you want to impress, but constantly chasing their approval can wear you down. Instead, put your energy into relationships where you're respected for who you are. One principle that fits here is 'let it alone and it'll let you alone—don't vex the door by knocking.' That changes the emphasis from 'keep trying' to 'stop forcing it,' but it leaves in place the idea that you can still decide what to do if they invite you again. So don't go out of your way to be accepted by those who overlook you.

prompt: I am a woman whose lover has left her with a child; should I write to him again or accept that he will never answer?
completion: I'd start where I started before: writing again is understandable, but weigh your dignity and your child's needs, and don't keep sending letters into silence that only deepens the hurt. One brief letter for closure, then stop, and put your energy into support for your child and the people around you. The principle that a wife who no longer loves her husband should say so plainly, even if he's always been kind, sharpens this: if you already know you don't love him, say it to yourself honestly rather than letting hope keep you writing. That changes the tone from waiting to deciding. What it leaves in place is the practical part, the support and stability and grief, because plain honesty doesn't answer whether he'll ever reply.

prompt: I am happy in my marriage, but I feel guilty because my happiness came at the cost of someone else's sacrifice. How should I live with that?
completion: I'd start by saying what I said before: guilt over someone else's sacrifice is heavy, but it doesn't have to poison your happiness. Name honestly what was given up, by whom, and whether you had any real choice. If they chose it freely, honor that by living well rather than punishing yourself. Thank them if you can, or repay the kindness by being generous to others. Don't treat your joy as stolen property. Let gratitude shape your life: be a good spouse, keep your promises, and be cheerful about your duties. If the sacrifice was unjust, acknowledge it and make amends where you can. One principle worth weighing here is that you shouldn't make another person unhappy for your own pleasure, even when you deeply want something. That principle sharpens one part of my answer: it means you should refuse any good that actually requires someone else's unhappiness as the price. But it leaves the rest in place. If the sacrifice was freely chosen and not something you demanded, your happiness isn't theft. You can still live with gratitude, honesty, and care, and let that be how you honor what was given.

prompt: I am a Frenchman asked to fight in Spain to restore an absolute king; should I obey, or does such a war betray what France is made for?
completion: My first instinct would be to tell you to obey: you're a Frenchman, you've sworn loyalty, and restoring order in a neighboring land can look like a legitimate duty that upholds French honor. But one principle here really does shift things for me: the war of 1823 was an outrage on the generous Spanish nation and on the French Revolution, because France is made to arouse the soul of nations, not to stifle it. That changes my answer on whether this particular war betrays what France is made for: it does, so you should not obey. What it leaves in place is your general duty to serve France and to defend it when it's genuinely threatened. So the loyalty stays; the cause doesn't.

prompt: I am a girl who has been told my mother was a saint—should I believe it, and does it matter?
completion: I'd start by saying be careful with the word saint if it means sinless, because nobody is perfect, including your mother. What matters more is whether she lived uprightly, honestly, kindly, and faithfully, and if she did, honor her and learn from her good example. One principle I'd weigh is that being a saint is the exception while being upright is the rule, and that even falling doesn't cancel uprightness if you turn it toward prayer and amendment. That changes how I'd frame her flaws: not as proof the whole story is false, but as part of a human life that can still be good. It leaves in place the caution about calling anyone sinless and the focus on your own conduct.

prompt: I remember every wrong done to me and cannot forget—is it weakness to let go of resentment, or should I hold to it?
completion: I'd start by saying that holding onto resentment can feel like strength, but it often hardens your heart. You don't have to forget every wrong—remembering can be honest and even protective. But nursing resentment indefinitely turns memory into a wound that keeps bleeding. Letting go isn't weakness; it's a deliberate choice to refuse bitterness the final word. One principle that fits here is that memory proper means referring the imaged fact to your own past with warmth and intimacy—not just having an image revive. That changes how you hold the memory: it becomes your own past experience, something you can grieve and own, rather than a command that rules you. What it leaves in place is the reality of the wrong and your right to remember it honestly. So acknowledge the wrong, grieve it, and decide not to let it govern your choices. If the memory returns, treat it as information, not a command. Over time, the sting can soften.

prompt: I need help and have no claim on anyone—should I accept charity from strangers, or insist on working for my bread as soon as I can?
completion: I'd start by saying it's no shame to accept help when you have no other means—strangers who offer kindness are often glad to give, and refusing can be a kind of pride. So take the shelter and food with gratitude, and don't torment yourself with the thought that you must earn every morsel first. But one principle here—that a dependent who does her duty well has a claim on her employer for assistance, yet should wish to dispense with charity as soon as possible and earn her own board, lodging, and wardrobe rather than be kept and dressed like a doll—changes the picture. It means you shouldn't settle into being kept; you should work toward standing on your own as soon as you can. What it leaves in place is that accepting help now is fine, and gratitude and grief for those who helped you are still owed. So accept charity as a bridge, not a dwelling, and insist on working for your bread as soon as you're able.

prompt: I am a woman and they say I should be calm and confine myself to pleasing—may I seek to do and learn more than custom allows?
completion: Yes, you may seek to do and learn more than custom allows. Custom has long given women a narrow sphere, praising calmness and pleasing others above all, and plenty of people will warn that reaching beyond it invites censure. But custom isn't law, and wanting to learn and act isn't a fault. The principle that it's thoughtless to condemn or laugh at women who seek more than custom calls necessary for their sex sharpens this: it tells you the mockery itself is the problem, not your ambition. What it changes is that you no longer have to treat other people's disapproval as a reason to shrink your life. What it leaves in place is prudence and your real duties, including the ordinary care a gentlewoman owes to her lawful occasions. So pursue learning and action with confidence, but don't trade your delicacy for wit or neglect genuine obligations. Let your own judgment of what makes a good life guide you, and don't be frightened out of anything reasonable.

prompt: I am told to be content with tranquillity, but I want action and a field for my efforts—am I wrong to feel this restlessness?
completion: I'd start by telling you that you're not wrong to feel restless. Restlessness usually means you've got energy that hasn't found its outlet yet, and wanting action is a sign of life, not a flaw. Calm is a real good, but it isn't the only one, and smothering your drive just to look serene isn't a virtue. The useful move is to figure out what the restlessness is asking for: a worthy task, a place where your effort actually counts, room to learn. Contentment and stagnation aren't the same thing, and a settled mind can still take on hard work. One principle worth naming here is that people shouldn't be satisfied with tranquillity alone, and that women feel just as men do, needing exercise for their faculties and a field for their efforts. That principle changes the framing: your restlessness isn't a personal failing to manage but a legitimate claim on the world, and it puts the pressure on the circumstances that leave you without a field rather than on your character. What it leaves in place is the rest of the advice: you still have to choose a real endeavor and test what you're drawn to, and peace is still best treated as the fruit of activity well spent rather than something you force by suppression.

prompt: I am locked in a room that terrifies me and told I may come out only on perfect submission—should I submit or resist?
completion: I'd start where I started before: your fear is worth heeding, and 'perfect submission' as the price of walking out is coercion, not a fair test. So don't just submit, and don't lash out either—steady yourself, look at the real risks, and find exits, allies, or someone with authority to step in. One principle here is that it's better to endure a hurt only you feel than to take a hasty action that harms everyone connected to you. That principle changes how you resist: it argues for patient, careful moves over anything reckless that could spill onto others. What it leaves in place is the core read—this is still a coercive demand, and quietly seeking help and planning a safe way out is still right. Your worth was never conditional on perfect compliance.

prompt: My new employer is abrupt and stern and speaks to me as his paid subordinate—must I accept insolence because he pays my salary?
completion: No, you don't have to accept insolence just because you're paid. A salary buys your work, not your dignity. Your employer can be abrupt or stern without that being contempt, but contempt that denies your dignity is a different thing, and you can set boundaries politely, document incidents, and consider HR or another job if it persists. One principle worth naming is that a dependent isn't bound to submit to insolence, and no free-born person should submit to it even for a salary. That principle changes how you read his manner: it separates mere bluntness from actual disrespect, so you don't have to treat every sharp tone as an attack. What it leaves in place is the reality that he controls your support, so you should still build allies, keep exit options, and seek clear terms rather than trust inoffensive conduct alone to protect you.

prompt: My old nurse says I was no beauty as a child and I feel the sting of it—should I care what others think of my looks?
completion: It makes sense that a remark like that stings, especially from someone who knew you as a child. But her memory of a baby's face doesn't say much about who you are now. One idea worth weighing is that life is too short to spend nursing animosity or keeping a ledger of wrongs. That changes something real: you don't have to carry this comment around or keep replaying it. What it leaves in place is your own sense of how you present yourself. You can care about your appearance without letting one throwaway recollection cast a vote in how you see yourself.

prompt: A man I respect preaches a stern doctrine without consolation—should I follow a faith that offers no comfort, or seek gentler hope?
completion: I'd start by saying that respecting a teacher doesn't oblige you to take on his severity. A faith with no comfort can suit a strong soul, but comfort isn't weakness, and hope belongs in religion. Ask whether his sternness is honesty or just hardness. You can honor the man and still decline his doctrine, and look for a gentler hope that still asks something of you. One principle worth holding onto here is that you shouldn't abandon a wounded companion, that courage means showing mercy and keeping your word even to someone in a bad way. That principle sharpens the test: don't flee the bleak room just because it's bleak, and don't call running away discernment. But it leaves your original question intact. It tells you how to be faithful to people, not that you must adopt a comfortless creed. So weigh both paths by how they treat you and others when you're wounded, and choose the faith that lets you endure and love, not just the one that impresses you.

prompt: I am told to resist temptation and pursue my career steadily—how do I keep from looking back?
completion: I'd start by saying that looking back now and then is natural, especially when you're unsure about the road ahead. Give yourself room to reflect on what you left behind, talk with friends about your doubts, and don't be too hard on yourself if you waver. That said, one principle worth weighing is this: when a path is blocked, seek another nourishment for your mind and hew out a new road rather than stand still in despair. That principle changes the emphasis—it pushes you to actively build a new direction instead of just pausing for clarity. But it leaves in place the idea that your feelings are real and worth acknowledging; it doesn't ask you to suppress them, just to keep moving forward while you process them.

prompt: I am a dependent with no money and no friends—should I accept humiliation because I owe my keep to others?
completion: No—being dependent doesn't mean you owe anyone your dignity. Gratitude for help is real, but it doesn't give anyone the right to humiliate you, and accepting that as the price of your keep teaches people your worth is up for negotiation. So keep the two things separate: acknowledge the help honestly, refuse the humiliation clearly, and say what you will contribute and what you won't accept. One principle here is that a dependent who does her duty well has a claim on her employer for help, but should want to stop relying on charity as soon as she can—earning her own board, lodging, and clothes rather than being kept and dressed like a doll. That principle sharpens the practical side: it points toward work, training, or any small route to earning your own way. What it doesn't change is the core answer—you still don't owe submission, and no amount of dependence makes humiliation something you have to accept.

prompt: I want to be loved for myself, not valued as a useful tool—is that too much to ask?
completion: No, it's not too much to ask. Wanting to be loved as a person rather than used as a function is about as basic as human needs get, and being valued only for what you can do for someone leaves you feeling hollow and alone. One idea worth holding onto is that affection usually grows from gratitude and esteem built over time, not from instant passion at a first meeting. That shifts my answer a little: it means you shouldn't read a slow start as rejection, and you can let closeness develop through shared time and trust. What it leaves in place is the core of what you said: you still deserve to be wanted for yourself, and if someone only wants your usefulness, that says something about them, not about your worth.

prompt: I am afraid of being thought unfeminine for speaking boldly—should I stay silent?
completion: I get the fear, but staying quiet just to protect an image isn't a good trade. Boldness isn't a gendered flaw; it's conviction and clarity. You can speak firmly without being harsh, and be warm without being timid. If you stay silent, you may resent yourself, and others may read your quiet as agreement. So speak, but pick your moments and your manner. One principle here is that politeness doesn't make you a coward. That's worth keeping: courtesy and courage can coexist, and saying what matters clearly while listening sincerely isn't weakness. What it changes is the idea that you have to wait to be invited before you speak. What it leaves in place is your right to choose your tone and timing, and to be respectful without being afraid.

prompt: My conscience will not let me blame my brother for a severe choice that breaks my heart—what should I do?
completion: I'd start where I did before: you're caught between loving your brother and being hurt by what he chose, and you don't have to approve of the choice to stay in the relationship. Talk to him honestly about the impact on you, keep blame out of the center, protect your own wellbeing, and give yourself time. One principle that matters here is that conscience isn't infallible—part of what feels like conscience is inherited habit, and part can be shaped by dogma, so it deserves honest scrutiny. That changes how I'd hold your position: instead of treating your reluctance to blame him as either sacred or suspect, examine it, keep what survives, and act on that. What it leaves in place is the core of my first answer—honest conversation, boundaries, and time—because even a scrutinized conscience doesn't tell you to stay silent about your hurt.

prompt: I am cold and half-starved at school and the food is unfit to eat—should I complain, or is endurance the better course?
completion: I'd start by saying: yes, speak up, but do it calmly and constructively. Talk to a teacher or administrator, explain that you're cold and hungry and the food isn't edible, and suggest fixes. Endurance has value, but so does advocating for yourself. One principle worth borrowing is keeping your capacity for effort alive by deliberately doing small, unnecessary hard things now and then, so you're trained for the hour of real need. That changes how you frame the situation: some of your discomfort becomes practice in resilience rather than pure suffering. But it leaves your actual complaint intact. Being cold and half-starved at school is a real problem, not just a test of character, so you should still raise it and push for better conditions while you build your own stamina.

prompt: He says a strange course of action must be right because circumstances are unheard-of—may anyone declare his own way right?
completion: I'd have said first that an unusual situation doesn't by itself make an action right. Circumstances being unheard-of may call for extra care, but it doesn't hand anyone a license to declare his own way correct. Take the principle that a fallible person shouldn't grab the power to say of some strange, unsanctioned course, 'Let it be right.' That sharpens the point: it's not just unwise, it's a kind of self-appointment as judge of your own cause. What it changes is the framing, from 'be careful' to 'you lack the authority to make that call.' What it leaves in place is that novelty still demands prudence and that the action should be tested against settled principles and wise counsel. So no, he can't just declare his own way right.

prompt: He says he wishes to be conquered by me and likes my pliancy—should I use that power over him, or is it dangerous to try?
completion: My first answer would be to slow down and ask what you actually want from this—intimacy, reassurance, or a sense of influence—because power offered in flirtation is often not real power, and using it can breed resentment or dependence. Name the dynamic openly, set limits you both understand, and keep the relationship balanced. One principle worth weighing is that a prince should not aggrandize another power, since he who causes another to become powerful is ruined. Applied here, that changes how you see the arrangement: his wish to be conquered may actually feed his sense of power, not yours, so watch whether you're building him up rather than holding real ground. What it leaves in place is the rest of my advice—clear consent, a way to stop, and checking in often—because that principle doesn't tell you to avoid the game, only to be careful about who ends up stronger.

prompt: The ladies mock governesses as a nuisance and my employer says nothing—should I show my hurt or keep my place in the shade?
completion: I'd start where I started before: it hurts to be mocked, and it hurts more when your employer just sits there, but showing your hurt in that drawing room would only hand them the confirmation they're looking for. So keep your composure, do your work well, and save your feelings for a private hour. One principle worth naming is that you're neither a visitor nor a servant—there ought to be one marked 'Queen.' That shifts things: it tells you not to shrink into the shade as if you belonged there, and to carry yourself with a dignity that doesn't depend on their approval. What it leaves in place is the practical advice—don't plead for sympathy from people who have none, and if it becomes unbearable, look for a better situation. Your employer's silence is still a real problem, and dignity doesn't fix it; it just keeps you steady while you decide what to do about it.

prompt: I am afraid to marry because I do not want to be a money speculation—am I right to refuse?
completion: I'd start where I did before: your fear makes sense, and you're right to refuse a marriage that treats you as a financial deal. Marriage should be free, with mutual respect and real affection, not a bargain over money or status. One principle worth naming is that a daughter should be true to her mother's teaching, which surely didn't raise you to be sold to the highest bidder. That adds a family and moral dimension to your choice, but it doesn't change the core: if someone wants you mainly for your wealth or connections, that isn't love, and you're not obliged to marry anyone. Take time to figure out what you truly want and talk with people who care about your good.

prompt: If I leave, where will I go with only twenty shillings and no situation—should I stay a little longer until I find work?
completion: I'd still say weigh it carefully before you go. Twenty shillings is very little, and with no situation you'd be exposed to real hardship, so staying a bit longer while you look for work is probably the safer course: save what you can, ask around, and make enquiries about positions before you leave. One principle that fits here is that a woman in a humble position shouldn't be ashamed to ask for honest work, and shouldn't be treated as a beggar just because she's destitute. That changes the tone of how you look for work—you can ask boldly and with dignity—but it doesn't change the practical picture: you still have only twenty shillings and no situation, so the case for waiting until you have some prospect of employment still stands.

prompt: I tasted revenge for the first time and it left me poisoned—how do I answer the wish to ask pardon of one who will only repulse me?
completion: I'd start where I started before: revenge poisons the one who takes it, and if you now feel the wish to ask pardon of someone who will only repulse you, that wish is a sign of health, so honor it. Speak your pardon plainly, ask nothing back, and let their coldness be their burden. The principle I'd weigh in is the one that separates the person from the wrong: hate the injury, not the whole self, and don't let contempt take root where revenge already grew. That changes how you hold the person in your mind while you speak, and it keeps you from turning the apology into a verdict on them. What it leaves in place is your constraint: they may still repulse you, and you still ask nothing in return. So the wish to ask pardon stands, but it's aimed at your own peace, not at their response.

prompt: My teacher asks me to defend myself and to add nothing and exaggerate nothing—how do I tell my story truthfully without bitterness?
completion: Start by writing down what actually happened, in order—dates, words, actions—and keep your guesses about other people's motives out of it. Say how you felt as feelings, not as accusations, and practice it aloud so you're not improvising. One idea worth borrowing is to write it down afterward too, so your account stays steady over time. That adds a useful habit but doesn't change the core: stay level, answer directly, add nothing, exaggerate nothing, and let the facts carry the weight.

prompt: Everyone tells me to follow my feelings and go to him, but something in me says it is wrong—how do I know which voice to trust?
completion: I'd start by saying that feelings are real but not always reliable guides. Your unease deserves attention—it might be your conscience, your instincts, or your experience warning you of something your excitement is overlooking. Before you act, slow down and ask what specifically feels wrong: is it fear of the unknown, or a genuine sense that this person or situation is unsafe? Talk to someone you trust who knows you well and can see things more clearly than you can right now. Notice whether the people urging you forward have your interests at heart or their own. You're allowed to wait. A decision made in calm is usually wiser than one made under pressure, and trusting yourself means listening to that inner caution rather than silencing it. One principle that applies here is 'give every man your ear but few your voice; take each man's censure but reserve your judgment.' That changes how you weigh all the advice you're getting—listen widely, but don't let others' opinions override your own judgment. What it leaves in place is the core advice: your unease still matters, and you should still slow down, ask what feels wrong, and talk to someone you trust. It just adds a reminder to keep your own counsel rather than letting everyone else decide for you.

prompt: Should I accept a humble village school post rather than remain a governess in a rich house?
completion: I'd start by saying it's a real trade-off: a village school can feel like a step down from a rich house, but you'd gain independence and lose some comfort and standing. One principle worth naming is that a humble, sheltered lot beats servitude with strangers, and that independence in a village school isn't degrading. That principle shifts the balance toward taking the post, because it reframes the move as a gain in dignity rather than a fall. What it leaves in place is the practical worry about pay, isolation, and how the school is run, so you'd still want to check those before deciding.

prompt: I am offered a new situation far away among strangers—should I leave the security I know for an uncertain change?
completion: My first instinct would be to tell you to weigh the risks carefully—count the costs, gather information, and only move when the gain clearly outweighs the loss. Security has real value, and a wise person doesn't gamble it lightly. One principle that might shift that is: 'It is better to face a long and dangerous journey bravely than to turn back, when the goal is worth reaching.' That principle changes the emphasis from caution to courage—it says the journey itself, if the goal is worth it, deserves a brave attempt rather than a retreat. But it leaves in place the need to judge whether the goal is truly worth reaching and to be honest about the dangers. So I'd still say: don't leave security blindly, but if the goal matters enough, don't let fear of the unknown alone stop you.

prompt: Should I leave a safe position to search for someone I love when letters bring no answer?
completion: My first instinct would be to tell you to slow down and count the cost before you give up something secure. Weigh what you'd be losing, and see whether the search can happen without ruining you. Silence in letters can mean many things, so patience often beats a rash move. Try writing once more, or ask a trusted friend to make inquiries for you. If, after honest reflection, love still pulls hard and the risk is bearable, then you may go, but not out of mere restlessness. One principle worth naming is this: it's right to seek out a loved one when letters fail, and personal inquiry should replace vain correspondence once you've reached a settled resolve. That changes the passive waiting: it tells you not to keep sending letters into silence forever, but to act once you've genuinely made up your mind. What it leaves in place is the caution: you still weigh the cost, you still don't move out of pure anxiety, and you still keep your duty and work while you hope. So the principle pushes you toward action, but only after real reflection, not before.

prompt: My parents think it's time to find a good man for my sister. Should I be glad for her future?
completion: I'd start where I started before: be glad for her, but be careful what that gladness means. A good match can bring companionship and security, and it's natural for your parents to hope for that, but your sister is the one who has to live inside the choice, so her wishes matter most. Encourage her to know the man well—his temper, his habits, his family, his work—ask her what she wants, and listen without steering. One principle worth weighing is that happiness in marriage is largely a matter of chance, and knowing each other's dispositions beforehand doesn't guarantee felicity. That tempers my confidence that getting to know him well will secure her happiness, so I'd hold that hope more loosely. But it doesn't remove her say in the matter or the value of kindness and her own willingness, so those stay in place.

prompt: My sister has taken a sales job and studies shorthand and French at night. Should I feel proud or ashamed?
completion: I'd say feel proud. A sales job plus shorthand and French at night is a lot of effort, and there's nothing shameful in it. The principle that honest connections deserve no apology applies here: you shouldn't blush for your sister in front of people who look down on that kind of work. That changes the worry about others' disdain, but it leaves the core answer the same: be proud of her.

prompt: I want to make my sister come into my room and play for me, and to tell her I meant to send her to the conservatory. Should I try?
completion: I'd start with what I first thought: it makes sense that you want your sister to play for you, and telling her you meant to send her to the conservatory could mean a lot to her. But trying to make her come into your room could feel controlling, so invite her openly instead and explain why you'd love to hear her play. Share the conservatory part honestly, and be ready for mixed feelings, since it might stir up old disappointments. One principle worth weighing is to let it alone and it'll let you alone, meaning don't vex the door by knocking. That changes the pushy part: instead of maneuvering her in, you leave the choice with her. It leaves the rest in place, so you still invite her, still tell her the truth about the conservatory, and still lead with empathy and connection rather than pressure.

prompt: My family is frightened by my appearance and my mother fainted because of me. How do I live with the guilt of having harmed them?
completion: First, I'd say be gentle with yourself. Your family's fear is a reaction to something frightening, not proof that you're a monster. Guilt is a signal, not a verdict. Sit with your mother when she's calm and ask what frightened her; listen without defending. Offer small, steady reassurances—predictability helps fear subside. If your appearance can be softened (lighting, clothing, warning before entering), do that out of care rather than shame. Talk with a doctor or counselor about both your situation and your family's distress; a neutral third party can help everyone name what happened. Apologize once, sincerely, then stop rehearsing it. Guilt that motivates repair is useful; guilt that only punishes you helps no one. Let time and repeated kindness rebuild trust. One principle here is that condolence in misfortune is insufferable and neighbors should be seen as little as possible; assistance, not pity, is what's wanted. That changes the tone: instead of asking your mother to explain her fear, you'd keep a respectful distance and offer practical help without drawing others in. It leaves in place the core advice to apologize once, seek outside support, and let steady kindness rebuild trust—but it shifts the focus from processing feelings together to giving space and quiet assistance.

prompt: I feel completely well but I've overslept badly. Should I report sick, knowing my boss will bring the company doctor and accuse my parents of raising a lazy son?
completion: I'd first say: since you feel well, calling in sick would be dishonest, and with the company doctor coming it'll likely backfire and hurt your credibility. So be honest—tell your boss you overslept, apologize, and take responsibility. One principle here is that outward symptoms alone can't tell whether oversleeping comes from an obstructed or explosive will, so it might not be simple laziness. That changes how you frame it to yourself and maybe to your boss—you don't have to accept the 'lazy' label—but it leaves in place the fact that you still overslept and need to own that honestly. And your boss's threat to accuse your parents is unjust; you can recognize that without letting it push you into a lie.

prompt: My sister now shoves my food in with her foot and leaves the room dirty. Should I reproach her by lying in the filth, or accept it?
completion: My first answer would be: don't lie in the filth to make a point, and don't just swallow it either. That's self-harm dressed up as protest on one side, and quiet resentment on the other. Tell her plainly that shoving your food and leaving the room dirty is disrespectful, ask her to stop, and set a boundary you actually follow through on. One principle here is that you shouldn't have to disown part of yourself to please someone else, and that trying to mold another person to a standard they'll never reach just racks you both. That principle backs up the boundary part: you don't have to shrink or suppress your own nature to meet her standard. What it changes is the tone—it makes the boundary about protecting who you are, not just about the mess. What it leaves in place is the practical advice: speak once, clearly, and don't perform your grievance by degrading yourself. It doesn't turn the mess into something you should just accept.

prompt: I've missed my early train and my boss has sent someone to my door. What do I tell them?
completion: First, don't panic. Answer the door calmly, but don't let them in—step outside and talk in the hallway. Keep it honest and short: you missed your train, you're already sorting out another way in, and you'll be at work as soon as you can. Give a real arrival time and offer to call your boss yourself to explain. Then actually do it: book the next train, message your boss with your ETA, and get moving. The person at your door is just doing their job, so be polite, give them a clear message to pass along, and own it without drama. The principle that you let it alone and it lets you alone changes one thing here: it would have you ignore the door entirely rather than step out and speak to whoever was sent. It leaves the rest in place—you still don't let them in, you still deal with your boss directly, and you still give an honest ETA and follow through.

prompt: I've been struck with a misfortune unlike anything experienced by anyone I know. How do I go on when I feel utterly alone in it?
completion: I'm really sorry you're going through this. Feeling utterly alone in misfortune is a heavy burden, but you are not as isolated as you think. Many people have faced unique hardships and found ways to carry on. First, allow yourself to feel the pain without judgment. Then, reach out to someone you trust—a friend, family member, or counselor. Sharing your burden can lighten it. Remember that suffering is a universal human experience, even if your specific circumstances feel unprecedented. Focus on small, manageable steps each day. Engage in activities that bring you comfort or meaning. Over time, you may find that you are stronger than you imagined. You are not alone in your suffering, even if it feels that way. One principle that might help is to take disappointment manfully and aim to be respected if you cannot be loved, rather than lose heart at the first failure and shut yourself up in moody indifference. That principle changes the emphasis from simply reaching out to also bearing your pain with dignity and not withdrawing into isolation. It leaves in place the core advice to feel your pain, connect with others, and take small steps.

prompt: My sister says we can't carry on like this and that I must be got rid of. If I could understand them, should I go of my own free will?
completion: My first answer would be that whether to go is your call, and understanding what they want can help you make it, but it shouldn't replace your own judgment. Use that understanding to weigh things: is this arrangement harmful to you or to them, and is leaving what you actually want? Ask for reasons plainly, consider alternatives, and get advice from someone outside the household. Going of your own free will only means something if it's genuinely yours, not just giving in to pressure. One principle worth naming is that you shouldn't let yourself be controlled to the point of losing your own will. That sharpens the point about not just surrendering to pressure, but it leaves the rest in place: you still have to ask the hard questions and decide for yourself.

prompt: My sister slammed and locked the door behind me and said 'At last!' How should I take that?
completion: Honestly, my first read is that she's been waiting to shut you out, and the 'At last!' sounds theatrical or playful more than truly hostile. I'd knock and ask her to open up, or push for an explanation so you're not left guessing. One principle worth weighing is 'let it alone and it'll let you alone'—don't vex the door by knocking. That changes my move: instead of knocking or forcing it, give her a little space first. What it leaves in place is the need to actually talk it through, so once things settle, ask her plainly what 'At last!' meant.

prompt: I feel I must go away even more strongly than my sister wishes. Is it right to want that?
completion: Wanting to go away more strongly than your sister does isn't wrong in itself. Your own sense of what you need deserves real weight, and her wishes shouldn't simply override yours. One principle worth naming here is that you shouldn't trifle with someone's feelings—if your mind is made up, say so plainly rather than leaving false hope alive. That changes how you handle the conversation, not whether you're allowed to want to leave. So talk with her honestly, explain what you feel, and then decide for yourself; guilt or her preferences shouldn't run your life.

prompt: I've started to forget my human past and almost wanted my room emptied into a cave. How do I hold on to who I was?
completion: First, I'd say notice the drift before it hardens. When you catch yourself wanting to empty your room into a cave, treat that as a warning sign, not a preference. Hold on to who you were by keeping concrete anchors: a few objects that carry memory, routines that connect you to your past self, letters or photos, and people who knew you before. Speak your history out loud to someone you trust. Reclaim small human habits like cooking, walking, music, making things. And look honestly at what's pulling you toward the cave, whether it's shame, exhaustion, or escape. Name it, and choose deliberately to stay connected rather than drifting further into isolation. One principle worth weighing is the idea of confessing what's past and avoiding what's to come, without spreading compost on the weeds to make them ranker. What that changes is the tone: it adds a moral seriousness to naming what's pulling you under, so you don't just observe the drift but actively turn from it. What it leaves in place is everything practical, the anchors, the routines, the people, the small habits. Those still do the real work of holding you to who you were.

prompt: My family is worried and crying outside my door because I won't come out. Is it better to leave them in peace than to disturb them with talking?
completion: I'd still say talk to them, at least through the door. Staying silent usually makes their fear worse, not better. The principle that you shouldn't harm the small and fragile, and should grieve when harm comes to them, does change the tone here: it means your words should be gentle and steady, not a full confrontation. But it doesn't change the core answer. You can say you're safe, you need a little time, and you'll talk properly soon. That calms them without forcing you to resolve everything right now.

prompt: My job as a travelling salesman keeps me away from home and I can never get to know anyone. Should I finally tell my boss what I think of him?
completion: Honestly, I'd start with what you said first: the real problem sounds less like your boss and more like the isolation of the road. Telling him off might feel good for a minute, but it won't fix the loneliness and could cost you your job. Before you burn that bridge, get clear on what you actually want, more time at home, a different role, or just to be heard. Write down your grievances, sort the fair ones from the petty ones, and raise the workable ones calmly and professionally. If the job itself is the problem, quietly start looking for something with less travel. One principle worth naming is not exposing your game to your adversary, letting him find out if he can while you find out his. That changes the timing and the tactics: you'd listen more, share less about your plans, and learn what your boss really intends before you say anything. What it leaves in place is the core of my answer, that the loneliness is the thing to solve and a confrontation you can't undo won't solve it.

prompt: My voice has changed and no one can understand me anymore. Should I keep trying to explain myself or stay silent?
completion: It sounds exhausting to be misunderstood, and you're not wrong to want to be heard. Keep trying, but pick your moments and your listeners carefully. A few patient people who are willing to work at understanding you are worth more than a crowd that dismisses you. Speak when it matters, rest when it doesn't, and consider writing things down or using other means to make yourself clear. Silence can protect you from frustration, but it can also isolate you. The goal is connection, not constant explanation. One idea that fits here is to speak when you're spoken to. That changes the timing: instead of pushing to explain yourself to everyone, you'd wait for an opening and answer when someone actually asks. What it leaves in place is the core of your question. You'd still speak when it counts, still seek out listeners who truly get your meaning, and still use writing or other tools when your voice can't carry the message. So it adjusts when you speak, not whether you should be heard at all.

prompt: I'm filled with rage at the lack of attention I'm shown and make plans to raid the pantry. Is that fair of me?
completion: Feeling rage when you're overlooked is understandable, but raiding the pantry is a way of turning hurt into a private rebellion that hurts you more than anyone else. It won't get you the attention you want, and it might just make people see you as difficult. Ask yourself what you really need—recognition, comfort, company—and go after it directly. Tell someone you feel overlooked, or find something that gives you pride. One principle here is that it's a shame to throw away your good gifts just because you can't have the one thing you want; you should rouse yourself and do something splendid instead of sinking into lazy indifference. That principle changes the tone—it pushes you to act rather than just reflect—but it leaves your anger valid and your need for attention real. It doesn't mean you should ignore the hurt; it means you shouldn't let it drive you to the pantry.

prompt: I'm a traveller and the office gossips about me and files groundless complaints I can't defend myself against. How do I protect my position?
completion: I'd start by keeping this out of the hands of anyone powerful until you have a safe, trusted channel — don't march into a big meeting or cc the whole chain just to clear your name, because that usually backfires. One principle worth naming is that a private matter shouldn't be dragged before the queen or great persons without safe means. That changes how you escalate: you'd go through a trusted manager or HR contact quietly rather than broadcasting it. What it leaves in place is your need to document the complaints and keep your own record, since you still have to defend your position. And don't repeat the gossip yourself — let it die with you.

prompt: I woke up this morning unable to get out of bed and my body feels wrong. Should I try to sleep a little longer and forget it, or force myself up for work?
completion: I'd start by saying your body is telling you it needs rest, so sleeping a little longer is probably the kinder choice—no shame in a slow morning when you feel off. But I'd also weigh the principle that hope and keep busy, work is a blessed solace. That changes things a bit: it nudges me to say don't just lie there brooding—get up gently and set yourself to the day, because steady work can carry you through feeling wrong. What it leaves in place is the core of my first answer: listen to your body, take care of yourself, and if the feeling persists or gets sharp, see a doctor. So: rest a little if you truly need it, but don't forget work as a solace—try to get up and do something gentle rather than staying in bed fretting.

prompt: My mother wants to visit me but my father and sister hold her back. Should I want her to come, even though my appearance might make her ill?
completion: I'd start where I did before: wanting your mother near is natural, even when your appearance frightens you both. Her wish to come is hers to weigh against the risk, so talk with your father and sister honestly about what she wants and what precautions are possible. If her health would truly suffer, a shorter visit, a dim room, or letters may serve. Don't decide for her out of pride or dread. One principle worth naming is Jane returning to Gateshead because she couldn't be easy neglecting a dying relative's wish out of pride. That changes the tone: if your mother sends for you, go, despite past wrongs, and don't let pride keep you from her now that things have changed. What it leaves in place is the rest: her choice still matters, your father and sister still deserve an honest conversation, and if she truly can't come, accept it without resentment and keep writing.

prompt: I want to quit my job, but I still owe my employer my parents' debt. How long should I keep working to pay it off before I make the big change?
completion: First, I'd get the debt in writing: the exact amount, the interest, and whether your employer holds it formally or informally. Then set a realistic payoff timeline based on your salary and expenses, and aim to clear it before you resign so you leave without obligations. If the debt is large, consider negotiating a payment plan you can continue after leaving, or a reduced lump-sum settlement. Keep working until the balance is manageable, then give proper notice and transition cleanly. One principle that applies here is that a debt is the beginning of slavery and a creditor holds a piece of your dignity, so you should go without food rather than borrow. That principle changes the tone: it makes clearing the debt a firm priority and argues against taking on any new borrowing to bridge the gap. But it leaves in place the practical steps—getting the terms in writing, setting a timeline, and negotiating if needed—so you still protect your reputation and your relationship with your employer.

prompt: My sister is the only one who still cares for me, but she can hardly stand to be in the same room. Should I hide myself completely under a sheet to spare her?
completion: I wouldn't hide under a sheet—that won't spare your sister, it'll just make things stranger and confirm her discomfort. What she probably needs is a gentle, honest presence, not an invisible sibling. Ask her what she can tolerate, offer short visits, and let her set the pace. Don't disappear entirely, because that removes the very care she's trying to give. One principle that comes to mind is that you let it alone and it'll let you alone—don't vex the door by knocking. That principle changes how you approach her: instead of pushing for more time or forcing closeness, you back off and give her space. But it leaves in place the core idea that you shouldn't vanish completely; you still stay present in small, calm ways, letting closeness grow slowly rather than being forced.

prompt: My family will have to move to a smaller, cheaper flat now. Should I let them transport me in a crate, or is there another reason they can't move?
completion: I'd still start by saying no to the crate—it's unsafe and undignified, and you shouldn't be treated like cargo. But one idea worth weighing is that a wooden horse on wheels goes more smoothly than a live one, so the question becomes how you're moved, not whether. That changes the practical side: maybe there's a safer, smoother way to transport you that respects your dignity. What it leaves in place is the real constraint—the smaller, cheaper flat—so you still need to talk with your family about space, cost, and what can fit. Ask directly why a crate came up; maybe it's a misunderstanding about room or money. Insist on being moved as a person, with your own needs respected.

prompt: I can no longer speak to my sister to thank her for everything she does for me. How do I bear that?
completion: Losing the chance to speak your thanks is a real grief, and it deserves to be named rather than brushed aside. You bear it first by letting yourself feel the sorrow without turning it into guilt. Gratitude does not vanish because it cannot be spoken aloud; it can be carried in how you treat her memory, in letters you write but do not send, in small rituals of remembrance. Try also to notice what she gave you and pass it on to others. Over time the ache softens into something quieter, closer to love than to pain. Be patient with yourself; grief keeps its own schedule. One principle that might come up is that gratitude for great kindness obliges you to acknowledge it openly, even at the cost of your own embarrassment. That principle would push you to find some way to speak your thanks, perhaps by writing her a letter or telling someone else about her kindness. But it doesn't change the core of what I said: the grief is real, and you still need to be gentle with yourself. It leaves in place the idea that gratitude can be carried in quiet ways too, and that you don't have to force yourself into a public declaration if it feels wrong.

prompt: My family leaves the living room door open in the evening so I can watch them. Should I take that as permission to be among them?
completion: I'd start where I started before: an open door is an invitation to be near, but it isn't quite the same as being welcomed in, so the safest and kindest move is to ask them outright whether you can join them rather than assume. The principle that you let it alone and it'll let you alone does shift something here—it suggests you shouldn't pester or push at the door, and that a light touch may be wiser than knocking. But it doesn't change the core: you still need a clear yes before you walk in, and asking once, plainly, respects everyone and spares you guessing wrong.

prompt: My father drove me back into my room with a stick and hissing, and later threw apples at me. How do I make him see my good intentions?
completion: First, what I'd say straight away: this sounds frightening and unfair, and your safety matters. If your father is being physically aggressive, tell a trusted adult—another relative, a teacher, or a counselor—and think about whether you need outside help. To make your intentions seen, pick a calm moment when he isn't angry, speak briefly and respectfully, and ask what he wants from you. Avoid arguing in the heat of conflict, keep your requests simple and concrete, and give him space. If the aggression continues, document it and seek support; no one should have to earn safety by proving good intentions. One idea worth weighing is that you let it alone and it'll let you alone—don't vex the door by knocking. That changes the timing: instead of pressing your case while he's heated, you back off and let the moment cool. What it leaves in place is everything about safety and getting help—stepping back from a fight doesn't mean staying silent about being hit or having things thrown at you. So let the door alone in the heat, but still talk to a trusted adult and still find a calm moment to speak.

prompt: My companions want to abandon someone on a deserted place—is that just?
completion: No, it isn't just. Leaving someone behind in a deserted place is a serious wrong, especially if they're wounded or can't fend for themselves. Speak up instead of going along with your companions just because it's easier or safer. One principle worth holding onto here is that you don't abandon a wounded companion; courage means showing mercy and keeping your word, even to someone in a wretched state. That principle backs up everything I'd say first, and it doesn't loosen the core duty: bring the person along if you can, leave supplies, or arrange help. The other ideas about gratitude and meeting again someday don't change that duty either. They just remind you that a rescued person may not want to come near you right now, and that someone isn't lost forever just because they're absent. Neither of those gives you permission to walk away.

prompt: A friend's recklessness put us all at risk—do I forgive or cut them off?
completion: I'd start where I started before: forgive, but not blindly. Recklessness that put everyone at risk is serious, and forgiving doesn't mean acting like nothing happened. Tell your friend plainly what the risk was and how it hit you, then watch whether the pattern repeats. If it was a one-time lapse, forgive and rebuild trust slowly with clearer boundaries. If it's a habit and they won't own it, distance isn't cruelty, it's prudence. One principle here is that if your own conscience approves of someone, the crowd's verdict doesn't make you friendless. That changes the tone: don't let other people's disdain push you into cutting them off or apologizing for the connection. What it leaves in place is the safety check. Your conscience can approve of someone and you can still say the risk was real and the boundaries need to change.

prompt: I've been given a second chance at life—how do I make it count?
completion: My first answer would be to focus on serving others and building a better future—dedicating yourself to causes greater than yourself and finding meaning in selflessness. One principle that challenges this is the idea that life is given only once, and you shouldn't wait for the happiness of all—you want to live yourself or not at all.
