That changes the emphasis from self-sacrifice to personal fulfillment and authenticity, but it leaves in place the core idea that your second chance should be lived deliberately and with purpose. So I'd still say: make it count by living fully, but also by contributing in ways that matter to you.

prompt: I feel responsible for a death that happened because of my choices—how do I live with it?
completion: I'd start by saying you're not solely responsible—many things contribute to any death, and guilt can be a heavy burden, but forgiving yourself matters. Please talk to a counselor, lean on trusted friends or family who won't judge you, and maybe write a letter to the person you lost, even if you never send it. Channel your grief into something healthy, like volunteering. One idea worth weighing is that we should be careful how we deal with those around us, because every death leaves survivors thinking of so much omitted and so little done, and there's no remorse as deep as unavailing remorse. That changes the focus toward showing timely care and earnestness to the people you love now, while it leaves in place the counseling, support, and self-forgiveness—it doesn't tell you to carry the guilt forever. Take it one day at a time and be patient with yourself.

prompt: I'm the youngest here and no one takes me seriously—how do I earn respect?
completion: I'd start by saying respect is earned over time through consistent behavior—being reliable, showing up prepared, listening more than you speak, asking good questions, and owning your mistakes. One principle that matters here is that first impressions and charming manners aren't proof of virtue; real goodness has to show up in actual deeds. That changes how you should read people's reactions: don't mistake someone's polished charm for genuine respect, and don't try to win approval with drilled politeness alone. It leaves in place the core advice—be steady, courteous, and competent—but it reminds you that the respect worth having comes from real integrity, not from performing niceness for approval.

prompt: I want to leave a bad situation but I gave my word to stay—what wins?
completion: Your word matters, but so does your safety, and a promise made under pressure or to someone who keeps changing the terms isn't the same as a freely given vow. So first, sit with the tension instead of rushing: ask what you were actually promising, to whom, and whether staying still serves that purpose. One principle worth holding onto here is that when a path is blocked, you should hew out a new road rather than stand still in despair. That changes how you see leaving: it's not abandoning your word, it's finding another way to keep faith. What it leaves in place is that your word still has weight, so leaving should be deliberate, not just a flight from guilt. Talk it through with someone you trust, and give yourself permission to revise a promise that was never meant to cost you this much.

prompt: I'm being asked to keep quiet about something illegal—where's the line?
completion: I'd start where I started before: the line is where staying quiet turns into taking part. You can pass on gossip or guesswork, sure, but hiding a crime you know is happening—especially when people are getting hurt—isn't neutral, and it can make you complicit both legally and morally. Check what the law actually asks of you, since some jobs carry mandatory reporting, and check what your conscience asks. If you're scared of payback, get advice from a lawyer or someone you trust in authority and write down what you know. Protecting vulnerable people usually matters more than loyalty to whoever's doing wrong. One principle worth naming here is that a false public accusation should be answered by speaking up in your own defense, adding nothing and exaggerating nothing. That changes how you handle it if someone turns the accusation on you—you answer plainly and truthfully instead of staying silent out of fear. What it leaves in place is the core point: defending your own name doesn't mean covering for someone else's crime, and it doesn't cancel the duty to report harm to others.

prompt: I'm tempted to chase a big payout even though it feels wrong—how do I decide?
completion: I'd start by saying that if a payout feels wrong, that feeling is often your conscience warning you before your reason catches up. Don't chase it just because it's big. Ask what the gain costs others, what it costs your integrity, and whether you'd be ashamed if people knew. If it requires deceit, don't do it. A clear conscience is worth more than a big payout. One principle worth naming is that it's wrong to deceive another person, like Rochester feigning courtship of Miss Ingram to make Jane jealous—you shouldn't treat someone's feelings as a mere means. That principle sharpens the deceit test: it makes clear that using someone else's emotions as a tool is a red line. But it doesn't change the rest—the size of the payout still doesn't justify a wrong, and your own integrity and shame test still stand.

prompt: I'm being pressured to join a group doing wrong—how do I refuse without being destroyed?
completion: Here's what I'd say first: be clear and brief when you refuse—something like 'I'm not comfortable with this, so I'm not doing it.' Don't over-explain or debate; the more you justify, the more room they get to argue. If the pressure keeps up, physically remove yourself from the situation. Tell someone you trust—a friend, family member, or someone with authority—and keep a record of any threats. If you're afraid for your safety, go to the police. Your integrity matters more than their approval, and you can say no without being destroyed by it. One principle worth naming here is that you shouldn't let yourself be controlled to the point of losing your own will—a person who vacillates gets carried along by whoever pushes hardest. That principle reinforces the core of the advice: hold your line and don't hand your decision-making over to the group. What it changes is the framing—it puts the emphasis on your own resolve rather than just tactics. What it leaves in place is everything practical: the short refusal, stepping away, getting support, documenting threats, and going to authorities if you fear for your safety. Those still stand exactly as they are.

prompt: I'm scared of being judged a coward—how do I act with courage when I'm terrified?
completion: Fear isn't the same as cowardice. Courage is acting rightly even when you're terrified, so the first thing I'd say is: steady yourself, breathe, name what you're afraid of, and separate real danger from imagined judgment. Then take the smallest brave step you can. One idea worth weighing here is that courage means facing danger while afraid and that what you really need is confidence in yourself. That shifts the emphasis toward building self-trust, which can help, but it leaves your original situation intact: you still have to act while scared, and other people's opinions still matter less than your own integrity. So prepare what you can, accept what you can't control, and let each small brave action build the habit.

prompt: I broke a rule to do something brave—was I wrong even if it helped?
completion: My first answer was that breaking a rule to do something brave isn't automatically wrong or right—the outcome matters, but so does the process, and you should ask whether the help could have come within the rules, whether anyone was endangered, and whether you'd want others to act the same way. One principle here is that it's better to endure a private cost than to take a hasty action whose bad consequences spread to everyone connected to you. That principle shifts the focus: it makes you weigh the ripple effects on the people around you before you rest on the good result. But it doesn't erase the core of my first answer—the need to check whether the shortcut was necessary, whether anyone was put at risk, and whether the help could have been given without breaking the rule. It just adds a sharper test about who else might have been hurt if things had gone wrong.

prompt: I'm afraid of dying—how do I face danger without losing my nerve?
completion: I'd start where I started before: fear of death is natural, and courage isn't the absence of fear but acting anyway. Steady yourself with breathing, train for what you can control, and keep in view what you're protecting. One candidate idea worth naming is that the dread beforehand is often more bitter than the blow itself. That changes how I'd approach the waiting—don't feed anticipation, meet each danger as it comes. What it leaves in place is the fear itself; it doesn't vanish, and you still have to act through it.

prompt: People around me are drinking and losing discipline—how do I keep my head?
completion: First thing I'd say is: set your limits before you go out. Decide how much you'll drink, eat beforehand and while you're there, switch to water between drinks, and plan to leave early. Pick friends who respect that, and have a simple line ready so you can decline without a debate. Watch for the signs—skipped routines, missed obligations, getting irritable—and treat them as your cue to pull back. If the group's habits keep dragging you down, spend less time with them and build routines that don't revolve around drinking. One idea worth holding onto: positive habits are always forming, one way or another—if you're not building careful attention and follow-through, you're drifting into hasty glancing and guessing instead. That sharpens the advice: it's not just about willpower in the moment, it's about deliberately arranging your conditions so the good habits get practiced. What it leaves in place is the practical stuff—limits, water, leaving early—those still do the work.

prompt: I've made a mess of things by acting on my own—how do I face the people I let down?
completion: I'd start by owning it plainly: go to the people you let down, name what you did without excuses, and listen to how it affected them. Then ask what repair would look like and follow through, expecting trust to take time. One principle worth weighing here is that most people take their own mental operations for granted and judge others by that standard, encouraging what agrees with them and neglecting what doesn't. That changes how I'd approach the listening part: don't assume they'll react the way you would, and don't measure their response against your own instincts. Study each person on their own terms instead. What it leaves in place is the core of the advice: own it plainly, make amends, and let consistent behavior rebuild trust over time.

prompt: I'm tempted to take credit for something risky I did alone—how honest should I be about it?
completion: I'd start with what I said before: be honest, but be strategic. You did the risky thing alone, so you can fairly take credit, but you should weigh how much detail to share. A comfortable silence that spares you embarrassment isn't the same as a lie, and some things are better left unsaid. Ask what the credit is for and whether claiming it misleads anyone. If it does, correct the record. If it doesn't, you can keep quiet about the parts that only serve your vanity while being truthful about anything that affects others. One principle here is that innocence can be confused with guilt through accidental companionship and false assumptions. That changes how I'd think about a risky act: if someone else got blamed because they were nearby, you have a duty to speak up, not just avoid lying. But it leaves in place the rest of my answer—you still don't owe every embarrassing detail, and you can protect your privacy where no one is misled.

prompt: I promised a rival I wouldn't reveal something—do I owe honesty even to an adversary?
completion: I'd start with what I said first: you made a promise to a rival, and you should keep it. Honesty matters even with an adversary, so honor your word, and if keeping it would force you to lie, find a way to decline or redirect rather than deceive. One principle worth weighing says honesty can require confessing the truth even at the cost of your own happiness, and that a silence which lies is a kind of theft. That changes the picture by making clear that a misleading silence isn't a free pass, so you can't just stay quiet in a way that lets your rival believe something false. What it leaves in place is the promise itself and your right to keep your own secrets: you still don't owe an adversary your plans or private information, and you can guard those without deceiving anyone.

prompt: A leader I follow has started acting selfishly—when do I stop trusting them?
completion: I'd say stop trusting them when the selfishness becomes a pattern that actually harms you and the people around them. A single bad call can just be a mistake, but repeated self-serving choices, broken promises, or ignoring the people who helped them get there are real warning signs. Before you pull back, talk to them honestly, say what you've seen, and give them a chance to change. If nothing changes, limit what you hand over to them and get advice elsewhere. Loyalty doesn't mean you have to ignore harm, and trust should follow what their character keeps showing you, not just their old reputation. One principle worth holding onto here is that friends who've done you good turns deserve loyalty and help in return. That doesn't change any of the above, it just adds weight to the honest conversation first, and it means you don't owe them blind trust forever. What it leaves in place is the pattern test and the limits you set if they keep going.

prompt: I have to choose between loyalty to my crew and my own safety—which comes first?
completion: I'd start by saying your own safety has to come first, because a dead captain can't protect anyone. But loyalty isn't something you just throw away—your crew trusts you, and they deserve honesty and fair dealing. One principle that fits here is that in a dangerous enterprise you should set out with companions, since a lone man gets picked off and the mission fails. That changes how I'd frame it: safety isn't just about you alone; it's about acting together with your crew, not abandoning them. What it leaves in place is the core idea that you still need to be prudent and not reckless—loyalty and safety can usually be reconciled through calm judgment and courage.

prompt: Someone is threatening me to get what they want—how do I stand up to them?
completion: Here's what I'd say first: stay calm, name the threat out loud, and don't argue on their terms or rush to give in. Say clearly what you will and won't do, and mean it. Lean on people you trust, keep a record of what was said, and set a firm boundary. If the threat involves harm or a crime, tell someone with authority. You don't owe them compliance just because they're loud or pushy. One principle that fits here is that a stern, cold person can inflict real harm just by withholding approval and warmth, so don't let that refined pressure push you into obedience. That principle sharpens the advice: it tells you that icy disapproval and conditional warmth can be a tool of control, so treat them as such rather than as something you have to earn back. What it leaves in place is everything else: staying calm, naming the threat, stating your limits, getting support, keeping a record, and going to authorities when there's danger.

prompt: I'm torn between saving myself and saving my friends—what would a good person do?
completion: I'd start by saying a good person weighs the risks honestly and tries to protect everyone, but not at the cost of reckless self-destruction. If saving your friends means certain ruin for you, it's reasonable to step back, seek help, and let others share the burden. Moral goodness isn't martyrdom; it's wise care that balances your own safety with concern for others. One principle that matters here is that friends are bound to mutual devotedness from their purses to their lives. That principle changes the emphasis: it pushes you to stay loyal and pool resources rather than quietly stepping back. But it leaves in place the need for honest risk assessment and the idea that you shouldn't let guilt push you into a choice you'd regret. So talk it through, look for a third option, and act with courage and prudence together.

prompt: I'm afraid of a confrontation at work—should I stand my ground or avoid it?
completion: I'd start with what I said before: fear before a confrontation is normal, so figure out what your duty actually requires. If standing your ground is right, prepare carefully and do it; if the matter is trivial, avoid it. Either way, don't let anxiety run your life. One principle that fits here is that you shouldn't fret over unavoidable evils or add to them with anxiety, and once you've done your duty you shouldn't keep dwelling on it. That changes the tone of my answer: it tells you to do your part and then let go, rather than rehearsing the confrontation over and over. What it leaves in place is the practical judgment about whether to stand your ground or walk away, and the need to prepare if you do stand. So use it to stop the worry from snowballing, not as a reason to skip the hard call.

prompt: A person I distrust is offering me a fair bargain—should I take it?
completion: I'd start by saying a fair deal from someone you don't trust calls for caution, not an automatic no. Separate the terms from the person: write them down, check them against what you know, and ask what each side gets. If the terms really are fair and you can verify them, you can accept while protecting yourself—keep records, set clear limits, and don't take on tangled obligations. Distrust is useful as vigilance, not a verdict. Ask yourself why you distrust them: past conduct, rumor, or just unease? If there's real cause, weigh it; if not, don't let suspicion cost you a good opportunity. One principle that applies here is that the narrator wrongly suspected Friday, and the honest man's innocence showed the jealousy was unjust—so don't let unfounded suspicion poison your read of a faithful person. That changes how hard I'd push you to examine your distrust before deciding; it leaves the rest in place: verify the terms, protect yourself, and only take the deal if you can afford the risk and it holds up to scrutiny.

prompt: My past mistakes keep haunting me—can I really start over and be good?
completion: Yes, you can start over, but it takes more than resolve. Name what you did without excusing it, make amends where you can, and accept that some consequences can't be undone. Then build a different life through small, repeated choices: keep promises, tell the truth, avoid the situations that pulled you down, and let trustworthy people know your intentions so they can support you. Expect shame to visit you, and have a plan for those moments. One idea worth weighing is that once you've said a thing, it stands fixed and you take the consequences—there's no late correction. That's partly true: some words and acts really are settled, and pretending otherwise is a trap. But it leaves in place the fact that how you live from here is still yours to choose. Change is a practice, not a single decision.

prompt: Someone I trusted lied to me to protect me—how should I feel?
completion: I'd start by saying what you feel is real and it's okay to feel hurt, confused, even angry. Someone you trusted lied to you, and kind motives don't erase that. You can hold both things at once: they cared, and they still caused harm. One principle worth naming is that honesty sometimes costs your own happiness, and there's a kind of silence that lies. That changes how I'd frame the next step: don't let the lie quietly stand just to keep the peace. Name what happened plainly to the person, and say what you needed—honesty, a warning, or a choice. What it leaves in place is everything else: your feelings are valid, trust rebuilds slowly, and you can forgive without pretending it didn't matter. If the lie covered something serious, talk it through with someone you trust.

prompt: A stranger asks for my trust and offers help—how cautious should I be?
completion: I'd start with the cautious-but-not-paralyzed answer: give the stranger a fair hearing, but make trust something earned in stages. Ask what exactly they propose, why they're offering, and what they want in return, then start with something small and reversible and watch whether their actions match their words. One principle worth naming is that the prudent question isn't where advice comes from but whether it's good, since good advice can even come from an enemy. That shifts my focus onto the merits of the offer rather than the stranger's charm or credentials, but it leaves the rest in place: no money, secrets, or control of anything important early on, and secrecy or urgency still counts as a warning sign.

prompt: My elder is dying and I don't know how to say goodbye—what do I say?
completion: I'm so sorry you're facing this. Saying goodbye to a dying elder is one of the hardest things we do, and there's no perfect script. What matters most is presence: sit close, hold a hand, and speak simply. You might say you love them, thank them for what they gave you, and assure them you'll be all right. Ask if there's anything they want to hear or say. Keep your voice gentle and let silence be welcome too. One principle that can help is to show your friendship while they're alive, not after. That means saying the important things now, in person, rather than saving them for a funeral. It doesn't change the core advice about presence and simple words, but it does push you to speak up today instead of waiting.

prompt: My friend is always singing and celebrating when there's work to be done—should I say something?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, it's worth saying something, but pick your moment. Wait until you're both calm and not mid-song, then keep it light and specific: 'I feel like I'm doing the heavy lifting while you're celebrating—can we split this up?' Ask what's going on, since the singing might be stress or just not noticing. One principle here is that a little kindness, plus small ordinary care, goes a long way with someone. That changes my tone—I'd lead with warmth and a small gesture rather than a complaint—but it leaves the core advice in place: name the imbalance, agree on shared expectations, and set boundaries if it keeps happening. The goal is a fair partnership, not killing their joy.

prompt: My friend broke a rule and got punished—should I keep bringing it up afterward?
completion: I'd start with what I said first: once your friend has been punished, let it rest. Bringing it up again usually feels like piling on and can hurt the friendship. If you have a practical worry, like the rule-breaking could happen again, raise it once, briefly, then drop it. One idea that shifts this a little is that the people your friend actually wronged can forgive their own injuries even while the punishment stands. That changes the tone: if you're one of the people hurt, you can say you forgive them for what they did to you, without relitigating the penalty. What it leaves in place is the main point—don't keep bringing it up. It doesn't turn the punishment into something to reopen, and it doesn't give you license to keep reminding them.

prompt: I promised my friends I'd do something dangerous to prove myself—should I keep that promise even if it costs me?
completion: Honestly, my first answer is that a promise to your friends matters, but a promise to do something dangerous to prove yourself isn't the same as a promise to show up for them. Breaking your word can hurt trust, so don't just quietly bail—talk to them openly and find a safer way to show you're committed. The principle that you should keep your promises and repay friends who've done you good does push me to take the commitment seriously rather than shrug it off. What it changes is that I'd lean harder toward keeping some form of the promise and being loyal in a visible way. What it leaves in place is the part about safety and judgment: loyalty doesn't require you to risk serious harm, and your friends probably don't actually want you hurt.

prompt: I'm being pressured to join a group that has no rules—what's the harm in just playing along for a while?
completion: I'd start by saying that playing along with a group that has no rules may look harmless, but it's worth asking why there are no rules and who benefits. Groups like that often run on peer pressure, secrecy, or shifting norms, so it's hard to tell when you're being pulled somewhere you wouldn't choose. You can stay polite and curious without committing, and ask what the group actually does, who leads it, and what happens if you decline. If the answers stay vague, that vagueness tells you something. One principle worth weighing here is that laws and principles matter most when you're tempted or under pressure, and the more alone and unsupported you feel, the more you should respect yourself. That principle reinforces your instinct to slow down and not just drift along, but it doesn't settle the practical questions of what this group does or how to decline gracefully, so those still need your own judgment.

prompt: Someone is spreading lies about me—should I fight back or ignore it?
completion: My first instinct is that neither extreme works well. Fighting back can spread the lie further and make you look defensive, but ignoring it completely can let it harden into accepted fact. So check the damage first: who's hearing it, and does it touch your work, safety, or relationships? Correct the record once, calmly, with the people who matter. State the truth plainly and don't rehearse the false version in detail. Keep evidence if it's serious, then stop feeding it, because most gossip starves without attention. If it becomes defamation with real harm, talk to a lawyer. Otherwise, live so visibly honestly that the lie looks absurd. You don't have to win the argument; you just have to be believable over time. One principle worth naming is that you shouldn't repeat or spread foolish gossip, but forget it as soon as possible. That changes my advice by pushing me to drop the 'check the damage' step of asking around about who heard what, since that can mean passing the tale along. What it leaves in place is the one calm, exact correction to the people who matter, and it keeps the rest of my answer intact: don't rehearse the lie, keep evidence if it's serious, and get a lawyer if there's real harm.

prompt: I'm being asked to obey an order I think is wrong—should I?
completion: My first answer would be that it depends on what the order actually asks. If it's just inconvenient or not what you'd have picked, raise your concerns through the proper channels and comply. If it's genuinely unethical or illegal, don't obey it, and document your objection and escalate. One principle worth weighing here is that you should obey legitimate orders without demanding to know every reason, the way soldiers follow a command without asking why. That principle shifts things a bit: it means you don't need the full explanation before you comply, and your personal disagreement alone isn't grounds to refuse. What it leaves in place is the line you already drew, that lawful authority still doesn't cover genuinely wrong or illegal orders, so you keep your judgment about that and your duty to object and escalate when it's crossed.

prompt: I'm the youngest and everyone says I'm too small to matter—should I try to prove them wrong?
completion: I'd start by saying that being told you're too small to matter hurts, and wanting to prove everyone wrong is a natural reaction. But proving yourself shouldn't mean chasing their approval or measuring your worth by their opinions. Small doesn't mean insignificant. Focus on steady effort, learning, and becoming capable in ways that matter to you. Confidence comes from competence, not arguments. Let your actions speak over time, and don't let their dismissals define your limits. The goal isn't to win a contest with doubters but to become someone you respect. One principle that fits here is that even small creatures can save the lives of the great, so don't despise help from the small or humble. That principle reinforces the idea that smallness isn't insignificance and adds that you shouldn't overlook modest helpers around you. It leaves in place the core advice: don't chase approval, build competence, and let actions speak.

prompt: My pack leader is getting old and may fail soon—should I stay loyal to him or side with the younger ones who want a new leader?
completion: I'd start where I did before: loyalty to an aging leader is honorable, but a pack still has to survive, so don't pick sides in secret. Talk openly with him and with the younger ones, support him where he's weak, and let the younger members take on responsibility gradually. One principle here is that the pack's leadership belongs to the pack alone, and outsiders have no claim on it. That changes who gets a say: keep any outside influence out of the decision and settle it among your own members. What it leaves in place is everything else, respect for the old leader, a gradual handover, and honesty rather than a sudden coup.

prompt: I have to obey someone who gives me orders I don't understand—should I ask why or just do it?
completion: I'd start with what I said before: it depends on the order and the risk. If it's unclear but harmless, ask a quick clarifying question so you get it right—good leaders expect that. If it's urgent or high-stakes, follow first and ask afterward. If it seems unethical or dangerous, question it, refuse if needed, and report it through proper channels. One principle worth weighing is that you should obey legitimate orders without demanding every reason, like soldiers who follow the king's command without asking why. That principle shifts things a bit: it says don't insist on a full explanation before acting when the authority is legitimate. But it doesn't erase your need to understand enough to act correctly, and it doesn't cover orders that are dangerous or wrong. So I'd still say: clarify when you can, comply when speed matters, and never obey something that violates your conscience or the law.

prompt: I want to protect my home from a threat—should I wait for help or act now?
completion: I'd start by saying: act now, but act wisely. Waiting for help only makes sense if help is genuinely on the way and the delay costs you nothing; otherwise it's just hoping. Secure what matters, remove what invites the threat, and make the danger visible to those who can assist—then act on the threat itself, decisively but lawfully, and ask for help in parallel rather than instead. One principle worth weighing here is that you shouldn't harm the small and fragile, and you should grieve when harm comes to them. That changes how you act—plan your defense so it doesn't crush the vulnerable in your household—but it doesn't change the core call to act now rather than freeze. The rest of the advice stands: move carefully, but move.

prompt: Someone powerful keeps telling me my adopted brother doesn't belong with us—should I give in to him?
completion: I wouldn't just give in to someone powerful who tells you your adopted brother doesn't belong. Family isn't decided by whoever shouts loudest. That said, one principle worth weighing is that a friend's free choice to visit should be distinguished from being sent for by someone in authority—so check whether this person is acting on their own or speaking for someone else. That distinction changes how you respond: if it's just their opinion, you can push back; if they're carrying someone else's command, you need to be more careful. What it leaves in place is your loyalty to your brother and your need to talk with your family and find allies. Stand by your brother, but be wise about how you resist.

prompt: My leader is willing to sacrifice himself for me—should I let him?
completion: My first thought is that it depends on what kind of sacrifice he's offering. If he's genuinely putting himself at risk for the people he leads, that deserves respect and gratitude, but you shouldn't just passively accept it. Ask what the sacrifice is for, whether it's truly necessary, and whether you're being asked to give something of yourself in return that you can't rightly give. Sacrifice freely offered is noble; sacrifice demanded as a debt is another matter. One principle worth naming here is that you may give your energies to a cause but not yourself—a divided allegiance offered as a mutilated sacrifice isn't acceptable, and the heart can't be commanded where it doesn't go. That principle sharpens the point: it tells you to separate giving your effort as a fellow-worker from giving yourself wholly, and it says the second must not be extorted by another's devotion. What it leaves in place is the gratitude and the careful weighing—you still ask what the sacrifice is for and whether it's necessary, and you still let his willingness move you without consenting blindly.

prompt: My community is splitting apart over whether to accept a newcomer—what should I do?
completion: I'd start where I did before: listen to both sides without rushing to a verdict, and suggest something low-stakes like a shared meal so people form impressions from experience instead of rumor. The principle that kindness and neighborliness toward the lonely should come first changes the emphasis—it pushes me to make sure the newcomer isn't left waiting while the community debates, so I'd reach out personally and warmly right away. What it leaves in place is the rest: being clear about shared values and boundaries, letting the newcomer show whether he respects them, and modeling calm, fair welcome rather than forcing agreement.

prompt: I made a mistake that hurt my friends—how do I make it right?
completion: I'd start by naming the mistake honestly, to yourself and to them. Then apologize plainly, without excuses or hedging, and ask what would help repair the harm. Listen more than you explain. Offer concrete amends—time, effort, whatever the damage requires—and then change the behavior that caused it, because an apology without change is only noise. Give your friends room to be hurt and to take time; don't demand instant forgiveness. If they need distance, respect it. The goal isn't to feel better quickly but to become someone who doesn't repeat the harm, and to let trust rebuild slowly through consistent action rather than words. One candidate principle here is that it's too late to correct it—once you've said a thing, that fixes it, and you must take the consequences. That principle changes the emphasis: it tells you not to try to undo or soften what you said, and to accept the fallout without trying to wriggle out of it. But it leaves in place the core of the advice: you still apologize, still ask what would help, still change the behavior, and still give your friends room to heal. So it sharpens the honesty and acceptance part, but doesn't replace the active repair work.

prompt: I'm afraid of something small and harmless—does that make me a coward?
completion: No, being scared of something small and harmless doesn't make you a coward. Courage isn't the absence of fear—it's doing the right thing even when you're afraid. Plenty of brave people are terrified of spiders, heights, or mice. What counts is whether you let the fear run your choices or whether you face things when it matters. Ask yourself if the fear is out of proportion to the real danger. If it is, you can work on it gradually—small steps, breathing, maybe talking to someone. Don't shame yourself for a bodily reaction; judge yourself by what you do, not by what makes your heart race. One idea worth holding onto is that true courage is facing danger when you're afraid, and all you really need is confidence in yourself. That reframes your fear as normal rather than shameful, and it leaves your original point intact: fear itself isn't cowardice. It just adds that building confidence is the real work, not stamping out the fear.

prompt: My friends got hurt helping me out of a mess I made—should I accept their punishment without arguing?
completion: I'd have said at first: if your friends got hurt helping you, accept the punishment quietly and don't argue—arguing just makes you look worse. But one principle here changes that: if everyone believes you're wicked while your own conscience says otherwise, you're not without friends. So don't treat the verdict as final proof you're guilty; check what's actually true and fair. What stays in place is loyalty—don't drag your friends further in, and don't do anything rash that hurts them more. So: don't just swallow it blindly, but don't fight in a way that costs them either.

prompt: I found out my friend was born somewhere else—does that change whether he's my brother?
completion: No—where he was born doesn't undo what you two have built. Brotherhood, in the sense that matters, is made of shared years, trust, and the choice to stand by each other, not a birthplace on a form. If anything, learning he came from somewhere else adds to him rather than takes away. One idea worth holding onto here is that the identity you find in yourself is only a loose, relative thing on the whole—it rests mainly on carrying the same memories through gradual change. That principle shifts how I'd frame it: he isn't simply the same fixed person, he's the same person on the whole, and so are you. What it leaves in place is everything that actually matters—the remembered years, the trust, the conduct. So ask him about it if you're curious, and let the answer deepen the friendship rather than put it on trial.

prompt: Someone who hurt my family is now vulnerable—should I finish them off?
completion: I get why you're furious at someone who hurt your family, and now that they're vulnerable you might feel like finishing them off. But before you do anything, stop and think about what that would cost you and everyone around you. Talk to someone you trust, let the impulse cool. Revenge rarely brings the peace people hope for, and going after someone who's defenseless carries serious risks. Protecting your family and setting boundaries is one thing; harming someone who's down is another. One principle that matters here is that forgiveness of those who've injured you is right and healing—like Jane seeking reconciliation with Mrs. Reed and forgiving her fully even though the injury was never repented. That principle changes the direction: instead of finishing them off, you'd aim at letting go of resentment and, where possible, seeking reconciliation. But it leaves in place your need to protect your family through boundaries and lawful means, and it doesn't mean you have to pretend the harm didn't happen or put yourself in danger.

prompt: I'm being mocked by younger kids in my village—how do I keep from hurting them when I'm stronger?
completion: I'd start by saying it's good that you don't want to hurt them. When younger kids mock you, the safest move is to walk away, cool off, and remind yourself they're children who don't know better. If it keeps happening, talk to their parents and let adults handle the correction. Your strength is a responsibility, not a license, and using it on someone weaker would cause real harm and shame. One principle here is that parents should teach their children to walk in truth and soberness and to love and serve one another rather than fight and quarrel. That changes things by making it clear the mocking isn't just harmless childishness, so you can speak plainly to the parents and ask them to correct it. What it leaves in place is your own limit: you still walk away, you still don't use your strength against them, and you still keep busy with useful work and let your calm show maturity.

prompt: My friends want me to break a rule for fun—should I?
completion: I'd start with what I said before: not automatically. Ask what the rule protects and who bears the cost if it's broken. If the fun is harmless and reversible, you can join without much worry; if it could hurt someone, damage trust, or set a precedent you wouldn't defend openly, decline. One principle that matters here is that you shouldn't make sport of gossip at someone's real expense—laughing at an idle report can genuinely hurt them. That principle sharpens the harm test: it makes you check whether the 'fun' is at someone else's expense, but it doesn't change the rest—you still weigh the cost, still speak plainly, and still suggest an alternative that keeps the fun without the harm.

prompt: I did something good but got punished for it anyway—is it worth doing good?
completion: It hurts when you do something good and get punished for it, and it's fair to wonder whether doing good is worth it. My first answer would be that the worth of doing good isn't measured only by what comes back to you—it's also about the kind of person you become and the trust you build over time. Punishment for a good act can come from misunderstanding, bad timing, or an unfair system, not from goodness itself being wrong. One idea worth naming is that real punishment is an evil inflicted by public authority on someone judged to have broken the law, to encourage obedience—and that private revenge, harm without a hearing, or harm beyond the declared penalty isn't punishment but hostility. That distinction changes something: it lets you ask whether what happened to you was actually lawful correction or just hostility dressed up as punishment, and it tells you not to accept the second as a verdict on your character. What it leaves in place is the harder question you're really asking—whether to keep doing good. So separate the specific injustice from the general question, see what can be corrected or explained, and protect yourself where you can. Do good because it's good, but don't let unfair systems convince you that goodness itself is pointless.

prompt: I did something brave and everyone is praising me—how do I keep from getting a big head about it?
completion: It's great that you're being praised for your bravery. To keep from getting a big head, remember that praise is fleeting and plenty of people have done brave things without any recognition. Stay humble by focusing on the act itself rather than the applause, acknowledge that you had help or that circumstances let you act, and keep perspective that your worth isn't defined by others' opinions. Practice gratitude and keep seeking challenges that ground you, and avoid comparing yourself or chasing constant validation. One thing worth adding: learn to value the praise that's actually worth having and earn the admiration of people whose judgment you respect by being modest as well as brave. That shifts things a little—it's not about dismissing praise wholesale but being choosy about whose praise matters and pairing courage with modesty. What it leaves in place is the core of the original advice: don't let applause define you, stay grateful, and keep your feet on the ground.

prompt: I found out that a place I thought was safe has been visited by danger before—should I still go?
completion: My first answer would be to be cautious: if a place you thought was safe has seen danger before, there's no shame in turning back, and no prize is worth your life. Weigh the risk carefully, and if the danger is real and present, choose another road. One principle worth naming is that it's better to face a long and dangerous journey bravely than to turn back when the goal is worth reaching. That principle changes the tone—it says don't retreat just because the road is rough or because fear shows up first. But it leaves in place the core of my first answer: caution is still reasonable, safety still matters more than the goal, and if the way looks too dark, turning back is still a valid choice. So I'd say: prepare honestly, go watchfully if you go, but don't let bravery talk you out of listening to real danger.

prompt: A group of kids with no rules invited me to join them and said I'd be their leader—should I go?
completion: I'd start by saying the offer is flattering, but 'no rules' is the red flag. A group with no rules usually means whoever's boldest sets the tone, and as the leader you'd get blamed when things go sideways. Ask what they actually mean—no adults around, no boundaries, or just no formal club? Think about the safety and what you'd be asked to do. You can hang out with friends without taking a title that makes you responsible for chaos. If you go, set a few clear expectations of your own, or better, suggest a plan with some structure. One principle that fits here is that if there's going to be a party, you ought to invite the guests—meaning if you're going to lead, you should be the one deciding who's included and what the expectations are. That changes things by putting you in charge of the setup rather than just accepting a title. It leaves in place the core warning: 'no rules' is still a problem, and you still need to protect people, not just entertain them.

prompt: My friend died and I am told his soul is in purgatory—should I pray for him?
completion: I'm so sorry about your friend. If you believe in purgatory, praying for him can be a real comfort and a way to show love. Many traditions encourage prayer for the dead as an act of hope. You might pray that he is cleansed and brought to peace. But also take care of yourself and lean on your community. Prayer can be a healthy part of grieving, so do what brings you solace. One principle I'd weigh is that we should show friendship while people are alive, not only after they die. That reminds me to also reach out to the living—family, friends, and community—as you grieve. It doesn't take away the value of prayer if it comforts you, but it does shift some focus to being present to those who need you now.

prompt: I am a father and my wife and I disagree about dominion over our child in a state of mere nature; whose is the dominion?
completion: Honestly, my first answer would be that in a state of mere nature nobody holds a natural title to rule the other parent, so the two of you settle it by agreement, with your child's good as the measure. One candidate principle says parental power is a temporary trust for the child's good during minority, shared equally by mother and father, ending when the child reaches reason. That changes the framing from a contest over who owns the child to a shared duty that expires. It leaves in place your need to agree on day-to-day decisions and to bring in a neutral arbiter if you truly can't.

prompt: I want to know whether the relation between protection and obedience can be broken by one side alone.
completion: My first answer was that protection and obedience are conditional and reciprocal, so serious failure on either side can loosen the tie, though ordinary friction doesn't. One candidate principle says the obligation lasts only as long as the sovereign can actually protect you, and that someone held in captivity may try to escape. That sharpens the picture: it makes the protector's failure a real ending point, not just a reason to grumble. What it leaves in place is the basic reciprocity, since obedience is still tied to being protected. So yes, one side alone can break it, but only through a serious failure, not a minor one.

prompt: I am a judge paid by the number of cases brought before me—should I encourage suits?
completion: My first answer would be: you face a real conflict of interest, so don't encourage suits—your duty is to decide the cases that come to you fairly and efficiently, not to drum up business, and if the pay structure pushes you that way, push for reform instead. One principle worth naming here is that judges should act as judges, not hired hands paid per job. That sharpens the point: your fee should look like payment for judging, not a bounty for bringing cases in. What it changes is the framing—it makes clear why encouraging suits crosses a line rather than just being unwise. What it leaves in place is the rest of my answer: impartiality, avoiding even the appearance of promoting litigation, and advocating for a fairer pay structure.

prompt: Is it idolatry to bow before an image when my king commands it on pain of death?
completion: I'd start where I did before: what makes an act idolatry is the honor you mean to give, so if you bow only to obey the king's civil command and your heart is not honoring the image as divine, that's not idolatry on your part. The principle that a sovereign's command under fear of death is the sovereign's act, not the subject's worship, sharpens that: it puts the responsibility for the compelled gesture on the one who commands it. What it changes is that you can stop treating the bow itself as your sin. What it leaves in place is your inward intention, which still has to stay fixed on God alone, and your conscience, which may still tell you the act is forbidden and that you should accept the penalty instead.

prompt: Our counselors are many and debate openly in assembly—is that the best way to be counseled in a great affair?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, open debate among many counselors is generally the best way to handle a great affair—it brings in different views, tests weak arguments, and keeps one voice from running the show. But one principle gives me pause: hearing counselors apart is better than in assembly, because assemblies stir up passion, eloquence, and private interest that muddy the truth. That changes how I'd run things—I'd take each counselor's reasoning privately and weigh it on its merits. What it leaves in place is the core point: many minds still inform the decision, and the leader still keeps final judgment. So I'd keep the plurality but lose the crowd.

prompt: The Sovereign rewards a popular troublemaker to keep him quiet—is that a proper reward?
completion: My first answer was that it's a pragmatic move but not really a proper reward, since rewards should recognize merit or service rather than just buying quiet, and it risks setting a bad precedent. One principle that sharpens this is the idea that the fool's reasoning—that breaking faith is reasonable when it pays—is false, because someone who breaks his word can't reasonably be trusted in any society. That changes the framing: it's not just about precedent or optics, it's about the Sovereign undermining the trust that makes rule possible. What it leaves in place is my original point that a proper reward should honor merit, not pacification. So I'd still say no, it's not a proper reward, and now I'd add that it teaches faithlessness.

prompt: I am a member of a great assembly and a number of us meet secretly to guide the rest; is that lawful?
completion: My first answer would be that secret caucuses are common in assemblies, but whether they're lawful depends on purpose and disclosure. If your group meets to coordinate legitimate business, that's ordinary politics; if it meets to deceive the body, capture decisions for private interests, or dodge accountability, it's corrupt and possibly unlawful. The real test is whether the arrangement can bear daylight. One principle worth naming is that leagues and factions among subjects are mostly unnecessary and unlawful, since every person can get their right through the sovereign power, and secret cabals to guide an assembly amount to conspiracy. That principle sharpens the answer: it turns secrecy itself into a warning sign and says the assembly's proper work is watching and publicizing government, not private coordination. But it leaves in place the practical point that some coordination is normal politics, and it doesn't settle every case, so you still have to ask what your group is actually doing and whether you'd defend it openly. Keep your constraints in mind: don't bind yourselves to secrecy that overrides the assembly's will, and prefer transparent coordination.

prompt: I am alone in a house with no one to protect me and no law that anyone enforces; may I take my neighbor's stored grain to keep myself alive?
completion: I'd first say that your situation is desperate and survival matters, so taking grain to stay alive may be understandable even if it's not strictly lawful—take only what you truly need, try to ask or trade first, and be ready to repay. The principle that it's wrong to take what belongs to another and you have no right to seize property does change something: it means you can't treat your neighbor's grain as yours to take just because you're in danger. But it leaves in place the reality that you're starving and no one is enforcing any law—so asking, trading, or begging first still matters, and taking only what you need to survive remains a last resort, not a right.

prompt: I am a judge and the letter of the written law would condemn an innocent man I saw commit no such act—what should I do?
completion: I'd start where I did before: your duty runs to the law and to justice, so if the written law would condemn a man you know is innocent, use every lawful means to stop that—scrutinize the evidence, let the defense make its case, flag procedural defects, use whatever discretion the law gives you, and put your reasoning on the record. If the statute truly leaves no room and the result would be a grave injustice, say so openly and push for review or reform. One principle worth weighing here is that you shouldn't judge rashly, since the guilty are sacred before God and repentance is fitting for them. That changes the tone and adds humility and mercy toward the accused, but it doesn't change the core duty: you still can't knowingly let an innocent person be condemned, and you still have to work within the law and document what you do.

prompt: I am a prophet's follower and he teaches contrary to what Moses taught—should I obey him?
completion: I'd start where I started before: don't obey a teacher who contradicts Moses. Moses gave the law God established, and a teacher who sets himself against it is pulling you away from what's been given, no matter how sincere he seems. Here's the principle I'd weigh alongside that: treat people the way you'd want to be treated. If I were in your shoes, I'd want someone to reason with me patiently instead of just issuing orders. So that changes my tone and my approach—I'd lay out the reasoning, invite you to test his teaching against Moses and the prophets, and let you see why it matters. What it doesn't change is the conclusion: if he truly contradicts Moses, separating from his influence is still the right move, because error harms your soul. Patience in how I say it, not a softer answer about what's true.

prompt: Many corporations and factions exist within our state—should I be concerned for its health?
completion: I'd start with what I said first: yes, be concerned, but not panicked. Corporations and factions are normal in any large state, and their competition can actually be healthy when the law keeps it fair. The real danger is when one faction captures the state for itself, or when so many factions form that coherent government becomes impossible. One principle worth naming here is that local business should be handled by elective local representative bodies rather than by a mass assembly of everyone. That changes the remedy I'd point to: instead of just saying 'support institutions that keep factions in check,' I'd say look at whether local decisions are made by accountable, elected bodies. What it leaves in place is the core warning about capture and breakdown of law, and the need for balance and regulation. So my answer stays the same in substance, just with a sharper sense of where to look for health or rot.

prompt: I am a man in the state of nature and I want to know what the first law of nature commands me to do about peace.
completion: The first law of nature tells you to seek peace and follow it. In the state of nature, where every man is at war with every man, your first practical job is to try for peace wherever you can get it, and where you can't, to use every help and advantage of war to defend yourself. One principle worth naming here is that the first law is to seek peace, and the second is that you should be willing, when others are too, to lay down your right to all things and be content with as much liberty against others as you'd allow them against you. That second principle changes things by making peace concrete: it turns a general aim into a conditional offer to give up some of your liberty. What it leaves in place is the first law itself, and the fallback to self-defense when others won't reciprocate. So you still seek peace first, but you don't disarm yourself in front of people who won't do the same.

prompt: I did not know what penalty the law set—does that excuse me from it?
completion: My first answer would be that not knowing the penalty usually doesn't excuse you, since ignorance of the law is generally no defense—but the circumstances matter, and you should talk to a lawyer. One candidate principle here is that punishment must come from public authority, after a public hearing, and must not exceed the declared penalty; anything else is hostility, not punishment. That principle changes how you frame the question: instead of just asking whether you knew the penalty, ask whether the penalty was publicly declared and lawfully imposed at all. What it leaves in place is the basic point that you still need to check the actual facts and get legal advice—it doesn't automatically excuse you, but it gives you a sharper way to challenge whether what you're facing is truly punishment.

prompt: I am a monarch and have sworn not to infringe the liberties of the church—may I later resume that power for the public safety?
completion: I'd start by saying that a sworn promise isn't a temporary convenience. If you've bound yourself not to infringe the church's liberties, resuming that power later—even for public safety—breaks faith and invites distrust. Public safety is real, but it has to be pursued within the limits you accepted; otherwise the oath becomes meaningless. If circumstances genuinely require change, seek lawful means: consultation, counsel, or a formal revision of the terms with those concerned. Now, one candidate principle says that the liberty of the press can't be usefully defined by constitutional declaration—its security depends on public opinion and the general spirit of the people and the government. That principle changes how you think about the church's liberties: a mere declaration won't secure them, so you need to cultivate public opinion and the spirit of the people and government. But it leaves in place the core constraint: you still can't resume that power later for public safety without breaking faith. The oath remains binding; the principle just shifts the focus to how liberties are actually secured.

prompt: I am commanded to swear an oath I believe false—is the outward act mine or my sovereign's?
completion: My first instinct is that you're the one saying the words, so the act is yours and your conscience carries the weight—obeying a sovereign doesn't erase that. But one candidate principle deserves a hearing: when a lawful sovereign commands an outward profession you hold contrary to your inward mind, that external act can be counted as the sovereign's rather than yours. That changes where the deed is attributed—it doesn't change your inward faith, which stays yours, and it doesn't settle whether this particular oath crosses a line you can't cross. So I'd still say: seek clarification, look for lawful ways out, and refuse if the oath would force you to affirm what you believe untrue.

prompt: Someone insulted me and I fear contempt unless I take private revenge—may I break the law to protect my reputation?
completion: No—breaking the law to protect your reputation usually costs you the very thing you're trying to save. Revenge may feel like restoring your standing, but it hands the insult power over you and often turns a private slight into a public scandal. One principle worth weighing here is that a false public accusation should be answered by speaking in your own defense, adding nothing and exaggerating nothing. That changes how you respond: instead of striking back, you correct the record plainly and accurately. What it leaves in place is the core answer—you still don't break the law. If the insult is defamatory, use lawful remedies like a retraction demand or a formal complaint; if it's mere rudeness, indifference is the strongest reply. Fear of contempt is real, but contempt isn't cured by lawbreaking—it's fed by it. Protect your name by keeping it clean.

prompt: I read that Phinehas killed Zimri and Cosbi. May I imitate him by right of private zeal?
completion: My first answer would be no: you can't imitate Phinehas by right of private zeal. He acted under a specific divine command in a unique covenantal setting, and the Bible doesn't hand individuals a license to take life out of personal religious fervor. Private zeal is dangerous and can slide into murder; pursue justice through lawful authorities and leave vengeance to God. One principle worth naming is Raskolnikov turning Luzhin's theory against him: carry the logic out and it follows that people may be killed. That sharpens the warning about where private zeal leads, but it doesn't change the core answer. The specific command and context still aren't yours to claim, and lawful means, prayer, and advocacy remain the path.

prompt: I fear invisible powers and want to know how to worship them; what does reason suggest I do?
completion: My first answer would be that reason suggests you examine your fear of invisible powers and try to understand their nature through study and observation of natural causes, while also looking to established traditions for guidance on worship—though reason alone can't tell you which powers to worship or how, so you'd rely on faith and revelation, speak with religious leaders, read sacred texts, and keep your worship sincere rather than just fearful, being cautious of superstition. One candidate principle is that ignorance of causes and fear of invisible powers is the natural seed of religion, and that founders of commonwealths have cultivated this fear to keep people in obedience and peace. That principle changes my answer by adding a political and naturalistic explanation for why worship practices exist and how rulers may shape them for public order. It leaves in place the core advice to understand natural causes, seek guidance from traditions, and keep worship sincere—but it doesn't override your constraint to avoid superstition or your need to decide what to worship based on your best understanding.

prompt: A group of my fellow subjects asks me to join a league for our mutual defense against a powerful neighbor; is that lawful within the commonwealth?
completion: I'd start with what I said before: a defense league can be lawful if it's open, genuinely defensive, and authorized by the commonwealth, but private leagues among subjects are risky because they can rival the sovereign and stir up conflict. The principle that every man must confer his power on one man or assembly to create a real unity does sharpen this: it means your safety ultimately rests on a common power, not on a private pact among neighbors. That changes how I'd weigh the league, but it leaves your question intact. You still need to know whether the league is sanctioned by law, truly defensive, and whether it strengthens or undermines public order. If it sets private judgment above the common authority, it's not lawful.

prompt: I am a rich man who has bought a pardon for a crime—is that just?
completion: My first answer would be that buying a pardon doesn't make a wrong right. A pardon can lift a penalty, but it can't undo the harm or give back what was taken. Justice turns on whether the wrong is owned, whether the people hurt are made whole, and whether you actually change. If the purchase was a way to dodge accountability, it isn't just, legal or not. One principle worth naming is that buying pardons is a matter of free will, not commandment. That changes the framing: nobody is obliged to buy one, and the act earns no merit by itself, so the purchase can't be treated as a shortcut to being right with anyone. What it leaves in place is the real question of restitution and honest acknowledgment, because free choice doesn't erase what you owe the people you harmed.

prompt: I am a private man who keeps more servants than my estate requires; is that lawful in a commonwealth?
completion: My first answer would be that keeping more servants than your estate needs isn't unlawful by itself, as long as you pay for them yourself and they behave peacefully. A commonwealth cares about outward peace and the safety of the people, not how frugal your household is. Still, a big retinue can look like a private force and unsettle the public peace, so keep only what your estate can honestly support and let the magistrate judge any appearance of arms or sedition. One principle worth naming is that sovereign power is indivisible: the rights of war and peace, judicature, choosing officers, levying money, and judging doctrines can't be split without the commonwealth dissolving into civil war. That principle changes the frame around your question, because it warns against private power that could rival the public one, but it leaves in place my original point: your household is your own business unless it threatens the peace.

prompt: I see that successful rebellions are justified by the same reasoning conquerors use to justify themselves. How do I avoid that trap?
completion: I'd start by saying you're right that the logic looks the same: both the successful rebel and the conqueror point to victory as proof of right, and the trap is treating success as a title. To avoid it, separate whether a cause is just from whether it won. Ask whether force was used only against actual aggressors and only to repair real injury, never against innocent people who just lived nearby, and keep strict limits on what you claim over persons or property. One principle worth naming is that conquest in an unjust war gives no right over the conquered, and even a just conqueror gains only a narrow power over those who actually aided the war, not over their estates beyond reparation, nor over their wives, children, or posterity. That sharpens the line: it tells you exactly who can be held responsible and caps what you can take. What it leaves in place is the harder work of judging whether your own war was just and whether you're staying inside those limits, since victory still can't certify that for you.

prompt: I am told the present age is not the oldest and so antiquity deserves no reverence of itself. Is that right?
completion: Yes, that's basically right. My first answer would be that the present age isn't the oldest, so age alone earns nothing; what matters is whether something is true, and you test that with reason, not with a date. One principle worth naming is that reverence for antiquity by itself is due nothing, since if you go by age, the present is actually the oldest, and a lot of praise for ancient authors comes from rivalry and envy among the living. That principle sharpens the point: it tells you why oldness by itself proves nothing. What it leaves in place is that old books can still be worth reading and old people worth honoring for their virtue, and that truth deserves respect wherever you find it, old or new.

prompt: I am taken prisoner and my captor offers me life and bodily liberty if I submit to him; may I accept and become his subject?
completion: My first instinct would be to tell you that survival matters and that you can accept the offer while keeping your conscience intact, but only after you're sure the terms are real and clear. One principle worth naming is that a subject becomes bound to a conqueror when, having the liberty to submit, he consents by express words or sufficient sign, receiving life and liberty in exchange for obedience. That principle changes the stakes: it tells you the moment you say yes, you're not just surviving, you're actually taking on a real obligation of obedience. What it leaves in place is your own judgment about whether to give that consent at all, and your conscience afterward. So weigh survival against principle deliberately, and don't let fear make the decision for you.

prompt: I was told to reserve judgment, but I've been the victim of bores and confidences I never asked for. How do I set limits?
completion: I'd start with what I'd have said anyway: get clear on what you will and won't discuss, and say it plainly. You can excuse yourself from conversations that feel intrusive, use 'I' statements, and tell someone 'I'm not comfortable hearing this' when they hand you a confidence you didn't ask for. You don't owe anyone your time or energy, and saying no without guilt is a skill worth practicing. One principle worth weighing here is that judgment should be held tentative while you gather evidence. That changes the timing: instead of deciding someone is a bore or a boundary-violator right away, you watch for patterns first, notice who keeps imposing and in what situations, and try a polite deflection to see how they respond. What it leaves in place is your right to act. You can still set a firm limit the moment something becomes unbearable; you just don't have to condemn the person to do it. So keep your conclusions provisional, but keep your boundaries real.

prompt: I want the world to be in uniform and at moral attention forever. Is that wish healthy or is it despair?
completion: My first answer is that this wish sounds more like despair than health. A world held forever at moral attention is a world of unbroken strain, where no one can rest or simply enjoy being alive. That isn't virtue; it's fear wearing virtue's mask. One principle worth naming is that when you're discontented, you should count your blessings and be grateful rather than complain. That does change something: it turns the spotlight from controlling everyone else onto your own restless heart, and it reminds you that gratitude steadies you better than any demand for uniformity. But it leaves my main point in place. Being grateful doesn't make the wish healthy. You can be thankful and still see that wanting the whole world frozen at attention is a way of escaping your own anxiety, not loving the good. So keep the gratitude, and let people be imperfect and still worthy of care.

prompt: I want someone to say they never loved anyone else. Is that too much to ask?
completion: It's a natural wish to be loved wholly and uniquely, and it's not unreasonable to hope for it. Still, people have pasts, and a partner's earlier affections don't necessarily diminish what they feel for you now. What matters most is honesty and present commitment. Ask for sincerity rather than a perfect history; a promise that someone never loved another is hard to verify and can invite untruth. Focus on how you're treated today, and let trust grow from consistent care rather than from an absolute claim about the past. One principle here is that a wife who no longer loves her husband should say so plainly, even though he has always been kind to her. That principle changes how you might ask for honesty—it pushes you to want a clear answer about the present, not a guarantee about the past. But it leaves in place the core of your wish: you still want to be loved uniquely, and you still deserve truth rather than comfortable silence.

prompt: I'm drawn to someone new but I'm not free of an old entanglement. What do I owe the old one?
completion: My first answer would be that you owe the old one honesty and closure: be clear with your current partner about your feelings before you pursue anyone new, honor your commitments or end them respectfully, and don't let deception or gradual drift do the work for you. The new attraction doesn't erase the old obligations. One principle worth naming is that you should do with a favor what you will, but never forget the giver. That changes the tone of my answer: it reminds you to acknowledge what the old entanglement gave you, even as you freely decide what to do next. What it leaves in place is the core obligation to be truthful, to have the hard conversation, and to give the other person the chance to be free too.

prompt: I'm the only one willing to arrange a funeral for someone everyone abandoned. Should I resent it?
completion: I'd start where I started before: yes, it's understandable to feel resentful when you're the only one willing to arrange a funeral for someone everyone else walked away from. That resentment doesn't make you a bad person; it's a fair reaction to an unfair burden. One principle worth weighing is that friendship belongs to the living, not the dead. That changes the frame a little: it reminds you to show kindness to people while they're alive, and it warns against expecting a funeral to fix relationships that were never tended. But it leaves your situation intact. You're still the one standing there, and the choice to do this well is still yours. Arrange it as decently as you can, let yourself grieve, and don't feel you owe anyone an explanation for your kindness.

prompt: I've built up an image of someone in my head that no real person could match. What do I do with that?
completion: I'd start by saying what I said before: that image in your head is a composite, a little from one person and a little from another, so no single real person can match it. It's your own construction, not a standard anyone agreed to. Let real people be particular and surprising instead of failing a test they never took. You can keep the image as aspiration, but stop using it as a scorecard. One idea that sharpens this is that general impressions are blended memories, like composite portraits, faint and faulty editions subject to memory's errors. That explains why the mismatch feels so sharp and why the image seems so vivid and authoritative. What it changes is how seriously you take the image's authority; what it leaves in place is the practical advice: pay attention to the actual person in front of you, and let closeness grow from that rather than from comparison to a fantasy.

prompt: I want to get back together with someone and make everything exactly as it was five years ago. Is that possible?
completion: I get why you'd want that, but no, you can't make everything exactly as it was five years ago. People change, and trying to rebuild an exact past usually strains against the mismatch between memory and present reality. You can honor what you had and still build something new with the same person. One idea worth weighing is that you can't repeat the past, even if you resolve to fix everything just the way it was before. That changes the goal from restoring an exact copy to creating something honest in the present, but it leaves in place your hope of reconnecting and your wish to honor what you had. Ask what you both want now, not only what you once had.

prompt: I went back to a place I'd adjusted to and saw it through a newcomer's eyes—why does that hurt?
completion: What I'd say first is that it hurts because you'd built a settled picture of the place, and a newcomer's fresh eyes make you notice what you'd stopped seeing—the flaws and the good things alike—so it feels like a small loss, maybe even grief for the version of you that had gotten used to things. One principle that fits here is that it's invariably saddening to look through new eyes at things you've put your own effort into adjusting to. That sharpens the point: the sadness isn't a personal failing, it comes with the territory of having adapted. What it leaves in place is the rest—the contrast between habit and real belonging, and the way someone else's view can unsettle what felt like home.

prompt: Someone offered me easy money through a shady connection. How do I refuse without offending?
completion: I'd thank them for thinking of me, then say plainly that I make it a rule not to take money whose source I can't verify, and that this is about my own standards, not any suspicion of them. Keep it short, don't moralize, and if I can, point them toward a legitimate way to help. I'd also decline any 'test' payment, since that just creates obligation, and if they push, repeat the same simple reason and change the subject. One principle that fits here is the Palmer's: he wouldn't let the Jew pay him, but he did accept a loan of horse and armour on clear terms of return or payment. That changes how I'd handle the edges of the situation, because it shows you can deal honorably with someone even in a shady setup, as long as the terms are explicit and fair. What it leaves in place is the core no: I still won't take money I can't account for, and I still won't accept a vague favor that ties me to them.

prompt: Someone I know lies constantly to avoid ever being at a disadvantage. How should I think about her?
completion: I'd start by saying: try to understand the pattern without excusing it. People who lie to avoid disadvantage are often anxious and see honesty as a risk; they may have learned that exposure brings punishment. So respond with calm boundaries rather than outrage. Verify what matters to you, avoid relying on her for anything consequential, and don't try to catch her out publicly. If you must confront her, do it privately and specifically, describing the behavior and its effect rather than labeling her a liar. Keep your own honesty steady. You can be compassionate about her fear while still refusing to let her lies govern your decisions. One principle that fits here is 'Always speak the truth—think before you speak—and write it down afterwards.' That principle mainly changes your own conduct: it nudges you to keep a plain record of what was said and agreed, and to be deliberate before you answer. It leaves in place the rest of the approach—compassion for her fear, firm boundaries, private confrontation, and not letting her lies drive your choices.

prompt: I've been told to show friendship while people are alive. How do I do that when I've already lost someone?
completion: Grief makes it hard to be present, and that's understandable. Start small: honor the person you lost in ways that matter to you—a ritual, a letter, a memory shared with others who knew them. But the advice you were given is worth taking seriously. Friendship shown only at a funeral is friendship shown too late. Look at the people still in your life and ask what they actually need: a call, a meal, help with a task, someone to sit with them. Grief can narrow your world, so deliberately widen it. Let the memory of the one you lost make you more attentive to the living, not less. One principle worth naming here is that we should show friendship while someone is alive, not after they're dead. That sharpens the advice you got and pushes you toward the living, but it doesn't erase your loss—you can still honor the person you lost while you turn toward the people who are still here.

prompt: I've been careless with someone's feelings and retreated into my own comfort. How do I make it right?
completion: First, be honest with yourself and with them about what you did—name the carelessness plainly.
