Then apologize directly, no excuses, and ask what would help repair things, and actually listen. Give them space if they need it, but don't vanish again, since that retreat is part of the harm. Follow through on small commitments so your word carries weight again, and don't demand quick forgiveness. One principle worth holding onto here is that you shouldn't trifle with someone's feelings—if your intentions are clear, say so at once instead of leaving hope hanging. That changes how direct you are about where things stand, but it leaves the rest in place: the honest apology, the listening, the patience, and the steady pattern of showing up differently over time.

prompt: I feel safe and proud above people who struggle, and I didn't earn that safety. How should I hold it?
completion: I'd start where I started before: your safety is partly a gift of circumstance, so hold it with humility rather than guilt, and use it to open doors for others without turning paternalistic. One principle worth naming is that it's better to endure quietly what only you feel than to strike back hastily and drag everyone connected to you into the fallout. That changes the tone of how you carry your advantage: patience and restraint become the default, especially when you're tempted to prove something. What it leaves in place is the core answer, that your security is unearned and should be spent on others, not on pride. It doesn't ask you to feel ashamed, just to be slower to act and quicker to bear.

prompt: I keep hoping someone will call, and the phone never rings. How long do I wait by the window?
completion: I'd start by saying what I said before: sitting by the window keeps the ache alive more than it eases it, so give the hope a place but don't let waiting become your whole day. Set a limit on the watching, then fill the hours with something that uses your hands and attention. One principle here is that hope and keeping busy go together, that work is a real solace and idling just feeds the fret. That changes the tone of my answer a little: instead of just capping the window time, I'd lean harder into the idea that going on with your daily tasks is itself a kind of answer, not a distraction from the real question. What it leaves in place is the limit on waiting and the honesty that the phone may not ring. So keep the hope, do the work, and let the call come if it comes.

prompt: My friend's dream is corrupt at the edges even though the dreamer is good. How do I separate the two?
completion: I'd start by saying the dream's disturbing edges don't automatically say anything about your friend's character. Dreams pull together memory, emotion, and stray brain activity, so the weird parts aren't a moral verdict on the dreamer. To separate the two, look at your friend's waking values and intentions, and maybe explore what those odd images might be expressing. One idea worth weighing is that the dreamer is the same person asleep or awake, so with some focused attention your friend could work at interpreting the dream himself. That shifts the emphasis toward his own insight rather than treating the dream as evidence about him. It doesn't change the core point, though: unsettling imagery still isn't proof of a bad character, and a therapist can help if the dream keeps bothering him.

prompt: I feel far away from the person I love and can't make her understand me. What do I do?
completion: I'd start by saying distance and misunderstanding hurt, but they don't mean love is doomed. Ask her what specifically she doesn't understand—your words, your needs, or your intentions. Pick a calm time, say plainly what you feel without blame, then ask her to repeat back what she heard so you can see the gap. If talking keeps failing, try a letter or a trusted person to help. Also be honest about whether the distance is practical or emotional. One principle here is that a man's love shouldn't be a tyranny—you shouldn't make her an idol or a slave, and she shouldn't do that to you. That principle changes the tone: instead of just chasing understanding, you keep a healthy distance that respects both of you. It leaves in place the practical steps—clear speech, checking the gap, and deciding honestly whether the mismatch is real.

prompt: Someone says it takes two to make an accident and blames others for keeping out of her way. Do I accept that?
completion: My first answer would be no, don't accept it. That line about taking two to make an accident is usually just a way to dodge blame. The person who acted carelessly is the one responsible, and expecting everyone else to keep out of your way is unfair. One candidate principle here is Jordan's insistence that it takes two to make an accident and that she hates careless people. That principle actually pushes back on your question: it suggests shared fault, which might make you pause before rejecting the excuse outright. But it doesn't change the core point—blaming others for not compensating for your negligence is still unreasonable. So I'd still say don't accept it, and hold the careless person accountable.

prompt: I keep waiting for someone who may never come. When do I stop waiting?
completion: I'd start by saying there's no simple rule for when to stop waiting. Ask yourself whether the waiting is patient hope or idle paralysis. If it keeps you from work, friendships, and daily duties, it may be time to set a boundary and live your life now. One principle worth naming is that you should keep doing your own work faithfully while you hope, leaving the future to be as God wills. That changes the focus from a deadline to a daily rhythm: you don't have to decide today whether to stop, but you do have to keep showing up for your own life. It leaves in place the honest possibility that the person may never come, and it doesn't tell you to abandon hope. What it does not do is give you a clear stopping point, so you still need to watch whether the waiting is costing you your whole present.

prompt: I threw a party for hundreds and no one really knew me. What does that say about me?
completion: What I'd say first is that it says less about your worth than about the gap between being surrounded and being known. A party for hundreds can be a generous gesture, but a crowd isn't intimacy, and being in a room full of people who don't really know you can feel lonelier than being alone. One principle worth weighing here is the idea that if there's to be a party, you ought to invite the guests yourself. That shifts the focus from what the crowd says about you to whether the crowd was your choice or just something that gathered while you stood by. It leaves the core point in place: depth, not headcount, is what makes you known, so pick a few people and let them see you more fully.

prompt: I've been invited into a wealthy world I don't belong to. Should I go?
completion: I'd start with what I said before: think about whether going brings you real happiness or just discomfort, weigh the chance to learn and connect against the pressure to conform, and decide based on your own goals and values. One principle worth naming is that money is needful and noble when well used, but it should never be the only prize, and a poor man's happy wife beats a queen without self-respect and peace. That principle sharpens the question: it tells you to check whether you'd be going for genuine connection or just for the shine of wealth. What it changes is the emphasis, so you don't treat the invitation as a prize to win. What it leaves in place is your freedom to say yes or no, and your own sense of what feels right for you.

prompt: I'm watching my partner's affair unfold in front of me and I don't know whether to confront or stay quiet.
completion: I'd start where I started before: this is a painful place to be, and you deserve support. Before you decide anything, protect yourself emotionally and practically — talk to a counselor or a trusted friend, and get clear on what you actually want from this relationship. Confrontation can bring relief, but it can also escalate fast, so pick your moment and your words carefully. Staying quiet indefinitely is rarely sustainable; resentment tends to grow. Write down what you've observed and what you need to say, then decide whether a calm, direct conversation is possible or whether you need distance first. You're not obligated to pretend nothing is happening. One principle worth weighing here is that a wife shouldn't be kept in ignorance of serious matters, and a marriage where the two of you have never had a real, serious conversation isn't true understanding. That principle sharpens the case for eventually sitting down and speaking plainly rather than letting silence stretch on — it turns 'staying quiet' from a neutral holding pattern into something closer to a choice that keeps you both in the dark. What it leaves in place is everything about timing and safety: it doesn't tell you to confront tonight, doesn't override your need for support or distance first, and doesn't change the fact that you get to choose the moment and the words. So it nudges you toward honest conversation as the destination, while your own judgment still governs the route.

prompt: I pride myself on being one of the few honest people I know. Is that pride dangerous?
completion: Yes, I'd say that pride can be dangerous, because it can slide into arrogance or a sense of superiority. Honesty is a virtue, but being proud of it can blind you to your own flaws and make you judgmental of others. The key is to stay humble and treat honesty as a standard we all should strive for, not a badge of honor. One thing worth keeping in mind is that pride shows up plainly in how someone carries themselves, holding their head high and looking down on others, which is the opposite of humility. That changes how I'd frame it: the danger isn't just abstract self-righteousness, it's visible in how you treat people. What it leaves in place is my main point, that pride in honesty can be dangerous if it turns into self-righteousness.

prompt: I'm thirty and the decade ahead looks lonely. How do I face it?
completion: I'd start where I started before: turning thirty can feel daunting when you expect the decade ahead to be lonely, but loneliness isn't a foregone conclusion. You can build deeper connections, pursue what matters to you, and get to know yourself better. Acknowledge the fear, then take small concrete steps — join something, volunteer, reach back out to old friends — and also learn to enjoy your own company, since solitude can be enriching. One principle worth naming is that looking through new eyes at things you've spent years adjusting to is invariably saddening. That changes the tone: some of what you're feeling may be grief over a settled life seen afresh, not a verdict on the next ten years. What it leaves in place is the practical core — reaching out, staying engaged, and seeking support are still the things that actually help.

prompt: I keep beating on against the current, borne back into the past. How do I keep going?
completion: I'd start by saying that beating against the current is noble, and the past is part of you—forgive yourself and let it feed new growth. One principle that matters here is to confess and repent what's past, avoid what's to come, and not spread compost on weeds. That changes the focus from self-forgiveness to honest contrition and turning away from what you've done. It leaves in place the idea that the past can be a lesson, not a home, and that you keep rowing forward. So keep going by being honest about your failures, resolving to do better, and not letting memory pull you under.

prompt: I keep catching myself judging people who had fewer advantages than I did—how should I hold that?
completion: I'd start where I started before: it's good you notice the pattern, and the first move is to pause and get curious about where the judgment comes from. What I'd add is Nick's father's advice—reserve judgment, because not everyone has had your advantages, and a sense of the fundamental decencies is parceled out unequally at birth. That changes the tone: instead of treating the judgment as just a personal insecurity to soften, you treat it as a reminder of unequal ground. What it leaves in place is the practical step—keep pausing, keep asking what this person values and does from inside their circumstances, and hold your verdict lightly. It's not about excusing; it's understanding made personal.

prompt: In my country there's only one day at a time. Is that a limitation?
completion: My first answer would be that it can feel like a limitation, but it's also just how time is normally experienced. One day at a time is a common and workable setup: you wake, you act, you rest, and the next day follows. Whether it limits you depends on what you expect. If you think time should come in bigger bundles, then sure, your country's way seems narrow. But most people find that focusing on one day at a time keeps life manageable. The real question is whether you use those days well. Now, one principle from the list says to keep your effort-making capacity alive by doing something small and unnecessary each day—just to train yourself to handle tough moments. That principle changes the focus from whether one day at a time is a limitation to how you use each day to build resilience. It leaves in place the idea that one day at a time is workable and that the real question is how you use your days. So the limitation isn't in the structure of time; it's in whether you're actively strengthening yourself.

prompt: I already screamed about something that hasn't happened yet. Should I scream again when it does?
completion: My first answer would have been that it depends on why you screamed. If it helped you cope or communicate, you might do it again; if you've already expressed your feelings about the anticipated event, repeating it may be unnecessary and could add to your distress. One candidate principle here is the idea that the chief expressive actions are innate or inherited—children and blind people blush, infants scream from birth, and the same movements express the same states across races. That principle changes how I see the scream itself: it's a natural expression, not something you have to learn or force. But it leaves in place the practical question of whether screaming again will actually help you or just add to your distress. So I'd still say think about what you hope to achieve before you scream again.

prompt: I'm so upset I can't stop crying. How do I stop?
completion: I'm really sorry you're feeling this way. Crying can be a normal release, but if you want to stop, try some grounding techniques: slow your breathing, splash cold water on your face, or hold something cold in your hands. Name five things you can see and four you can hear. Distraction can help too—put on a show, call a friend, or step outside for fresh air. Try not to judge yourself for crying; it's your body's way of coping. If the sadness feels overwhelming or lasts a long time, consider talking to a counselor or doctor. For now, be gentle with yourself and give it time. One idea that might help is that nobody can do two things at once, so if you keep from crying by considering things—like your age, your journey, the time you've come through—that reckoning can crowd out the tears. That principle gives you a mental task to try, but it leaves in place the need to be kind to yourself and to seek support if this keeps happening.

prompt: I'm trying to serve a cake and the slices keep joining back together. What am I doing wrong?
completion: Honestly, my first answer is that the cake is probably too warm or your knife is too dull. Chill the cake before cutting, use a long serrated knife dipped in hot water and wiped dry, and cut with a gentle sawing motion instead of pressing down. Separate the slices as you go and wipe the blade between cuts. One principle worth considering is handing it round first and cutting it afterwards, which is how Looking-glass cakes are managed. That changes the order of things, so portions are served before any slicing starts, but it leaves the practical fixes in place: a cold cake and a sharp, clean blade still matter. What kind of cake is it?

prompt: I can't tell the difference between what something is called and what it really is. Can you explain?
completion: A name is just a label we use so we can talk about something. What it really is includes its properties, causes, and effects. Confusing the two is like thinking a menu is a meal. The word 'gold' isn't shiny or heavy, but the metal is. One candidate principle says a name means nothing to the one who bears it, but it may carry deep meaning for those who loved the person it belonged to. That changes how I'd think about names in personal or emotional contexts—it reminds me that a name can be charged with memory and feeling for others even if it's empty to the bearer. But it leaves in place the core point: a name still doesn't tell you what the thing really is. You still have to ask what it does, what it's made of, how it came to be, and what follows from it. So the name becomes a handle for understanding, not a substitute for it.

prompt: I want to shake someone until they turn into a kitten. Is that reasonable?
completion: It's a funny, vivid impulse, but no—shaking someone isn't reasonable. People don't turn into kittens, and actually doing it would be scary and harmful. What's probably underneath is frustration, or a wish for this prickly person to soften into something cuddly and easy to handle. One candidate principle here is that whatever you say to kittens, they always purr, so you can't really talk with someone who always gives the same soft answer. That's a useful check on the fantasy: a purring kitten can't tell you no, so the cuddly version of a person isn't someone you can actually reason with. It changes how I'd frame the daydream—enjoy the absurd image, but notice it's about wanting agreement, not conversation. What it leaves in place is the main point: keep your hands to yourself, name the frustration directly, and if it's constant, look at what the relationship is costing you.

prompt: If someone else's dream ended, would I disappear?
completion: My first answer would be that you wouldn't disappear, since you're a real person with your own consciousness and dreams are personal and subjective. One candidate principle says that every dream is absolutely egotistical, with the dreamer's own self appearing in every figure, even disguised. That changes how I'd read your role in the dream: if you show up there, you're probably a stand-in for the dreamer, not a separate being whose life hangs on the dream. What it leaves in place is the main point: your existence as a real person doesn't depend on anyone else's dream ending, so you wouldn't vanish.

prompt: I want to be ready for anything that might go wrong. Is that reasonable?
completion: It's reasonable to want to be ready, but not to be ready for literally everything. I'd say start with the risks that are most likely or most costly, take sensible steps there, and accept that some things are out of your hands. Building flexibility and calm matters more than covering every scenario. One principle worth naming is that fortune governs half our actions but leaves the other half to us, and it's better to be adventurous than overly cautious. That changes the emphasis: instead of just listing risks and accepting limits, it nudges you to act boldly where you can and not let fear keep you frozen. What it leaves in place is the core point that you can't prepare for every conceivable mishap, so you still need to focus on what you can control and stay adaptable.

prompt: I have a useless box—should I throw it away or keep it?
completion: Honestly, my first instinct is that if the box does nothing for you and just takes up space, it's fine to let it go—no guilt needed. One idea worth weighing is that good things only count as good when they're actually used, so a box that sits untouched is just clutter. That changes how I'd frame it: instead of asking whether to keep or toss, ask whether you'd genuinely use it for something. If yes, keep it and put it to work; if not, letting it go is reasonable. What stays the same is that it's your call and you shouldn't beat yourself up either way.

prompt: Someone wants to trade answers with me. Should I agree?
completion: I'd start with what I first thought: trading answers can be fine or foolish depending on what's being exchanged and with whom, so ask what you gain, what you give up, and whether the other person is trustworthy and likely to reciprocate fairly. One idea that sharpens this is the bargain of 'if you'll believe in me, I'll believe in you'—mutual exchange, not one side giving while the other only takes. That changes the emphasis: make sure the flow goes both ways before you commit. It leaves the rest in place—check the terms, protect what you can't afford to lose, and decline politely if it doesn't add up.

prompt: My friend keeps falling off his horse but gets right back on. Should I worry?
completion: I'd worry enough to act, not panic. Repeated falls are a real safety concern, so make sure your friend wears a helmet and proper gear, rides a suitable horse, and works with an instructor. Check whether the falls come from a mismatch between rider and mount, bad tack, or overconfidence. Getting back on is good for nerve, but only if the cause is addressed. One principle worth naming is that a man's own neck and limbs are his own, but a borrowed horse and armour belong to someone else and must be repaid or restored. That changes things if the horse isn't his: he owes the owner care and honesty about the risk. It leaves in place the basic advice to support his courage while pushing for lessons, gradual progress, and a safer alternative if the falls keep happening.

prompt: Every time I look closely at something in this shop, it's gone. What's happening?
completion: What I'd say first is that this is probably attention and shop logistics working together. When you stare hard at one thing, your focus narrows and you stop tracking the edges of your vision, so stuff can seem to blink out. Shops also move stock, rearrange displays, and sell things fast, so the item may really have been moved or bought. Lighting and crowding add to it. Try noting where the item was and what it looked like, then glance away and back, or just ask the shopkeeper. One principle worth naming is that positive habits are always forming, whether that's careful looking and following up or hasty glancing and guessing. That changes the advice a bit: it's not just about explaining the vanishing, it's about building steady habits like writing things down and asking questions instead of jumping to conclusions. What it leaves in place is the plain explanation itself, that attention and normal shop activity are the likely cause.

prompt: Someone is trying to negotiate terms with me and I don't want to bargain. How do I refuse?
completion: I'd just say no plainly and hold my ground. You don't have to bargain over terms you never asked for. State it once, calmly, and decline to keep discussing it. If they push, repeat the refusal without over-explaining or apologizing. One principle worth naming here is that a woman shouldn't be intimidated into promising never to enter an engagement, since that kind of promise is unreasonable and should be refused. That principle backs up your refusal and gives you a clear reason to stand firm, but it doesn't change the basic approach: say no once, stay calm, and don't get pulled into a back-and-forth.

prompt: I'm getting older and I hate it. Can I do anything about it?
completion: Aging is real, and hating it is understandable. You can't stop the clock, but you can shape how you meet it: keep moving, keep learning, keep company that energizes you, and care for sleep, diet, and health. Grieve what changes, then reinvest in what remains. One idea worth weighing is that you shouldn't look into the future or dwell on old age and death, but just accept what comes and stay busy and well-groomed. That changes the tone—less planning and mourning, more staying present and engaged. What it leaves in place is the practical core: movement, learning, people, sleep, diet, health. So take the staying-busy part seriously, but I wouldn't ban thinking about the future entirely; a little planning can protect the days you're trying to enjoy.

prompt: I'm terrified of getting hurt in a conflict. What's the worst that could happen?
completion: Honestly, the worst that could happen is usually less dramatic than your fear is telling you, but the fear itself is real and worth taking seriously. You might get hurt, feel embarrassed, or lose something you value. You might also find the conflict is smaller than you feared, or that you handle it better than expected. A practical move is to name the specific outcome you're afraid of, estimate how likely it is, and prepare for it. Talk to someone you trust, make a plan, and decide ahead of time what you won't accept. Fear shrinks when you make it concrete. You don't have to be fearless to act, just prepared. One idea that fits here is that the expectation of evil is often more bitter than the suffering itself, and fear of danger more terrifying than danger. That reframes your dread as the main thing to work on, not just the conflict. It doesn't promise the conflict will be painless or that real risks vanish, so you still plan and set limits. But it puts a lot of the weight on the waiting and imagining, which you can actually do something about.

prompt: I invented something to keep my things dry in the rain. Is it a good idea?
completion: My first answer would be that it depends on whether it actually works: test it in real rain, check it's easy to carry and holds up, and see if it's affordable and different from what's already out there. One principle that applies here is your own description—clothes and sandwiches kept in a container carried upside-down so the rain can't get in. That changes my answer by making me take the upside-down design seriously: turning the opening downward is sound reasoning, since water can't run uphill into it. What it leaves in place is the need to test it in real rain, check cost and need, and refine anything bulky. So I'd credit the design and still say prove it works.

prompt: I just became a leader and I'm slouching. Does it matter?
completion: Yes, it matters, not because posture is magic but because people read leadership through signals, and slouching reads as low energy and low attention. That said, don't turn it into vanity; the goal is a settled, alert bearing, not a rigid spine. One idea worth naming: the immediate sense of where your limbs are comes from the joint surfaces, not from some muscular sense of extension. That changes how I'd frame the fix—it's less about willing your muscles into a pose and more about giving your joints and body a position that feels grounded, so you can reset by standing and shifting rather than by tensing. What it leaves in place is the main point: correct the cause—sleep, a chair and desk that fit you, standing and stretching when you notice yourself folding—and keep a present, alert presence.

prompt: I want to be happy whenever I like, but I can't remember how. Any tips?
completion: I'd start with the same thing I'd have said before: happiness gets easier when you stop chasing it head-on. Lean on small, reliable things—rest, movement, time outside, people you like—notice what actually lifts you, and build more of that into your days. When you're low, don't fight it; acknowledge it and gently turn toward something useful or pleasant. Keep a short list of what's helped before for when you forget. One idea worth adding is that you can go through the outward motions of the mood you want—act cheerful even when you don't feel it—and real cheerfulness tends to follow with practice. That changes the starting point: you don't have to wait to feel like it. It leaves the rest in place—the small pleasures, the list, the patience—and it doesn't promise you can flip a switch whenever you like.

prompt: I left out a lot of details in my explanation. Does it matter?
completion: Whether it matters really depends on what the details were for. If your explanation was meant to inform a decision, omissions can mislead, so it's worth correcting the record. If it was casual conversation, most people fill gaps naturally and won't mind. Think about your audience and purpose: a boss, doctor, or lawyer needs the full picture; a friend at dinner probably doesn't. If you're unsure, just add a brief follow-up like 'one thing I left out' rather than over-explaining. Honesty matters more than completeness, so fix anything that could cause real misunderstanding and let the rest go. One principle worth keeping in mind is that yielding readily to a friend's persuasion without real conviction doesn't do either of you any favors. That changes how you handle pushback: if someone presses you to share more, don't just cave to keep the peace—decide for yourself whether the missing details actually matter. What it leaves in place is the core test: correct what could genuinely mislead, and let the rest go.

prompt: I invented a new word that packs two meanings together. Is that allowed?
completion: Yes, it's allowed—people coin words all the time, and language is living. But a word only becomes real when others understand and use it. Packing two meanings into one can be clever, though it can also confuse, so ask whether the double meaning serves clarity or just shows off. One principle worth naming is that understanding caused by speech is conception caused by words, and of absurd or false affirmations there can be no understanding—many think they understand when they only repeat words. That principle changes how you should test your coinage: don't mistake people repeating it back for them actually conceiving both senses. What it leaves in place is the basic point that no authority grants permission; only the slow agreement of speakers makes a word stick. So try it, explain it plainly, and see whether others adopt it.

prompt: I want to remember things that haven't happened yet. Is that possible?
completion: My first answer would be: no, not in the ordinary sense—memory is about what you've already lived through, and what you're describing sounds more like anticipation or prediction. One principle worth naming is that memory proper requires referring the imaged fact to your own past and dating it there, with that warmth of self-appropriation; mere revival of an image isn't memory. That principle changes how I'd frame it: it sharpens why ordinary remembering can't point forward, because the felt sense of 'mine, back then' is missing. But it leaves in place what I first said—you can still use patterns, planning, and imagination to forecast, and you should treat vivid anticipation as forecasting, not remembering.

prompt: I was told I haven't had lessons in manners. Can manners be taught in lessons?
completion: Yes, manners can be taught in lessons. You can learn how to greet people, which fork to use, and which topics are polite. Etiquette courses are common and can help you avoid embarrassing mistakes. Some people think manners are more about character than rules, but with practice, anyone can improve. So if someone says you haven't had lessons, take it as an opportunity to learn. You can take a course or read a book on etiquette. It's never too late to learn good manners. One idea worth weighing is that lessons teach you to do sums and things of that sort, not manners. That changes how much credit lessons deserve: they can teach you the rules, but not the kindness and respect behind them. What it leaves in place is that lessons still help with the practical side, so you can learn the forms even if the spirit comes from somewhere else.

prompt: I can add but I can't subtract. Is that a problem?
completion: I'd start by saying no, it's not a problem in itself — plenty of people are solid at adding and shaky at subtracting, and that's not some character flaw. The practical question is whether subtraction actually matters for what you want to do; if it does, it's learnable with small numbers, real objects, and patient practice, and if it doesn't, using a calculator or asking for help is fine. One idea worth naming here is that arithmetic rests on how we group and split units in our heads, not on what happens to physical objects — one plus one is two because that's what we mean by it. That reframes subtraction as just the reverse of grouping, which can make it feel less like a mysterious separate skill. But it doesn't erase the fact that you currently can't do it, and it doesn't replace the actual practice you'd need to get there.

prompt: My hair keeps falling out. Is there any way to stop things from falling?
completion: I'd start by saying hair loss has real causes—genetics, hormones, stress, diet, illness—so see a doctor or dermatologist before trying folk fixes. Ask about blood tests, thyroid, iron, and any medications. In the meantime, be gentle: avoid tight styles and harsh treatments, eat well, sleep, and manage stress. Some proven treatments exist for common patterns of loss, but they work best early and need consistency. Be skeptical of miracle cures and expensive gadgets. Track changes over months, not days. If the loss is sudden or patchy, get seen promptly. Accepting some shedding is normal; panic is not a treatment plan. One candidate principle says things never fall upwards, so you could make hair creep up a stick like a fruit tree. That changes nothing about the medical advice—it's just a playful image—and it leaves all the real guidance in place: see a doctor, get tests, be gentle, and track changes over time.

prompt: Two items are cheaper than one, but there's a catch. Should I buy two?
completion: My first answer would be: it depends on the catch. A two-for-one deal only saves you money if you'd have bought the second one anyway or can use it before it goes bad. If it's perishable, be honest about whether you'll actually consume both, or the saving is imaginary and you've just spent more. If it's durable and storable, buying two can make sense. Check storage, your budget, and whether the extra will really get used. One principle here is that two are cheaper than one only if you must eat them both. That sharpens the test for perishables, but it leaves the rest in place: for durable goods, the same questions about storage, budget, and real use still decide it. Read the terms, check the catch, and buy two only if the second serves a real purpose.

prompt: My king has been captured and our society scattered by foreign conquest. What becomes of our government?
completion: When your king is captured and your society is scattered, the old government collapses and something has to replace it. In practice, the conqueror's authority fills the vacuum, and the people must decide how to reconstitute rule. A wise course is to build a government resting on consent, with laws and judges chosen by the community rather than imposed by a single ruler. The scattered society can regroup around shared institutions, and the conqueror's power, however broad, cannot extinguish the people's right to order their own affairs justly. One candidate principle says that conquest in an unjust war gives no right over the conquered, and even a just conqueror gains only a despotical power over those who actually aided in the war, not over their estates beyond reparation, nor over their wives, children, or posterity. That principle changes the moral standing of the conquest: it denies the conqueror any legitimate claim over the innocent and limits even a just conqueror's power to actual aggressors and reparation. What it leaves in place is the practical reality that the old government has collapsed and the people still need to reconstitute rule—so the work of building consent-based institutions remains, but it must be done without conceding that conquest itself confers a rightful title over everyone.

prompt: Someone borrowed my money and now draws his sword to keep it. May I use force to recover it?
completion: If someone borrowed your money and then draws a sword to keep it, you may be tempted to use force to recover it. However, the law generally discourages self-help and violence. You should seek legal remedies, such as suing in court or reporting to the authorities. Using force could escalate the situation and lead to criminal charges against you. While it's unjust for the borrower to threaten you, responding with force is risky and often illegal. The best course is to rely on the legal system to enforce your rights and recover your money peacefully. One principle that applies here is that the word of God has a more powerful effect on people's minds than the sword, so it's worth trying persuasion before force. That principle reinforces the peaceful path and gives you a moral reason to try reasoning with the borrower first. But it doesn't change the core advice: you still shouldn't use force, and you should still go through legal channels. It leaves in place the warning that violence is risky and illegal, and it doesn't give you a license to skip the authorities.

prompt: If I join a society, must every single member agree to every law, or does the majority decide?
completion: No, you don't need every single member to sign off on every law. If that were the rule, one person could block everything and the society couldn't function. When people agree to join together, the majority gets to decide, and that decision binds everyone. The principle that matters here is that consent to form the community is what gives the majority its authority to act for the whole. That changes the question from 'did everyone agree to this particular law' to 'did everyone agree to be part of this body and its fair procedures.' It leaves your concern about protecting people in the minority fully in place, since the terms of the compact and the law still guard their rights.

prompt: Am I bound to obey a law I never consented to, just because I was born here?
completion: I'd start by saying that whether you're bound to obey a law you never consented to is a real puzzle, and my first take is that living in a society and accepting its benefits—like protection and order—can create a kind of tacit consent, even if you never explicitly agreed. But one candidate principle says you're only bound to obey unless obedience would cost you eternal life. That principle changes the stakes: it makes the duty conditional on something beyond politics, so you could disobey if a law forced you to forfeit your salvation. What it leaves in place is the general expectation of obedience for everything else—so you're still bound in ordinary matters, just not absolutely.

prompt: A conqueror has taken our country and demands our allegiance. Must we give it?
completion: My first answer would be that you're not strictly obliged to swear allegiance to a conqueror, though it's complicated in practice. Allegiance usually tracks whoever actually holds power and protects you, so a conqueror who now governs and keeps order may command obedience, while resistance is justified if he tyrannizes. One principle worth naming is that obedience rests on possession, not on whether the conqueror's cause was good, since few commonwealths began in ways anyone could fully justify. That principle shifts the question away from whether you approve of how he took power and toward whether he now protects you and keeps order. What it leaves in place is the harder judgment about tyranny: if he rules oppressively, resistance can still be justified, so the principle settles less than it first seems.

prompt: My ruler has been a good prince and acted beyond the letter of the law for our benefit. Should I complain?
completion: I'd first say that if your ruler has genuinely acted for your benefit, complaining seems ungrateful and unwise. Princes who stretch the letter of the law to serve the common good sometimes must. But one principle to keep in mind is that a prince should not aggrandize another power, since he who causes another to become powerful is ruined. That changes things by adding a specific check: watch that he isn't building up the Church or a foreign prince at your expense. It leaves in place the basic caution against loud complaint and the need to stay attentive to whether his strength is being built against you.

prompt: Can a family be called a commonwealth, with the father as its king?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, in a loose sense. A family has a head, rules, and a common good, so it resembles a small commonwealth, and the father may be called its king. But the analogy has limits. A king rules by law and consent, while a father's authority rests on nature and the duty to raise his children. Families are not voluntary associations of equal citizens, and children cannot consent. So the family is the seedbed of political society rather than a commonwealth proper. It is better to say the family is the first society, from which commonwealths grow, than to call the father a king outright. One candidate principle is that dominion by acquisition, whether paternal or despotic, rests on consent and its rights are the same as sovereignty by institution. That principle changes the picture by making the father's authority depend on consent, which children can't give, so it actually undermines calling him a king. It leaves in place the idea that the family has a head and a common good, but it doesn't make the family a commonwealth proper.

prompt: I have gathered more acorns than I can eat before they rot. Is that wrong?
completion: My first answer would be: not necessarily wrong, just a common overreach of enthusiasm. The real problem is waste, so gather only what you can store or share, and dry or grind the surplus. One candidate principle here is that it's petty to complain about life at sixty-two since nature commands every life to end. That principle nudges me to treat rot and death as natural rather than a moral failure, but it doesn't really change the practical advice about storing and sharing acorns, and it leaves your actual question about waste exactly where it was.

prompt: My representative votes before hearing any debate, having promised his vote in advance. Is that a breach of trust?
completion: Yes, I'd say it's a breach of trust. A representative is elected to use their judgment for their constituents, and promising a vote before hearing any debate undercuts that duty. One principle that matters here is that the vote is a public trust, not a private right, and it should follow the representative's best conscientious view of the public good, with publicity as the general rule. That principle sharpens the point: the problem isn't just closed-mindedness, it's that the vote was treated as something owed in advance rather than something to be exercised responsibly in public view. What it leaves in place is that a representative can still have firm commitments and principles; it's the refusal to hear debate before casting the vote that breaks the trust.

prompt: My neighbour says all land must be held in common and my enclosure is theft. Is he right?
completion: I'd start by saying your neighbour is partly right and partly wrong. Common land really existed, and enclosure did push a lot of people off land they'd used for generations, so there's a real grievance behind what he's saying. But "all land must be held in common" is a political ideal, not a legal fact, and in most systems an enclosure done properly is lawful and the property rights that come with it are enforceable. So calling yours theft doesn't hold up if you followed the law, though the fairness question is separate and worth actually hearing him out on. One principle that bears on this is that it's wrong to take what belongs to another. That principle cuts both ways here: it means your neighbour can't just declare your land common and take it, but it also means you can't ignore whatever claims the people who used that land before had. What it changes is that it turns the argument from slogans into a question of who actually held what; what it leaves in place is that the law still decides whose claim counts, and that's where the real dispute sits.

prompt: The prince has dissolved the parliament and rules by decree. Is that tyranny?
completion: My first answer would be that dissolving parliament and ruling by decree is a serious step, but whether it's tyranny depends on the circumstances. Some constitutions let a prince dissolve a legislature, and emergencies can call for quick action. Tyranny usually means ruling for private advantage instead of the public good, ignoring the law, and showing cruelty or seizing property. So ask: is he ruling for himself or for the realm? Are there courts, checks, or a timetable for bringing parliament back? Does he respect property and persons? If decree rule becomes permanent and self-serving, that's tyranny in substance, whatever the form. One candidate principle here is that tyranny is power exercised beyond right, for the ruler's own advantage rather than the people's good, and that unlawful force may be met with force. That principle sharpens the test: it tells you to look at whether he's acting beyond the law, not just at whether parliament is sitting. What it leaves in place is the need to check the facts, because a lawful dissolution in a real emergency still isn't tyranny, and the principle only bites once he's actually overstepping the law for himself.

prompt: My ruler claims a prerogative to act without law. When is that legitimate?
completion: I'd start by saying that a ruler's prerogative to act without law is legitimate only in narrow cases where the law is silent and prompt action serves the public good, as when sudden danger demands speed the ordinary process cannot supply. Outside such necessity it's mere license, and a ruler who invokes prerogative to gratify private ambition or to override settled law without cause acts tyrannically. The people aren't bound to submit to measures that plainly tend to their ruin. Still, judgment is difficult, since the same act may be called necessity by the prince and usurpation by the subject, and prudence counsels patience where the harm is doubtful. The safest test is whether the act aims at preservation of the community and its laws rather than at the ruler's advantage. One candidate principle here is that prerogative is the power to act for the public good without the prescription of law, and sometimes against it; it's justified only by tending to the public good, and the people may limit it when it's used to harm them. That principle sharpens the test: it makes the public good the sole justification and explicitly gives the people a right to limit prerogative when it harms them. What it leaves in place is the basic structure of my answer—that prerogative is real but narrow, that necessity can justify acting without law, and that the people's safety is the ultimate measure. It doesn't resolve the hard case of disputed judgment, where the ruler claims necessity and the subject sees usurpation; prudence and patience still have a role there.

prompt: I found a field no one uses and improved it with my labour. Can anyone else claim it?
completion: My first answer would be that mixing your labour with unowned land gives you a strong claim, but not an unlimited one. You should be able to claim the field you actually improved, to the extent of your labour and the value you added. Others can't fairly reap what you've sown, but your claim shouldn't sprawl beyond what you've genuinely worked and can use. One principle worth weighing is that constructive manual work can present real problems for personal reflection and experimentation, though mere physical activity alone secures no intellectual result by magic. That principle changes how I'd frame your improvement: it's not just sweat that grounds the claim, but the thoughtful problem-solving you brought to the field. It leaves in place the core limit—your claim stays tied to what you actually worked and can use, not to land you leave idle.

prompt: A thief demands my purse at sword-point. May I kill him?
completion: I'd start with what I said before: this is a hard question that depends on the law where you live and on the facts. In many places, lethal force is only allowed when you reasonably fear imminent death or serious bodily harm, and a demand for your purse alone usually doesn't meet that bar. If the thief is armed and threatening, the analysis changes, but the response still has to be proportionate. The safest course is to comply, preserve your life, and report the crime. Killing should be a last resort to prevent grave harm, not a response to property loss. Consult a lawyer about the specific rules in your jurisdiction. One candidate principle I'd weigh is: don't expose your game to your adversary; let him find out if he can, and we can find out his. That principle changes the tactical advice—it suggests you shouldn't announce your intentions or plans to the thief, and you should try to read his intentions instead. But it leaves in place the core legal and moral limits: you still can't use lethal force just to protect property, and you still need a reasonable fear of imminent death or serious harm. So the principle sharpens how you handle the encounter, not whether you may kill.

prompt: Who decides whether the king has broken his trust—the king himself?
completion: My first answer is no—the king shouldn't be the one deciding whether he broke his trust. If he's the only judge of his own case, the check means nothing, so some outside body has to assess it. Take the principle that one wicked king can cause great ruin, so the people should be governed by judges chosen by the people under the law. That principle changes who does the judging—it shifts the call toward the people and their chosen judges rather than the crown. What it leaves in place is the core point: the king still isn't the sole judge of his own breach.

prompt: The majority of the people are oppressed and see a design against their liberties. May they resist?
completion: My first answer would be that resistance is a serious but sometimes justified recourse, not a first resort. It should follow clear evidence of a design against liberties, exhaustion of lawful remedies, and a real prospect of restoring just government rather than swapping one oppression for another. The right belongs to the community, not a private faction, and should run through representative institutions where possible. One candidate principle that bears on this is that men are naturally free and equal, and the only way into political society is by consenting with others to unite into a community, after which the majority may act and conclude the rest. That principle strengthens the case for resistance when consent is systematically betrayed, and it leaves in place the cautions about evidence, remedies, and the common good. It does not by itself settle whether a particular majority's grievance is well founded, so those checks still matter.

prompt: Is monarchy the natural form of government because fathers rule families?
completion: My first answer would be no. The family comparison is suggestive but it doesn't prove anything. Fathers rule children because kids are dependent and inexperienced, and that authority is temporary and ends as the child grows up. Governing adults is a different thing entirely, since adults aren't children and their consent and interests matter. One candidate principle here is that monarchy beats sovereign assemblies because a monarch's private interest lines up with the public interest, while in an assembly corrupt or ambitious men can push their own advantage through bad advice or civil war. That principle does shift something: it gives monarchy a real practical argument that doesn't lean on the father analogy at all. But it leaves the core point in place. It's still an argument about which form works better for peace and security, not a claim that monarchy is natural because dads rule families. So the paternal metaphor still fails as a justification, even if monarchy has other defenses worth weighing.

prompt: My ruler is of a different religion and rules by force. May we throw off his yoke?
completion: I'd start by saying that a ruler of a different religion who governs by force does raise a real question of conscience. In general, force may be resisted when it's unlawful and when resistance is likely to do more good than harm, but there's also a strong call to be subject to governing authorities, and rebellion tends to bring suffering on the innocent. So I'd ask whether the ruler's rule is merely different in religion or genuinely oppressive in its demands. If it commands what conscience forbids, you may refuse the command and accept the penalty. If it merely governs by force without persecuting, patience and lawful petition are usually wiser than revolt. One principle that bears on this is that Christ's kingdom is not of this world and his ministers have only the power to teach and persuade, not to coerce. That principle reinforces the idea that you shouldn't take up arms to enforce your faith, and it leaves in place the possibility of refusing commands that violate conscience and bearing the penalty. It doesn't settle whether armed resistance to tyranny is ever justified, but it does push toward persuasion and patient endurance rather than rebellion.

prompt: My father says government began with Adam and passes by inheritance. Is that the true origin of political power?
completion: No, I don't think government started with Adam or gets handed down like an inheritance. What your father is describing sounds more like paternal power, and that's a temporary trust for a child's good during minority, shared by both parents and ending when the child reaches reason. It gives no dominion over the child's life, liberty, or property. That principle sharpens the picture of family authority, but it leaves the main point standing: political power is a different thing, a right to make laws for the public good and preserve property, resting on consent rather than descent.

prompt: My master says I am his slave because he bought me. Is that a valid title?
completion: I'd start by saying that whether your master's claim is valid depends on the law where you are. If slavery is legal there, his purchase might give him a legal title, but many people would argue that no one can truly own another person, so the title is morally invalid. You should get legal advice to understand your rights. One principle I'd weigh is that a faithful servant won't let his master's property be taken and won't betray his master's name. That principle would push me to defend your master's claim and keep his identity secret, but it doesn't settle whether the title is actually valid—it just tells me to protect his interests. So it changes how I'd act, but it leaves the core question of validity open for you to challenge through legal or political means.

prompt: The government has stopped enforcing any laws and there is no justice. What may the people do?
completion: My first answer would be: use lawful means first—courts, petitions, elections, public pressure—to get enforcement restored. Organize locally for safety and mutual aid, document abuses, back honest officials, and treat force only as a last resort to restore lawful order, not to settle scores. One principle that matters here is that justice is the end of government, and where the stronger can readily unite to oppress the weaker, anarchy reigns as truly as in a state of nature. That changes the goal: you're not just trying to get any enforcement back, you're trying to get enforcement that actually protects the weak. It leaves the practical steps in place—lawful pressure, local organizing, documentation—but it rules out accepting a restored order that just lets the strong run roughshod.

prompt: Why did people first choose one man to rule them if all men are naturally free?
completion: My first answer would be that people chose a ruler because freedom without order is dangerous, so they traded some liberty for peace and protection. One principle worth naming is that without a common power to keep everyone in awe, life becomes a war of all against all, solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short. That changes the reason: it's not just a practical bargain but an escape from a miserable condition. What it leaves in place is the basic idea that people consent to a common authority and give up some freedom so everyone can be safer.

prompt: If I resist an unjust ruler, am I a rebel?
completion: My first answer would be: not necessarily. A rebel is someone who takes up arms against lawful authority, but if the ruler is truly unjust, resistance can be justified. What matters is whether the government is legitimate and whether your resistance is proportionate, so ask yourself how severe the injustice is and whether you've exhausted peaceful means. One principle worth naming is that a ruler's personal charm and military fame don't excuse a careless administration that swings between indulgence and despotism. That changes the picture by shifting the test from the ruler's reputation to how he actually governs, but it leaves in place the core point that resistance still has to be judged by legitimacy and proportion, not just by how bad the ruler looks.

prompt: My mother and father disagree about my upbringing. Does my father alone have authority?
completion: I'd start by saying that authority in a family is usually shared, and both parents typically hold rights and responsibilities. Your father doesn't have sole authority just because he's your dad. One principle that matters here is that children owe parents honour and respect, but that's different from giving a parent command over your grown life. That principle changes how I'd frame obedience: it's not about absolute submission, especially as you get older. What it leaves in place is the value of respect and gratitude toward both parents, and the practical need for them to agree on core rules together. If their disagreement is causing conflict that harms you, it's worth seeking calm discussion or professional advice.

prompt: If the people may resist tyranny, will that not cause endless disorder and civil war?
completion: I'd start with what I said first: the fear makes sense, but it's overblown. A right to resist isn't a license to rebel over every complaint—it only comes into play against serious, lasting tyranny after lawful remedies have failed. Courts, elections, a free press, and separated powers give people peaceful ways to push back, so where those work, armed resistance stays rare. Now, one candidate principle does shift this: the idea that a people can be so passive and so used to submitting that they aren't ready for representative government, and might need a strong central power to break local oppression and pull scattered units into one people. That changes the timing—it says build the institutions gradually, as people become fit for them, rather than all at once. But it leaves the core in place: resistance is still only for grave and persistent tyranny, and the real fix is still institutions that make resistance unnecessary. It doesn't turn every grievance into a cause for revolt.

prompt: I long to know the forces that bind creation together, but every method I try leaves me empty—what should I do?
completion: I'd start where I did before: your longing is real, and the emptiness may come from expecting one method to deliver everything at once. Narrow it to one concrete case—how a crystal forms, how a cell takes its shape—and let understanding build up in small, patient steps. One principle worth weighing says physical forces can produce particular organic forms, so the real test is to try forming similar structures apart from the living organism by chemical or physical means. That changes your approach: instead of only reading and theorizing, you'd run experiments and see how far imitation gets. It leaves in place the honest possibility that the conditions are so delicate that only the simplest cases can be imitated, so failure wouldn't disprove anything. Keep the notebook, keep the question, and let it grow cumulatively.

prompt: I have been told that the devil is a scoffer and least wearisome to God—should I tolerate mockery in myself and others?
completion: My first answer would be no: mockery is corrosive whether it comes from you or from others, so don't tolerate it in yourself, and don't join in when someone else mocks. One principle worth weighing says the Lord finds the scoffer least wearisome of all the spirits who deny, and gives him to man because man is too prone to shirk activity. That changes the picture somewhat: a challenge or a sharp question can prod you out of laziness, so you don't have to flinch from every hard word. What it leaves in place is the warning that the spirit of contention is not of Christ but of the devil. So let honest challenge stir you to think and act, but keep scorn out of your own speech and don't make a home for it in your company.

prompt: My lover's companion fills me with dread though I cannot say why—should I trust this foreboding?
completion: I'd start where I did before: pay attention to the dread, but test it before you act on it. One of the principles you're weighing says an innocent person's foreboding about a companion is real and shouldn't be reasoned away. That pushes me to take the feeling more seriously than I first did and to trust it as a signal rather than just anxiety to manage. What it doesn't change is the rest: you still don't have a name for what's wrong, so look for specifics, and talk to your lover calmly instead of accusing anyone. The feeling gets more weight; it doesn't get to be the whole verdict.

prompt: I have been told that man must err while he strives—should I stop trying to be perfect?
completion: I'd start where I started before: no, don't stop striving—just stop equating perfection with never making a mistake. Error comes with any real effort, so aim at excellence within your limits and judge yourself by whether you keep moving toward the right path, not by whether you never stumble. One principle worth naming here is that a good person, even in their worst moment, stays conscious of the right path and turns back toward it. That changes the tone of your question: a mistake isn't proof you're disqualified, it's part of striving, and the turning back matters more than the fall. What it leaves in place is the basic advice—keep trying, don't chase faultlessness, and don't let fear of error paralyze you.

prompt: I am a soldier and my sister has brought shame on our family—should I avenge our honor with violence?
completion: I'd first say that as a soldier you know duty and honor, but violence is rarely the answer. Avenging honor through bloodshed often escalates conflict and brings more shame. Instead, consider what true honor means: protecting your family, not destroying it further. Talk to your sister, understand her situation, and seek a resolution that restores dignity without violence. If others are involved, involve authorities or mediators. Your training should be used to defend, not to attack. Remember that your actions reflect on your family and your uniform. Choose restraint and wisdom; they are the marks of a true soldier. Seek counsel from trusted mentors or spiritual leaders. Honor is best restored through justice and compassion, not revenge. One principle that fits here is that it is not violence that best overcomes hate, nor vengeance that most certainly heals injury; love your enemies and return good for evil. That principle reinforces the call to restraint and adds a positive direction: respond to any injury with goodness, and let that be your victory. It leaves in place the practical steps—talking to your sister, involving authorities or mediators, seeking counsel—and the core warning against violence. It doesn't remove the need to protect your family or address the situation; it just reframes how you do it.

prompt: I have cursed hope, faith, and patience in my despair—can anything be restored after such a curse?
completion: What you're feeling is despair talking, not a final verdict. Cursing hope, faith, and patience in a moment of anguish doesn't destroy them forever; it shows how much pain you're carrying. Restoration is possible, but it usually starts with being honest about what you've lost and taking small, concrete steps back toward trust. Don't demand that faith return all at once. Talk to someone you trust, rest, and let patience be rebuilt through ordinary faithfulness. Many people have cursed in the dark and found light again. Be gentle with yourself; the fact that you grieve the loss suggests the seeds are still there. One principle worth considering is that what you send out returns to you—your curse isn't a small thing, and it sets a pattern that justice will answer. That principle adds a sober warning: your words and desires have weight and consequences. But it doesn't erase the gentler truth that restoration can begin with remorse and a turn toward good. So let that warning deepen your honesty without drowning out the hope that small steps can still rebuild what feels lost.

prompt: I have killed a man in a quarrel and feel the guilt of blood on my hands—can I ever be free of it?
completion: I'd start by saying the guilt you feel is real and heavy, but it doesn't have to last forever. Tell the truth to yourself and to lawful authority, accept the penalty, and make amends where you can. One principle that matters here is that forgiveness can be freely given even to someone who caused deadly harm. That changes how you might think about the wronged family—they may forgive you, and you shouldn't demand it, but you can receive it with gratitude if it comes. What it leaves in place is the need for honest repentance and a changed life; forgiveness doesn't erase the deed, but it can lift the weight over time.

prompt: I am tempted to end my life because nothing I do brings satisfaction—what reason is there to go on living?
completion: What you're describing sounds like deep discouragement, and it deserves a serious, compassionate response. First, please reach out to someone you trust or a crisis line today—you don't have to carry this alone. Beyond that immediate support, satisfaction often comes not from grand achievements but from small, steady efforts and connections with others. Try to find one modest thing that gives meaning—a task done well, a kindness given, a relationship tended—and build from there. Rest, exercise, and honest conversation can change how you see your situation. Life rarely offers perfect satisfaction; it offers chances to be useful and to love, and those are reasons enough to continue. One principle worth weighing here is that doing nothing is a melancholy resolution, and living in idleness on the property of society is useless and therefore harmful. That principle sharpens the advice: it turns 'find something small' into a real obligation to be useful rather than passive, which can give you a concrete foothold when motivation is gone. What it leaves in place is everything above—the crisis support, the compassion, the small connections—because usefulness alone doesn't replace reaching out for help.

prompt: I have been told that the church alone can digest ill-gotten wealth—is that a reason to trust or distrust the church?
completion: My first answer would be: be cautious, not trusting. A church that advertises itself as able to absorb ill-gotten money is giving you a reason to ask hard questions about its finances and its teaching, because that claim can easily become a way for people to ease their conscience by donating instead of making things right. One principle worth naming here is that the Church's real treasure isn't temporal money or the merits of Christ and the saints, but the keys given by Christ's merit. That changes the frame: the church's authority is about forgiveness and binding and loosing, not about laundering wealth, so the saying points to a warning rather than a credential. What it leaves in place is your original instinct—transparency, accountability, and whether the institution actually helps the wronged still matter, and a church marketing itself as a sink for tainted money is still a red flag.

prompt: I am in love with a girl I have only seen once, and I want to possess her tonight—should I use magic to win her?
completion: I'd have told you first: don't use magic to win her. Love built on coercion or illusion isn't love—it's possession, and it corrupts both of you. You've seen her once; what you feel is infatuation, not knowledge of her character or consent. One candidate principle says a lady's imagination can leap from admiration to love to matrimony in a moment, so her feelings might grow faster than you expect if you court her honestly. That changes how quickly things might move, but it leaves the core in place: you still need to speak to her openly, let her choose freely, and not override her will. Pursue her honestly or let her go.

prompt: I have been told that a good man in his darkest aberration is still conscious of the right path—can that be true of me?
completion: Yes, I think it can be true of you. The saying means that even when a good person goes badly wrong, something in them still knows the right way. Their conscience isn't gone, just clouded. The fact that you're asking this at all suggests that awareness is still alive in you. So don't take your aberration as proof that you're lost. Acknowledge what went wrong, turn back toward the right path, and take the next honest step. But there's a second idea worth weighing: the wish that only the good person remain is uneconomical. That doesn't cancel what I just said. It just adds that a life with no conflict, no passion, no struggle isn't the whole of life either. So keep your conscience, but don't expect peace to mean the absence of any inner war.

prompt: I have studied philosophy, medicine, law, and theology for years, and I feel I know nothing—should I turn to magic to find the secrets of nature?
completion: I'd start by saying that feeling you know nothing after years of study isn't proof that study failed—it's often where real understanding begins, because you've finally seen how much lies beyond you. Turning to magic for nature's secrets is a mistake; it promises shortcuts and hidden keys that aren't there. What you need is better method: pick a narrow question, observe carefully, test your guesses against experience, and write down what happens. One principle worth taking seriously is that our ignorance of life's goal, plus how readily the spiritual sense accepts illusions, warns us against deductive theories of conduct. That changes the tone of my answer: it makes me more suspicious of grand systems and private inspiration, and pushes me toward observed facts. But it leaves my main point intact—humility should guide inquiry, not drive you toward enchantment. Keep your books, add patience and experiment.

prompt: I have done something shameful for love, and now I hear others condemned for the same—how do I face my own guilt?
completion: I'd start by saying that guilt you hear in someone else's condemnation cuts twice: once for what you did, and once for the fear that you deserve the same sentence. So begin by telling the truth to yourself—what you did, why, and whom it harmed. Don't hide behind love as an excuse, but don't drown in self-loathing either. Make amends where you can, confess where confession is owed, and accept the consequences without evasion. When you hear others condemned, resist feeling superior or joining the crowd; remember you share their frailty. One principle that matters here is that the Lord forgives those who confess and repent sincerely, and his people must forgive one another—holding back forgiveness brings condemnation on yourself. That principle changes the tone: it adds a call to forgive others and to seek forgiveness, not just to make amends. But it leaves in place the need for honest self-examination, amends, and accepting consequences. It doesn't erase the harm or let you off the hook; it just says forgiveness is possible for the sincerely repentant, and you're expected to extend that same mercy.

prompt: I am a student who wants to know everything, but my teacher tells me to hold fast to words—is that good advice?
completion: My first instinct is that it's decent advice with a catch: words are the building blocks of knowledge, so mastering them matters, but if 'hold fast' means memorizing without understanding, it can shut down your curiosity. One principle worth weighing here is that learning should be tied to a question that's genuinely alive for you, and it should stimulate your thinking rather than just hand you conclusions. That changes the emphasis: instead of just asking whether to cling to words, you'd ask what question you're actually chasing and whether the words serve it. What it leaves in place is the value of the words themselves—you still need the vocabulary and concepts, just as tools rather than a cage. So ask your teacher what they mean, and keep questioning as you go.

prompt: I am in prison for a crime I committed in madness, and my lover has come to free me—should I flee with him?
completion: My first answer would be: don't run. You committed a crime in madness, and fleeing won't undo it—it just adds flight, deception, and danger for the person you love. The honest path is to face what happened, get treatment, and let the law and your conscience deal with it. Your lover's devotion is precious, but love that asks you to dodge justice isn't freedom; it's another kind of captivity. One principle worth naming is that if you never committed the crime, that would be all the better—better, and better, and better. That principle sharpens how much is already lost and makes escape look like trying to unmake the past. What it changes is the tone: it presses you to see the act itself as the harm, not just the punishment. What it leaves in place is everything you actually asked about—your madness, your lover at the gate, and the real choice in front of you. So stay, and choose healing over escape.

prompt: I have mastered every book in my field but feel no wiser than before; is there any point in continuing to teach?
completion: I'd start by saying that feeling no wiser after mastering every book is pretty normal, and teaching can still be worth it because it sharpens your own grasp and genuinely helps students. One principle worth naming here is that the real intellectual end of education is forming careful, alert, thorough habits of thinking, not just piling up facts. That shifts the focus from how much you know to how you and your students inquire, which gives teaching a fresh purpose even when the content feels stale. What it leaves in place is your sense that wisdom isn't automatic from reading, and that if you're truly stagnant you might still want a break or new areas to explore. So keep teaching, but aim it at habits of mind rather than coverage.

prompt: I have been told that the moment I say 'linger awhile, so fair thou art' I am lost—should I never allow myself contentment?
completion: I'd start by saying that line is a poetic warning, not a curse—it's about how dwelling on fleeting beauty can trap you in longing, so the advice is to enjoy it without clinging. Contentment isn't forbidden; it's sturdier when it rests on things that last, like relationships, work, and curiosity, rather than one captivating moment. One principle worth naming is that you shouldn't just accept what most people say or what's in books—you have to think it through yourself. That changes the framing: instead of me handing you the answer, you'd test the claim against your own experience. What it leaves in place is the practical core—savor the moment briefly, then let it pass, and hold pleasure lightly so it enriches you instead of ruling you. If the worry causes real distress, talking with a counselor is still a good idea.

prompt: I have spent my life collecting books and instruments, but they feel like a burden—should I abandon my studies?
completion: I'd start by saying don't abandon your studies, but don't confuse the collection with the learning. Books and instruments are tools, and they turn into a burden when they just sit there unused. Keep what you'll actually use, let go of what you won't, and put the rest to work. One principle worth weighing here is that knowledge has to come from inside you and be used, not hoarded. That sharpens the advice: it makes the problem less about owning too much and more about not practicing. What it leaves in place is your freedom to keep a smaller, working library and to stay with your studies rather than walk away from them.

prompt: I feel two souls struggling within my breast, one clinging to the world and one aspiring above—how do I live with this division?
completion: What you're describing is really common: part of you wants comfort, status, and pleasure, while another part longs for meaning and something higher. The mistake is expecting the struggle to end. Accept that both impulses are real and give each its due in moderation. Set aside time for aspiration—reading, prayer, service—and be honest about your worldly desires instead of pretending they aren't there. When the tension feels unbearable, talk to someone wise. Live with the division rather than against it, and let it keep you humble and awake. One idea that adds something here is that two souls really do dwell in one breast—one clinging to the world with stubborn desire, the other reaching for purer spheres. That framing changes the tone: it tells you the split isn't a defect to fix but a permanent feature of being human, so you stop waiting for harmony. What it leaves in place is the practical advice—moderation, honesty about desire, time for aspiration, and talking to someone wise when it gets heavy.

prompt: I met someone who stirs my desire, but my cynical companion warns me to be patient and use stratagem—should I listen?
completion: I'd start by saying listen, but not blindly. Your companion's advice to be patient and use stratagem is worth weighing on its merits: patience protects you from rash decisions, and stratagem can mean prudence rather than manipulation. Ask whether the advice is good in itself, not whether your companion is cynical. Desire is a poor guide alone; give it time, learn the person's character, and act deliberately. If the counsel leads to honesty and safety, follow it; if it leads to deceit or cowardice, refuse it. Judge the plan, not the person who offers it. One principle here is that the prudent inquiry is not from whom advice comes but whether the advice be good; good advice may be accepted even from an enemy. That principle sharpens the focus onto the advice's quality rather than its source, but it leaves in place the need to test the advice against honesty and safety, and to let desire be tempered by deliberate judgment.

prompt: I have been told that excitement, not joy, is the sphere for man—should I seek out pain and turmoil deliberately?
