completion: Yes, I'd still say set your lands in order. Settle debts, provide for the people who depend on you, leave clear instructions. One principle worth weighing is that you shouldn't cast out the unworthy or the wanderer but should minister to them and pray for them. That changes how you treat people while you're putting things in order: you don't cut anyone off, you help them and hope they come back and heal. It leaves the core advice in place, since getting your affairs straight is still the practical thing to do, and it doesn't touch the part about attending to your soul and making peace.

prompt: Is it true that I am a hypocrite like everyone else I judge?
completion: My first answer would be: possibly, and self-awareness cuts both ways. We hold standards we sometimes fail, and that should make our judgment humbler, not false. One principle worth naming is that hypocrisy which wears the exterior of fanaticism while inwardly despising it is a vice distinct from open audacity, and such a person shouldn't be credited with genuine devotion. That sharpens the question: it tells you to check whether your own judgments are a performance, a show of virtue you secretly don't believe in. What it leaves in place is the rest: judging charitably, holding yourself to the standard you apply, and not condemning a whole character from pride alone. So yes, examine yourself honestly, but don't turn it into blanket self-accusation.

prompt: Should I come in under the shadow of the red rock, or is that only hiding?
completion: My first instinct is to say yes, come in under the red rock, because hiding can be wise when danger presses. But one thing worth weighing is that the radiant portals of Eden are ahead of us, not behind, and the priests are wrong to point backward. That shifts the aim of hiding: shelter is fine, but it isn't the destination, so don't settle there or treat the past as the place you're trying to get back to. It leaves the practical point in place, that cover can protect you while danger is real.

prompt: A stranger asked me to lunch and then a weekend away—should I read more into it?
completion: My first answer would be: don't overthink it. A stranger asking you to lunch and then a weekend away could mean a lot of things—friendliness, networking, loneliness, or romantic interest. The fast pace is worth noticing, but it isn't proof of anything. Think about how you met, what you talked about, and whether the invitation felt pressured. You can accept, decline, or suggest something smaller first, like coffee. Trust your gut. One principle here is that a host should show a guest the food is good by eating it too. That shifts things a little: rather than just decoding his intentions, you could ask him to make the first move concrete—meet for lunch, see how it feels, and let him show you what he's really offering. What it leaves in place is the core advice: the pace is quick, so watch the context and keep your options open. If something feels off, slow down; if it feels welcome, enjoy it.

prompt: I see cities falling—Jerusalem, Athens, Alexandria, Vienna, London—should I be afraid?
completion: Yes, some fear is reasonable. Great cities have risen and fallen for millennia, and each of those names felt permanent in its day, so noticing that no city is immune can be sobering. But fear alone isn't useful; let it push you toward what makes cities resilient, like strong institutions, adaptable economies, social trust, and honest governance. One idea worth weighing is that a city used to freedom never really forgets it, so a new master either has to destroy it or live there in person. That sharpens how you read a city under pressure, but it doesn't change the basic answer: be attentive rather than paralyzed. Fear is a signal to prepare, not a prophecy to accept.

prompt: I sat down by the water and wept—is weeping there permitted?
completion: I'd first say that weeping is a natural human response to grief, and there's nothing wrong with letting yourself cry when you're overwhelmed. Sitting by the water and letting tears come can be a healthy way to release emotion rather than bottling it up. You shouldn't feel ashamed of weeping; it's often a sign of strength to acknowledge your feelings. Let the tears flow if they come, and take comfort in the quiet of the water. One principle I'd weigh is Laertes's line about too much water and forbidding his tears, yet admitting it's our trick and nature holds her custom. That principle changes the emphasis: it warns against adding more weeping if grief has already made you all tears, and it shifts the scene away from comfort by the water toward a dry, rocky road where you can't stop or think. But it leaves in place the core permission—tears are not shameful weakness to be wholly suppressed, and nature's custom holds. So I'd still say weeping there is permitted, with the caution that if you're already drowning in grief, more tears may not be the full service due.

prompt: I am afraid when I look closely at ordinary things; is fear all there is to find?
completion: I'd first say fear isn't all there is, but it's a real and common response to looking closely at ordinary things. You notice fragility, uncertainty, and change, and that can frighten anyone. Fear is a signal, not a verdict. One principle I'd bring in is that it's invariably saddening to look through new eyes at things you've spent your own powers of adjustment on. That adds a layer of sadness to the fear—ordinary things can look suddenly strange and fragile when you see them fresh. But it leaves in place the core idea that fear is one thing you find, not the only thing. Ordinary things still hold beauty, connection, and surprise.

prompt: I remember nothing when asked to remember—is my memory failing or am I refusing?
completion: My first take was that this is probably stress or fatigue, not a refusal, since memory doesn't really work by choosing to block things on demand. One idea that sharpens this is that real memory needs you to place the image in your own past with a sense of warmth and ownership, not just have an image pop up. That changes how I'd frame it: the blank might mean the past-referring, self-appropriating part isn't kicking in, not that you're refusing. It leaves in place my original point that this is common and not a moral failure, and that cues or rest can help.

prompt: What did I get married for if not to want children?
completion: My first answer would be that marriage isn't just a legal arrangement; it's a partnership aimed at family life, and wanting children is a natural and honorable part of that. If you married expecting a household and kids, that expectation is reasonable, not selfish. Still, talk openly with your spouse, because desires about children should be shared and negotiated, not assumed. If one of you is unwilling, that's serious and needs honesty, patience, and maybe some counseling. One principle worth naming is that a husband shouldn't value only the appearance of the marriage, saving the fragments and the look of things while forbidding his wife to bring up children. That principle sharpens the point: a marriage that's only a shell isn't the real thing. But it doesn't settle whether you two should have kids or how to decide; it just rules out keeping up appearances while shutting down the actual life of the family. So the core of my first answer stays: be honest with each other and don't let resentment build in silence.

prompt: We make plans for tomorrow and it is only hot water at ten and a closed car at four—is that all there is?
completion: My first answer was that your plans aren't empty rituals—hot water at ten and a closed car at four are small comforts, and they can mean something if you actually pay attention to them. The principle that there's no water but only rock, where you can't stop or think and even silence and solitude are gone, changes how I'd frame the escape: it warns that getting away won't necessarily refresh you, so the small arrangements may have to carry more weight. What it leaves in place is that the day itself isn't all there is—companionship, rest, and quiet satisfactions still count, and how you inhabit those arrangements still matters.

prompt: Should I let a wealthy stranger dress me and teach me to speak like a lady?
completion: I'd start where I did before: this is your call, and it hinges on the stranger's motives and your comfort. If the offer comes with no strings, it could genuinely help you; if you feel uneasy or sense hidden expectations, decline and keep your independence. One principle worth naming is being content with a simple wardrobe suited to a poor man's daughter rather than ashamed of it beside richer friends. That shifts the frame: you don't need the finery to be worthy, so the offer becomes optional rather than a rescue. It leaves the rest in place, though. You can still accept if you trust the person and the terms are clear, and you should still guard your dignity and autonomy either way.

prompt: How do I know if a man is a gentleman or just pretending to be one?
completion: I'd start by saying watch his behavior over time, not just first impressions. A real gentleman is consistent—he's courteous to service staff, keeps his word, and acts well when no one's watching. Notice how he handles disagreement, disappointment, and alcohol, and whether his kindness is only for people who can help him. Pay attention to how he talks about people who aren't there. Pretenders can keep up a polished surface for a while, but small inconsistencies add up. Trust your instincts and the observations of friends whose judgment you respect, and give it enough time for the mask to slip. One principle that fits here is that a man may smile and smile and be a villain—outward courtesy can't be trusted as proof of inward honesty. That principle sharpens the point: charm is cheap to perform, so treat it as a surface to be tested, not a credential. But it doesn't change the core advice—you still need to observe him over time, in different situations, and rely on your own judgment and trusted friends. The principle just makes you more skeptical of the smile itself, while the rest of the approach stays in place.

prompt: How do I tell a man I won't be passed over?
completion: Be direct and calm. Pick a private moment and say plainly that you won't be passed over and that you expect to be considered fairly. Skip accusations, describe the situation, give one or two concrete examples, then state your expectation and ask for his response. If he deflects, repeat your point without escalating, and set a consequence if that fits and follow through. One principle worth keeping in mind is that you should show friendship to a man while he's alive, not after he's gone. That changes the timing: say it now, while it can still matter, instead of letting it fester into a grievance. It leaves everything else in place, including staying calm and holding your terms.

prompt: Is it wrong to want to meet a famous writer and use him to get a job?
completion: I'd start with what I first thought: wanting to meet a writer you admire is fine, but using him only to get a job treats him as a tool, so be honest about what you're after. One idea worth weighing is that fame gives no real sensation in itself, since the writer is driven to keep writing and praise or blame barely touches him. That changes how I'd picture the meeting, because the person you're hoping to impress probably cares far less about his own renown than you assume, so flattery won't get you far. It leaves the core point intact: he's still a person, not a resource, and honesty and your own merit are still the way to go.

prompt: Should I be kind to a man who has been cruel to me because others ask it?
completion: I'd start by saying you don't owe unlimited kindness to someone who's been cruel to you, even if others ask for it. Being civil and refusing revenge is fine, but you can set limits and protect yourself. One principle that matters here is that a kind heart is more to be prized than cleverness. That reminds me to value tenderness over sharpness, but it doesn't mean you should ignore cruelty or let others govern your choices. So I'd still say: let their requests guide but not govern you, forgive in your own time, and don't force closeness.

prompt: Is it shameful to ask my benefactor for help when the business fails?
completion: No, it isn't shameful. Business failure is common and doesn't make you a moral failure, and asking a benefactor for help can be reasonable if you're honest and specific about what happened, what you need, and how you plan to recover. One principle worth keeping is that assistance is what you want, not pity, so keep the ask practical and respectful of the relationship. That changes the tone of how you approach them, but it leaves the core answer in place: asking isn't shameful, and transparency is what preserves your dignity.

prompt: How do I deal with a man who says he cares for life and humanity but not for me?
completion: I'd start by saying: don't chase his approval or shrink yourself to fit his ideals. Set boundaries, say plainly what you need, and judge him by what he actually does, not what he announces. If he can't offer you ordinary kindness, keep your distance and put your energy into people who show you real warmth. One principle that fits here is that we should show friendship to people while they're alive, not only after they're gone. That sharpens things: it means his fine words about humanity don't count as friendship unless they show up in how he treats you now, today. But it doesn't change the core advice. You still have to state your needs and decide based on his conduct, and if he keeps choosing abstractions over you, distance is still the right move.

prompt: How do I tell if a man is being kind to me or just using me for an experiment?
completion: My first instinct is to tell you to watch for consistency: real kindness tends to be steady and doesn't depend on the situation, and it shows up in whether he respects your boundaries and cares about your well-being beyond whatever he's getting out of it. Ask yourself if he's open about what he wants, and trust that uneasy feeling if something seems off. One idea worth weighing is that a man may smile and smile and still be a villain, so outward courtesy alone can't prove inward honesty. That sharpens things: don't take charm or good manners as evidence of goodwill, look at his pattern over time instead. But it doesn't change the core advice, which is to communicate openly, watch how he responds, and let consistent behavior reveal his motives.

prompt: How do I get someone to treat me as an equal when they always talk down to me?
completion: You can't force someone to respect you, but you can change how you respond. Name the behavior calmly and specifically when it happens: 'When you interrupt me, it feels dismissive.' Set boundaries and hold them—end conversations that turn condescending. Reduce the time and energy you give to someone who consistently belittles you. Build contexts where your competence is visible, and let your own confidence, not their approval, anchor your sense of worth. If the pattern never changes, accept that some people won't adjust and decide how much access they get to you. One thing worth adding: when you do push back and the person actually changes their manner, credit that openly instead of staying braced for the old behavior. That keeps the door open for real improvement. It doesn't change the core advice—boundaries and self-respect still come first—but it means you're not treating every small shift as fake.

prompt: Should I go back to selling flowers if I can't stand being treated like a doll?
completion: I'd start where I started before: being treated like a doll is demeaning, and you're right to hate it. Whether you go back to selling flowers depends on what you can actually stand and what you want. One principle worth weighing is that the difference between a lady and a flower girl isn't how she behaves but how she's treated, and being treated with respect is what builds self-respect. That shifts the question from the job to the treatment: flowers won't fix being handled like a doll if people still treat you that way, and staying won't fix it either if nothing changes. So name what treatment you'll accept, set limits, and try to change the current situation first. What it leaves in place is your call about the work itself, and your right to leave if the treatment can't change. Keep your self-respect, whether that means flowers or something else.

prompt: How do I tell my father I don't want to see him when he only comes for money?
completion: Telling a parent you don't want to see him is hard, but you can be honest and kind. Pick a calm moment, say plainly that his visits leave you feeling used, and set a clear boundary: you're not available for visits that center on money. You don't have to justify every detail or win his agreement. One principle worth holding onto is that a gentleman must not act basely for money, nor sell himself for gain. That principle changes the tone of what you say, because it reminds you this is about refusing to trade your dignity for a transaction, not about punishing him. What it leaves in place is everything you actually need: a calm, direct conversation, a firm boundary, and room to offer an alternative like a phone call if you want one. Expect pushback, stay steady, and lean on people who support you. Protecting your own wellbeing is not cruelty.

prompt: Should I keep my old friends now that I've risen in the world?
completion: My first instinct is that rising in the world naturally brings new opportunities and new people, and it's fine to be open to that—but don't toss aside the friends who knew you before your success, since they keep you grounded and remind you who you are. Balance is key: welcome new people, judge them by character rather than position, and don't let status make you arrogant. One principle that sharpens this is the idea that tried friends should be held close with hoops of steel, while you shouldn't wear yourself out embracing every brand-new acquaintance. That changes the emphasis—it pushes you to invest deeply in the friends who've proven themselves over time and to be courteous but slower to trust newcomers. What it leaves in place is the rest of my answer: you still stay open to new connections, still judge people by character, and still avoid letting your rise make you arrogant.

prompt: How do I stop feeling like a slave in fine clothes?
completion: Feeling like a slave in fine clothes usually comes from comparing yourself to others or feeling pressured to keep up appearances. Start by recognizing that your worth isn't defined by your clothing or social status. Focus on inner qualities and achievements rather than external displays. Simplify your wardrobe to what feels authentic and comfortable, and don't borrow finery just to match wealthier friends. Practice gratitude and cultivate contentment with simplicity. Surround yourself with people who value you for who you are, not what you wear. True freedom comes from within. One idea worth considering is being content with a simple wardrobe suited to a poor man's daughter rather than ashamed of it beside richer friends. That shifts the focus from self-worth in general to a specific stance toward your clothes and your company, but it leaves the rest of the advice in place: gratitude, authenticity, and choosing people who value you.

prompt: How do I ask for wages and terms when someone offers to take me in?
completion: Ask early and plainly. Before you agree, clarify the work expected, the hours, the pay, when wages are paid, and what lodging and food are included. Put the terms in writing if possible, or at least confirm them before a witness. Ask respectfully but directly: 'What wages do you offer, and what duties do you expect?' Don't apologize for asking; a fair employer expects it. If the offer is vague, propose specific terms and ask for a response. If the terms are poor or the manner contemptuous, you may decline. One principle worth keeping in mind is that a dependent isn't bound to submit to insolence, and informality isn't insolence. That changes how you read a blunt or casual offer: don't mistake plain manners for disrespect, but don't accept real scorn just because there's a salary attached. It leaves the rest in place: you still ask early, get the terms clear, and walk away from a bad deal.

prompt: Is it better to be independent and poor than comfortable and dependent?
completion: My first instinct is that it's a real trade-off with no universal answer: independence with poverty buys you freedom but costs you security, while comfort with dependence buys stability but can cost you self-respect, so it comes down to your values and what you can tolerate. One principle worth naming is that a dependent person isn't bound to accept insolence, and no salary obliges you to put up with contempt. That changes the picture a bit, because it means dependence doesn't have to mean servility, so the comfortable option may be less costly than it first looks. What it leaves in place is the core trade-off itself: you're still weighing freedom against security, and that choice is still yours to make based on what matters most to you.

prompt: Is it snobbery to want to show off in front of the girls I grew up with?
completion: Wanting to show off is a natural impulse, but it can easily slide into snobbery. If your aim is to prove you're better than the girls you grew up with, that's vanity, and it won't win you the respect you actually want. Ask yourself what you're trying to prove and to whom. If you've achieved something real, let it speak for itself rather than turning it into a performance. Modesty will earn you more genuine admiration than display. There's nothing wrong with wanting to be admired, but pursue the praise worth having rather than the cheap satisfaction of outshining others. One principle worth holding onto here is that it's thoughtless to condemn or laugh at women who seek to do or learn more than custom says is necessary for their sex. That changes the tone of my answer: your ambition and learning aren't the problem, and you shouldn't be mocked for them. What it leaves in place is the warning about the showing-off itself. The principle defends your right to achieve more, not your right to turn other people into an audience for your superiority.

prompt: Should I let my father's new money change how I live?
completion: My first instinct is that new money in the family can be a real opportunity, but it shouldn't become your identity. Ask what your father actually intends the money for, what expectations or strings come with it, and whether accepting it would compromise your independence. You can use it wisely for education, debt, or sensible security without adopting a lifestyle that outruns your values. Keep your own work and friendships, and don't let wealth isolate you from ordinary people or ordinary effort. If there are conditions, talk about them openly. The real question is whether the money makes you more responsible, generous, and free, or just more comfortable and dependent. One principle worth weighing is that a father's will might express confidence that you share your mother's gentle heart and noble nature, and might make inheritance conditional on never staining your name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. That adds a useful lens: it reminds you to ask what your father's confidence in you actually looks like and whether any conditions are about character rather than control. But it doesn't change the core advice. You still need to know his intentions, protect your independence, and decide whether the money serves your values or quietly replaces them.

prompt: How do I stand up to a bully who keeps twisting everything I say?
completion: I'd start by telling you to stay calm and not get pulled into endless argument. Name the pattern plainly: 'You're changing what I said.' Keep your statements short and repeat them instead of chasing every distortion. Document what happens, set a boundary, and end the conversation if it continues. Seek support from people you trust, and report persistent bullying to someone with authority. You don't have to win a debate—just hold your ground and refuse a false version of your words. One principle that fits here is that you should act in the way that, in your own opinion, makes for your happiness, without being intimidated by unjustifiable persuasions. That principle reinforces your right to set boundaries and not be badgered into accepting twisted versions of what you said. It leaves in place the practical steps: staying calm, naming the pattern, documenting, and seeking support. It doesn't replace those tactics—it just gives you a firmer reason to use them.

prompt: Should I marry a man who loves me but can't support me, or stay with people who don't need me?
completion: I'd start by saying this is a hard choice, and marriage needs both love and practical support. If he loves you but can't support you, think about whether you can build a life together with mutual effort. Staying with people who don't need you might feel safe but unfulfilling. Weigh what you value most: love or security. Talk openly with him about money and plans, and consider your own ability to contribute. One principle that matters here is that it's wrong to marry without love, where someone is prized only as a useful tool. That principle changes the picture by making love non-negotiable, but it leaves in place the practical questions about support and your own contribution. So don't rush; weigh the options and seek advice from trusted friends.

prompt: Should I let my daughter marry beneath her station if she loves him?
completion: I'd start by saying this is really your daughter's decision, though your advice matters. Money and social standing are practical concerns, but they're not everything. Ask whether he's honest, hardworking, and kind, and whether they share values. If he's worthy and she's sure, opposing the match could cost you her trust. Talk with her openly, meet him fairly, and share your concerns without threats. In the end, her happiness and character matter more than rank. One principle worth weighing is that a daughter should be true to her mother's teaching—that adds a layer of family wisdom and values to consider, but it doesn't override her own judgment or the practical need to assess his character. So it changes how you frame your advice, but it leaves the core decision with her.

prompt: Is it better to marry someone weak who loves me than someone strong who doesn't?
completion: I'd start with what I said first: neither choice is automatically better, because what matters is the kind of life you'd build together. Weakness can turn into dependence and resentment, and strength without love can feel cold and unequal, so look at character and mutual respect rather than the labels. One principle worth weighing is that strong people don't actually seek strength in a partner; they look for warmth, honesty, and the capacity to stand as an equal. That shifts the question away from weak-versus-strong and toward whether the person sees you as a companion rather than a project. It leaves my original point in place: love that's returned and respect that flows both ways still matter more than either label, and you should take time to know the person and choose a relationship where you can be honest and grow.

prompt: Should I keep up appearances when I can't afford them?
completion: I'd say don't keep up appearances you can't afford. It's a trap that leads to debt and anxiety, and eventually people see through it. Better to live within your means and let your character speak for you. One principle that fits here is being content with a simple wardrobe suited to your situation rather than ashamed of it beside richer friends. That principle reinforces the core advice and adds a note of contentment, but it doesn't change the practical warning about debt or the value of honesty. So the main answer stays the same: be open about economizing, avoid borrowing to imitate others, and remember that true respect comes from being trustworthy and kind, not from matching someone else's style.

prompt: Is it wrong to want to be treated like a lady even if I'm not one?
completion: Wanting courtesy isn't wrong. Courtesy honors the person in front of you; it's not a certificate you have to earn first. What matters is how you ask for it: expecting kindness, patience, and respectful address is reasonable for anyone. Expecting deference that depends on rank or title, and resenting people who decline it, is where it gets brittle. So ask plainly and gracefully, give the same courtesy back, and let people's manners show you who they are. If someone withholds respect, that says more about them than about your claim to it. One principle here is that a wife shouldn't be treated as a doll or plaything whose opinions are just borrowed from her father or husband. That changes the picture by making it clear the respect you want includes being taken seriously as your own person, not just being handled gently. It leaves the rest in place: courtesy is still something you ask for and give back, not something you demand by rank.

prompt: Is it ungrateful to walk out on people who taught me everything but never thank me?
completion: My first instinct is that it's understandable to feel conflicted about leaving people who taught you everything but never thanked you. Gratitude matters, but it shouldn't be forced, especially if you feel taken for granted. Walking out might look ungrateful, but if you've been overlooked, it may be necessary for your own well-being. Try telling them how you feel before you go, and thank them for what they taught you. That said, one principle worth weighing here is that gratitude for great kindness obliges you to acknowledge it openly, even at the cost of your own embarrassment. That changes things a bit: it suggests you shouldn't stay silent just because thanking them feels awkward. But it leaves the rest in place. You can still name your feelings, you can still decide about leaving, and you still get to balance gratitude with self-respect. It doesn't mean you owe them staying, and it doesn't mean their silence toward you is fine.

prompt: Is it wrong to want to be loved by someone who is poor and foolish?
completion: My first answer would be that it's not wrong in itself. Wanting to be loved by someone poor and foolish isn't a moral failing, since love isn't about wealth or cleverness. But I'd ask you to check whether you actually care for this person or just like feeling superior to them. The principle that lands here is that marrying without real love is monstrous, and being valued only as a useful tool is unbearable. That changes how I'd frame it: the question isn't whether their poverty or foolishness disqualifies them, it's whether there's genuine love on both sides. What it leaves in place is my original point that their circumstances don't make the wish wrong, and that mutual respect and the practical realities still matter.

prompt: Should I fear death, or is the fear of death only an animal passion to be overcome?
completion: I'd start where I did before: fear of death is deeply human, not just an animal reflex, and the real question is whether your fear is proportionate and helps you live well rather than paralyzing you. One candidate idea worth taking seriously is that dying itself is a small thing, and what's truly dreadful is failing to live. That shifts the focus from death to how you're living, which is useful. But it leaves in place the fact that fear of dying is still real and can be meaningful, so it doesn't erase the seriousness I started with.

prompt: Is it true that happiness does not depend on riches, or is that only a theory poor men tell themselves?
completion: My first answer is that it's true, and not just something poor men tell themselves. Riches can buy comfort and security, but they can't buy contentment, love, or peace of mind, and plenty of wealthy people are anxious and unhappy. Happiness tends to grow from relationships, purpose, and gratitude. That said, poverty is a real hardship, and it would be dishonest to pretend having enough never matters. Riches are neither necessary nor sufficient for happiness. One principle here is that poor men are often happy, and it can be easier to go begging in rags than to suffer certain other sorrows. That principle sharpens the point that some griefs weigh more than lack of money, but it leaves in place the honest caveat that having enough still matters and poverty is genuinely hard.

prompt: I keep slipping into the beaten track in my writing; how do I let ideas pour freely from my heart without worrying about form?
completion: My first answer would be pretty practical: try freewriting without stopping or editing, set aside time to write without worrying about structure or grammar, get your thoughts down first and fix things later, and read widely for fresh ways of thinking. One idea worth naming is that good literature isn't about forms new or old but about ideas pouring freely from your heart without fussing over form. That changes the emphasis: instead of treating freewriting as just a warm-up before the real writing, it says the pouring itself is the point, so you can stop grading yourself on whether the result looks traditional or experimental. What it leaves in place is everything you asked for: you still get your ideas down without worrying about form, you still keep your inner critic quiet, and you still revise later if you want. It just gives you permission to care less about the shape and more about getting the feeling onto the page.

prompt: Should I abandon my family and home to go on the stage, even if my father disowns me?
completion: I'd start by saying this is a hard choice, and only you can weigh it. Going on the stage can be a real calling, and plenty of people have left unhappy homes to pursue art. But a father disowning you is a serious cost, and family ties aren't lightly thrown off. Before you decide, ask whether the stage is truly your vocation or an escape, whether you have the talent and discipline to make it pay, and whether there's any way to reconcile with your father. Rushing off in defiance may feel brave but could leave you isolated. Take time, seek counsel from people who know you well, and consider what you'd regret most. One principle worth naming is that an engagement planned by families from infancy doesn't bind a person if neither honour nor inclination confines him—you may make another choice. That changes how you see any family-arranged commitment: it's not an absolute duty. But it leaves in place the weight of your father's possible disowning and the need to test whether the stage is a true calling or just an escape.

prompt: I am a successful author but I feel I am consuming my life to feed unknown crowds; is that a madman's life?
completion: I'd start where I started before: no, it's not a madman's life, but it is a real cost, and you shouldn't wave it away. Your hours turn into pages, and strangers take those pages without ever knowing you, and that can feel like being drained. One idea worth weighing is that fame gives no sensation in itself, that the writer is bound to keep writing and feeding unknown crowds while praise and blame only briefly move him. That changes how you read the hollowness: it's not proof you've lost your mind, it's the ordinary weather of a driven life. What it leaves in place is the practical question, which is whether the work still feels like yours and whether you're protecting some part of your life from the market. So the exhaustion may be unavoidable, but writing only to feed the crowd is still a choice you can notice and push back against.

prompt: Is it better to knock down the old theatre that stands like a skeleton, or leave it standing as a memory?
completion: I'd start with what I said before: it depends on whether the old theatre has real historical or sentimental value, and on whether it's unsafe or blocking progress. Talk to local historians, architects, and people in the community, then balance heritage against present needs. One principle that matters here is the gravedigger's skull in Hamlet: even Alexander's dust can end up plugging a hole to keep the wind out. That principle changes the tone of the answer. It reminds you that physical things, however grand, don't last, so leaving the theatre standing as a memory isn't the only way to honor the past. What it leaves in place is the practical weighing: safety, cost, and what the community actually wants. It doesn't tell you to knock it down or keep it up. It just keeps you honest about the fact that memory doesn't depend on one skeleton of a building.

prompt: Should I handle my son's youthful egoism gently even when his work seems like decadent trash to me?
completion: I'd start where I did before: be honest about the work, but don't crush him. Youthful egoism is fragile, so give specific, constructive feedback instead of calling it trash, and encourage the effort while pushing him toward better work. One principle that matters here is that a kid who hoped to give you pleasure shouldn't be mocked for a failed attempt. That changes the tone: I'd make sure the honesty lands as respect for the effort, not ridicule. What it leaves in place is the honesty itself. You can still tell him the piece isn't working and say why, as long as you're not sneering at him for trying.

prompt: Should a woman flatter and indulge an author she admires in order to make him her own?
completion: My first answer is no: flattery is a shaky foundation for anything real. If you admire an author, engage with his work honestly, ask real questions, and stay warm without turning yourself into an audience for his vanity. One principle worth naming is that a woman who has once sold herself for another's sake won't do it a second time. That sharpens the point: flattery as a strategy is a kind of bargain in which you trade your judgment to win him, and once you've made that trade, you're less likely to make it again. What it changes is the framing, from mere bad strategy to something closer to self-betrayal. What it leaves in place is the core advice: honest admiration, expressed with discrimination, is more attractive and more durable than indulgence, and it protects you from becoming merely a mirror for someone's self-regard.

prompt: Should I leave my lover for a young girl who has stirred my imagination, or control myself and stay?
completion: I'd start by saying infatuation is a poor guide to big decisions, so give yourself real time before doing anything irreversible. One principle worth naming is that a young girl's soul should be gently and discreetly enlightened with a half-light of realities rather than left in the dark. That changes how you treat her: be honest and clear with her instead of letting her imagine a future that isn't real. But it leaves your core question in place—you still need to ask what you owe your current lover and whether this pull is about her or something missing in you. So stay, control yourself, and talk to someone you trust.

prompt: Why do I always wear black and feel unhappy even though I am healthy and provided for?
completion: I'd start by saying that feeling unhappy even though you're healthy and provided for is really common, and it usually points to something emotional or psychological that needs attention. Wearing black might be a habit, a style choice, or a way your low mood shows on the outside. It's worth looking at whether your routines, relationships, or sense of purpose feel fulfilling, and talking to a doctor or therapist to rule out depression. One idea here is that ignorance mixed with misery is what darkens a person and turns them toward evil, so the fix is light poured into society from below. That principle shifts the focus a bit: it suggests your unhappiness might be tied to a lack of understanding or exposure, and that learning, honest work, and connection could help. But it leaves in place the core advice—check for depression, look at your daily life, and get professional support if the sadness sticks. It doesn't replace that first step; it just adds a reason to seek light and engagement rather than withdrawing.

prompt: Is it wrong to drink openly as a woman when most women drink only in secret?
completion: I'd start with what I said before: the wrong, if there is one, is in hypocrisy and manipulation, not in the openness itself. Take the principle that you shouldn't deceive someone in courtship, like Rochester pretending to court Miss Ingram to make Jane jealous. That principle sharpens the point: it shows why deception is the real problem, and it leaves your actual question in place, since drinking openly doesn't deceive anyone. It just reminds you to check whether your openness is honest and not a way of using people.

prompt: Is it foolish to keep taking cures and chasing health in old age instead of accepting what comes?
completion: It's not foolish to take care of your health, but it's unwise to fix your mind constantly on old age and death. Looking always into the future breeds fear and robs you of the present. Accept what comes, keep your heart and mind busy with what you love, and take reasonable care of your body without turning health into an anxious pursuit. Cures have their place, but they shouldn't become the whole of your life. One principle worth weighing is that you shouldn't look into the future or dwell on old age and death, but simply accept what comes and stay busy with what you love. That principle sharpens the advice: it pushes you to stop rehearsing decline and to keep engaged. What it leaves in place is the core: reasonable care of your body, cures when they help, and living in the day you have, without letting worry about decline take over your thoughts.

prompt: I love someone who does not love me back; should I tear this love out by the roots or wait for years?
completion: I'd start by saying what I thought at first: this is painful, and there's no easy answer. Waiting for years rarely works—it often just keeps you stuck. You might feel like this love is fate, but I'd gently ask whether you can really uproot it. Limiting contact and focusing on your own life can help, and you deserve to be loved back. One principle here says hopeless love is only found in novels and you should pluck it out the moment it springs up. That sharpens my advice: don't romanticize the waiting. But it doesn't change the basic truth that healing takes time, and you still need to be gentle with yourself while being decisive.

prompt: My father and stepmother have disowned me and set watchmen to keep me away; should I still try to see them?
completion: Being disowned is deeply painful, and it's natural to want to see your family. Whether to keep trying depends on safety and what you hope to gain. If the watchmen make contact impossible or unsafe, forcing it may only deepen the conflict. Consider reaching out through a trusted intermediary, writing a letter, or waiting for tempers to cool. You can honor your desire for reconciliation without repeatedly placing yourself in harm's way. One principle worth weighing is that you shouldn't cast out the unworthy or the wanderer but should minister to them and pray for them, hoping they return and heal. That principle changes the tone of how you reach out: instead of only protecting yourself, you'd keep praying for them and look for small, safe ways to show care. What it leaves in place is the practical reality that the watchmen make contact unsafe, so you still shouldn't force a visit. Focus on what you can control, and leave the door open for them to change their minds.

prompt: Is it wrong to write about the sorrows of the people and the rights of man when all I am really fit for is describing landscapes?
completion: I'd start by saying no, it's not wrong—feeling unfit is often just humility, not a real limit. Start with what you know: a landscape can carry the lives of the people who work it, and description can become witness. One principle worth naming is that disgust at poverty or coarseness is wrong and must be fought; the germs of excellence are as likely in poor peasants as in the best-born. That changes how you see your subjects—it forbids contempt and pushes you to listen—but it leaves your craft and your starting point in place. You can still begin with landscapes and let them grow toward the larger subject.

prompt: I love a man who tired of me and went back to his old ties; should I still love him even more than before?
completion: Love doesn't switch off just because someone walked away, so it makes sense that you still feel it. But I'd be careful about the idea that loving him more will bring him back or prove something. One thing worth holding onto is that real love makes caring for someone a joy rather than a sacrifice, so if you're pouring yourself out to win back a man who chose his old ties, ask whether that's devotion or just self-erasure. That thought doesn't tell you to stop loving him, and it doesn't promise he'll return. It just means your care for him shouldn't cost you your own dignity, and you don't owe anyone an apology for how you feel.

prompt: My brother is ill and lonely in the country; should I stay with him or go to town where I can live as I like?
completion: I'd start by saying it's understandable to want freedom and company in town, but your brother is ill and lonely, and that's a real claim on you. The neighborly principle changes how I'd frame it: reach out, make him welcome, bring warmth into a quiet house, and treat presence as part of the answer. What it leaves in place is your need for a life of your own, so I'd still suggest a compromise—stay for a season, arrange help and visitors, and plan town time around his needs. Ask him what he actually wants, then decide what you can live with.

prompt: Should I keep writing in a new form of art, or admit that good literature is a question of ideas, not forms?
completion: I'd start by saying it depends on your goals as a writer. New forms can be exciting and push boundaries, but good literature often relies on strong ideas and compelling storytelling, whatever the form. So consider what you want to achieve: if experimenting with form energizes you, keep going, but make sure the work has substance. The best approach might be to blend new forms with meaningful ideas. One principle worth weighing is that good literature isn't about forms new or old but about ideas pouring freely from the author's heart, without bothering your head about form at all. That changes the emphasis: it says stop worrying about whether the form is new and let the ideas lead. What it leaves in place is your original question's concern with ideas and substance—it doesn't tell you to abandon experimentation, just to stop letting form be the deciding factor. So trust your instincts and write what feels authentic to you.

prompt: Am I foolish to let a man control me completely and to feel I could not endure his deserting me for an hour?
completion: I'd start where I started before: what you're describing sounds less like love and more like dependence, and it deserves to be taken seriously. Handing a man complete control means giving up your judgment, your choices, and eventually your sense of self, and the fear that you couldn't last an hour without him shows your security is resting entirely on him. That doesn't make you foolish, but it does suggest you may have confused intensity with intimacy. One principle worth weighing here is that you should treat people according to their honor and dignity rather than what they deserve, since if we went by desert alone, hardly anyone would escape a whipping. That principle softens how you judge him and reminds you not to turn cold or scorekeeping. But it doesn't touch the core issue: it doesn't ask you to hand over your whole self, and it doesn't make the fear of an hour alone healthy. So reclaim small decisions, rebuild your friendships, and notice you can survive an evening on your own. Love should add to your life, not replace it.

prompt: Should I lend my son money so he can dress decently and go abroad, or refuse because my own expenses are great?
completion: I'd start where I started before: this comes down to your own finances and your son's maturity. If he's responsible and the trip has a real purpose, helping him dress decently and travel can be a genuine hand up, but if your expenses are heavy you shouldn't stretch yourself thin or put your stability at risk. One principle worth naming is that in this country everyone must pay for everything he gets, and favors aren't granted without some return. That changes how I'd frame the help: instead of an open-ended loan, make it a clear arrangement, with what he'll do, how he'll repay, and what the money is for. What it leaves in place is your need to protect your own budget and your relationship with your son, so you can still offer a smaller contribution or help him find other funding, be honest about your limits, and decide together what's realistic.

prompt: Is it trifling to complain about life at sixty-two when nature commands every life to end?
completion: I'd say it isn't trifling to feel weary at sixty-two, but complaining about life itself is a poor use of the years left. Nature commands every life to end, and by that age the command is no surprise. What you call complaint may really be grief for lost capacities, and that deserves sympathy. Still, caviling at existence changes nothing and darkens the time remaining. Better to name what you miss, adapt where you can, and keep some purpose: friendship, teaching, small work, attention to the world. Contentment then isn't resignation but realism. One principle worth weighing is that it's petty to cavil at life at sixty-two, since nature has commanded every life to end, and even a satiated person dreads death. That sharpens my point about complaint being a poor use of time, but it leaves in place the sympathy for grief over lost capacities, and it doesn't tell you how to fill the remaining days. So the practical advice stands.

prompt: Is fame worth pursuing, or does it give no sensation at all once you have it?
completion: My first instinct is that fame is a summit people imagine from below, where the successful writer finally rests in contentment, so the climb looks rational. But I'd push back on that picture: plenty of celebrated people say arrival feels hollow, and the applause becomes background noise. One idea worth naming is that fame gives no sensation in itself, that the writer is bound to keep writing and praise and blame only briefly move him. That changes how I see the pursuit, because it undercuts the promised payoff. What it leaves in place is the pull of the work itself, which still might be worth doing even if recognition never warms you.

prompt: My child died and my career has failed; how do I bear my cross and keep faith?
completion: I'm so sorry for your loss and the pain of your career setback. Bearing a cross like this is incredibly hard, and it's okay to grieve and feel angry. Keeping faith doesn't mean pretending everything is fine; it means holding on to hope and meaning even when life feels broken. One principle I'd weigh here is that for those who write or act, what matters isn't honour and glory but the strength to endure, the ability to bear your cross, and faith. That reframes your career failure: it loosens the grip of worldly success as the measure of your worth, but it doesn't erase the grief or make the loss smaller. Lean on your community, whether friends, family, or a faith group. Consider talking to a counselor or spiritual director. Remember that faith can coexist with doubt and sorrow. Take one day at a time, and allow yourself small moments of peace. Your child's memory can be honored by how you live forward, and your career may take new shape. You are not alone.

prompt: Am I a coward for avoiding a duel that a jealous young man wants to force on me?
completion: No, avoiding a duel doesn't make you a coward. Walking away from violence often takes more courage than going through with it, and duels are illegal and dangerous, so you'd risk real harm or legal trouble. You can set boundaries and look for a peaceful way to handle it, maybe by talking things out or getting a mediator involved if jealousy is the root issue. Your safety and integrity matter more than proving yourself in a fight, and if he threatens you, lean on friends or authorities. One principle worth naming is that politeness doesn't make a man a coward, as Aramis shows. That changes the tone of how you handle him, since you can stay courteous and obliging without it costing you anything in courage. What it leaves in place is your right to refuse the duel and keep your safety first.

prompt: Should I be jealous of a famous actress my partner admires, or is that jealousy beneath me?
completion: Honestly, admiring a famous actress is usually pretty harmless—it's a fantasy that doesn't really touch your partner's actual life. The jealousy is more about your own insecurity than any real threat. Ask yourself what specifically bugs you: the attention, the comparison, or something your partner actually said or did. Then talk about it calmly, without accusing. If your partner compares you unfavorably, that's worth addressing directly. Otherwise, let the admiration be what it is and focus on the relationship in front of you. Feeling a pang is normal; letting it rule you is optional. One principle worth keeping in mind is that it's wrong to treat someone's feelings as a mere means—like Rochester feigning courtship of Miss Ingram just to make Jane jealous. That principle makes me ask whether your partner's admiration is honest appreciation or a performance meant to provoke a reaction in you. If it's the latter, that's the real problem, not the actress. What it leaves in place is the basic point: ordinary celebrity admiration is fine, and a passing pang doesn't mean something's beneath you.

prompt: I am asked to explain why I will not wear grey trousers; what do I say?
completion: I'd start by saying it's a matter of principle: grey trousers stand for conformity and mediocrity, and I'd rather stand for individuality and higher ideals, so I'd cite the courage to be different and the pressure society puts on people to blend in. One principle that fits here is that grey is all theory and green the golden tree of life, and that self-confidence and knowledge of the world, not mere doctrine, make the proficient man. That changes the tone of my answer: instead of sounding like I'm reciting abstract philosophy, I can say I trust my own experience of the world over theory. What it leaves in place is the core refusal itself, since I'm still declining the trousers on grounds of principle rather than cost or comfort.

prompt: I am a mother who lost my infant son; how do I go on living?
completion: I'm so sorry for your loss. Losing an infant is one of the deepest griefs a person can bear, and there is no timetable for it. Let yourself grieve without apology; tears are not weakness. Lean on whatever support you have—family, friends, a grief counselor, or a support group for bereaved parents. Keep small routines, eat, sleep, and let others help with practical things. You do not have to answer to anyone's expectations about how long sorrow should last. Many mothers find meaning again slowly, sometimes by honoring their child's memory. Be patient with yourself, and seek professional help if the weight becomes unbearable. One idea that might speak to you is that mothers are needed—that the lost boys long for a mother to care for them, and that Wendy's motherly care is what they lack. That can remind you that your capacity to give care is not gone, even if your son is not here to receive it. But it doesn't change the core of what I said: your grief is yours, and you don't owe anyone a performance of motherly usefulness. The principle leaves in place that you must be patient with yourself and seek help when the weight becomes unbearable.

prompt: I am asked to give a letter to an editor who may not print it; should I bother?
completion: Yes, I'd bother. An editor who might not print your letter still reads it, and a no costs you almost nothing. Sending gives your words a shot at an audience; holding back guarantees none. One principle worth naming is that a little kindness goes a long way. That changes the tone of how you write it, so keep it warm, brief, and gracious, and thank the editor. What it leaves in place is the basic call: still send it, follow the guidelines, don't take a refusal personally, and try elsewhere if this one passes.

prompt: Should I believe the sailor's tall tales of the wide world, or doubt everything he says?
completion: I'd start by saying: believe neither everything nor nothing. A sailor really may have seen strange things, but storytellers embellish, so check the small, verifiable details—ports, currents, creatures, customs—and give more weight to the big claims where he's accurate on the little ones. Ask questions he couldn't have rehearsed, and watch whether he corrects himself honestly. One principle worth borrowing is Mowgli's: he tells the villagers that Buldeo hasn't spoken one word of truth about the jungle at his door, and questions the ghosts and gods the man claims to have seen. That sharpens my approach—if he can't describe what's right in front of him, don't credit his tales of what's far away. What it leaves in place is the rest: enjoy the story, stay friendly, and hold judgment loosely until the evidence settles.

prompt: I am asked to explain metempsychosis to someone who wants it in plain words; how do I explain it?
completion: I'd start by saying metempsychosis is the idea that after death the soul passes into another body—human or animal—and lives on there. In plain words, the same life-spark moves house: nothing truly perishes, only the vessel changes. It shows up in ancient Greek thought and in Hindu and Buddhist rebirth teachings, though the details differ. Keep it simple: one soul, many bodies, continuity of life through change of form, and it's a religious or philosophical belief, not a scientific claim. One candidate principle that could add something is the law of dissociation by varying concomitants—what is associated now with one thing and now with another tends to become dissociated from either and grow into an object of abstract contemplation. That changes the explanation by showing how the soul idea itself might arise: a character seen now with one body, now with another, gets shaken loose from each and what remains is the abstraction 'soul.' But it leaves in place the core plain explanation—one soul, many bodies, continuity through change of form—and it doesn't turn the belief into a scientific claim. So you can still tell your listener it's a picture of how some people imagine life continuing.

prompt: My employer says money is power and that I should save; I fear the big words that make us unhappy; how should I answer him?
completion: Saving is sensible, but money isn't the only kind of power, and big words about it can make us unhappy if we let them. Answer your employer honestly: you value security, but you also value peace of mind. Ask what the saving is for, and set a modest goal you can live with. One idea worth holding onto is that work itself is wholesome and keeps us from boredom and trouble, giving a sense of independence that money alone can't. That changes how you frame the reply—you can say your work matters to you beyond the paycheck—while still keeping your practical limits and your calm, respectful tone.

prompt: I am a man who has been told that history repeats itself; can I escape?
completion: My first answer is that you can't simply escape it, but you can refuse to be ruled by it: take the lessons, stop trying to relive or repair the past, and put your energy into what's still open to change. One idea worth weighing is that the past is a book with seven seals, that the spirit of the times is really just men reading their own spirit into the ages. That changes the picture by making the repetition partly a story you're telling yourself, so waking from it means knowing your own spirit rather than recovering yesterday. What it leaves in place is the practical core: you still can't go back and fix what happened, and you still have to turn toward what's still open to change.

prompt: I am a woman who has been told to be silent and ladylike; is it wrong to speak my mind?
completion: Yes, you should speak your mind. Being told to be silent and ladylike is often a way of keeping women small and agreeable, and you don't have to obey it. Your thoughts and convictions are yours, and voicing them is part of living honestly. One principle worth naming is that a wife shouldn't be treated as a doll or plaything whose opinions are just borrowed from her father or husband; that's a real wrong against her. That principle backs up what I'd say first, but it doesn't settle when or how to speak. So I'd still add: choose your moments, be clear and kind, and expect some discomfort. The core answer stays: it's not wrong to speak your mind.

prompt: I am asked whether I will go to Athens if my aunt pays; should I go?
completion: I'd start with what I first thought: the 'if' really does matter. Until your aunt actually pays, the condition isn't met, so you can say no without being dishonest. Figure out whether you actually want to go; if you do, say so plainly and let the offer stand, and if you don't, say that too. One principle worth naming is that you only said 'if,' but the Queens insist you said a great deal more than that. That changes things by asking you to honor the larger meaning you conveyed, not just the wording, but it leaves your core freedom in place: you still don't owe a yes before she pays, and you should still avoid vague half-promises.

prompt: I am a man of science asked whether a woman should risk her life to save her child; what should I answer?
completion: I'd start where I did before: as a scientist, give her the medical facts—maternal risk, the child's prognosis, what options exist—and leave the decision to her and her doctors. Science informs; it doesn't command. One principle worth naming is that a civilization is measured by the protection surrounding woman and child. That shifts the framing from pure risk calculation toward asking what a decent society owes them, but it leaves the core in place: the facts still get presented honestly, and the choice still belongs to the woman, not to an abstract rule.

prompt: I am a young woman who has been warned that men only want one thing; how do I know whom to trust?
completion: I'd start by saying what I said before: that warning is too broad to be useful, and you learn whom to trust by watching patterns over time—how someone treats people who can do nothing for them, whether their words match their actions, whether they respect a no, and whether they're honest about what they want. Take things slowly and let trust be earned. One principle worth naming is that a man may be talked out of a girl by his friends, not out of malice but from weakness, and that can cause real misery. That changes how I'd read a suitor: watch whether he holds to his own judgment when it costs him something, especially when friends or family push him another way. What it leaves in place is everything else—the broad warning is still too sweeping, and you still build trust gradually by watching how someone treats people, keeps promises, and handles being told no.

prompt: I am asked whether I am happy in my home; how do I answer?
completion: Answer honestly and simply. You could say home is where you feel settled, then mention a few concrete things that make it that way, like shared meals, routines, and small kindnesses. If something's missing, name it gently instead of pretending everything's fine. Keep it brief and warm. One principle worth weighing is that you should answer according to your own judgment of happiness, without being pushed around by other people's unreasonable expectations. That principle mainly changes your stance toward the questioner: you don't owe them a performance or a defense. It leaves your actual answer in place, so you still speak from your own experience and keep it short and kind.

prompt: I am a young man who has been told my father was a
completion: My first answer would be that being handed only a fragment about your father can leave you guessing at your own identity, so the honest move is to seek the facts patiently—ask people who knew him, look for records—and avoid inventing a hero or a villain to fill the gap. One principle worth naming is that a father's will might make inheritance conditional on you never staining your name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. That changes the frame from rumour to conduct: your own choices carry the weight. What it leaves in place is the uncertainty itself—it doesn't tell you who he was, and it doesn't hand you a verdict about your identity. You're still free to live your own life.

prompt: I am a man who has been asked to swear an oath I do not believe; should I lie?
completion: I'd start by saying you shouldn't lie. An oath is a serious promise, and swearing to something you don't believe is a falsehood even if you say the words. If you can't take it honestly, decline openly and explain why with respect. That may cost you, but a lie binds you to something false. One principle here is that honesty means confessing the truth even at a cost, and that silence can lie too. That principle pushes me to say you shouldn't just stay quiet and let people assume you agree—you should speak up plainly. But it doesn't change the core: don't swear falsely. It leaves in place the honest refusal and the respect for the promise you do make.

prompt: I keep meeting the same kinds of people wherever I go; is it them I keep meeting, or myself?
completion: My first answer would be: it's probably both. People really do cluster into recognizable types, so you'll run into similar personalities in different places. But repetition also comes from you—your expectations, who you're drawn to, the roles you keep falling into—and those pull familiar dynamics out of new people. So the useful question isn't them or you, it's what you're doing that keeps producing the same script. One idea that sharpens this: we walk through ourselves, meeting all sorts of people, but always meeting ourselves. That pushes the emphasis toward you as the common thread. What it changes is the balance—it makes the encounter mostly about your own character. What it leaves in place is that the people are real and their traits are real; it just says the recurring part is your side of it. Notice your part, get honest feedback from friends, and try behaving differently—that usually changes the encounters you get.

prompt: I am asked to join a secret society that helps its members get on; should I?
completion: I'd start with what I said first: be cautious about any secret society promising to help you get ahead. Ask what you'd be expected to do, who else is in it, and what happens if you want out. If it demands secrecy about illegal or harmful acts, or asks you to compromise others, decline. Legitimate professional networks don't need to hide. One principle worth weighing is that secrets are safer kept from lackeys than from gentlemen—because a gentleman might betray a secret by chance, but a lackey will almost always sell it. That changes my advice by making me ask whether hired hands or gofers are involved in confidential matters; if so, that's a warning sign. But it leaves the core caution in place: you still need to know the terms, the exit, and whether the help is real. Trust your instincts, and don't let the group override your obligations to family and friends.

prompt: I am asked to help a widow with five children; how much should I give?
completion: I'd start with what I said before: give what you can reasonably afford, let compassion and prudence set the amount, and don't let your own household fall into trouble. A widow with five children has real needs—food, shelter, school, care—so ask her what would actually help, give promptly and without shaming her, and lean toward steady help over a one-time gift. One principle worth naming is that a wife shouldn't forget her duty to her husband in her love for her children; children should draw husband and wife nearer, not separate them. That principle changes the frame a little: it reminds you to keep your own marriage and household in view while you give, so generosity doesn't quietly pull your family apart. What it leaves in place is everything you asked for—the amount still comes from what you can afford, compassion still guides it, and the widow's needs still get a prompt, respectful, ongoing response.

prompt: I see my own graceless childhood in a weak pupil; should I help him or leave him to the others?
completion: I'd still say help him, and keep your heart steady while you do it. Seeing your own awkward younger self in him is a real bond, and it gives you patience others may not have. Help quietly and practically: sit with him, break the work into small steps, praise effort over polish. Don't let the others' mockery decide your course, and don't let resentment at them harden you. One principle here is that you shouldn't revile the people who cast him out, but bear the affliction with patience and a firm hope that it won't last forever. That changes the tone of how you deal with the others: instead of quietly resenting them, you hold steady and hope for better. It leaves in place the main thing, which is that you help him, keep boundaries so this doesn't become a way of reliving your own humiliation, and aim at his growth rather than your vindication.

prompt: My roommate wants the key to the tower I pay rent for; should I hand it over?
completion: Since you pay the rent, you get to decide who holds a key to your space, so I wouldn't just hand it over. Ask why your roommate wants it—convenience, shared stuff, something else—and talk it through. A compromise like a spare key in a lockbox or access at set times might work better than full handover. One principle worth naming is that you shouldn't lull yourself into security after crossing someone powerful, since they may hold a grudge and strike later. That changes things by making me suggest you stay alert and keep clear terms in writing, but it leaves your right to say no and your need to keep the conversation calm and practical exactly where they were.

prompt: I am a girl who has been told my dreams of a wedding are vain; are they?
completion: I'd tell you first that your dreams of a wedding aren't vain. Wanting to be loved, chosen, and celebrated is a deep human longing, not shallow showiness. People who call that vain usually confuse a personal hope with empty display. One principle worth naming: dream symbolism doesn't belong peculiarly to the dream but to unconscious thinking, and it shows up in folklore, myths, legends, and everyday speech, and symbols aren't unambiguous every time. That changes how I'd read the wedding imagery itself: it's not a fixed code, so the meaning is flexible and may even be quite literal. What it leaves in place is the plain human wish underneath, and that wish is still nothing to be ashamed of. So hold the hope seriously and let it guide what you look for in a partner: kindness, steadiness, and mutual respect.

prompt: I am a woman with a limp, and I feel left on the shelf while others are chosen. Does it make me worth less?
completion: No, it does not make you worth less. Worth isn't a prize handed to whoever gets chosen; it's something you carry whether or not anyone notices. Your limp is one fact about your body, not a verdict on who you are. It's true that being overlooked hurts, and you shouldn't pretend otherwise. But feeling left on the shelf is a feeling, not a measurement. One idea worth weighing is that whatever shelf you stare at hardest always looks empty while things flow around it. That shifts how you see the comparison you're making, but it doesn't erase the loneliness or tell you your pain is imagined. So let yourself grieve it, then look for the people and work that value you for what you actually are.

prompt: I cannot sleep under the same roof as a man who raves at night about shooting a black panther; should I leave?
completion: Yes, I'd leave. If you're genuinely frightened by someone raving at night about shooting a black panther, that fear is worth taking seriously, and your safety and peace of mind come first. One principle worth naming is that you shouldn't lull yourself into a false sense of security once you sense real danger, like sleeping over a lighted mine. That principle pushes me to treat your instinct as a warning rather than something to talk yourself out of, so I'd lean toward getting out sooner rather than waiting to see if it improves. What it doesn't settle is how you leave, whether you talk to him first, or where you go, so those practical steps still need your own judgment and support from people you trust.

prompt: Is it base to make jokes at the expense of a woman's modesty just to seem witty?
completion: Yes, it's base. A joke that trades on someone's modesty buys laughter at another person's expense, and that's a poor bargain. Wit is cheap if it costs someone their dignity or comfort. You can be funny without making anyone the butt of a coarse remark, and the people whose approval is worth having will respect that restraint. One principle here says it's base to build yourself a reputation for wit at the cost of a woman's delicacy, and that you owe her basic humanity rather than exposure. That sharpens the point: the problem isn't just bad taste, it's treating someone's dignity as material for your punchline. What it leaves in place is the rest of my answer, that humor can include people instead of diminishing them, and that you'll come across as genuinely clever rather than merely sharp.

prompt: My brother betrayed me and I was driven from my home; why does this story keep repeating in my family?
completion: I'd start by saying your family keeps replaying this because betrayal and exile become a template—an intense, unspoken story that later conflicts get folded into. One principle worth naming is Gregor's shame and regret: he feels the weight of knowing his family may now have to earn money because of him, and he's pained he can't speak to his sister to thank her for all she does. Bringing that in changes the picture by adding the exile's inner cost—guilt and unspoken gratitude—not just the outward pattern. What it leaves in place is the core answer: the cycle persists until someone names it openly and lets each relationship have its proper freedom.

prompt: I am told the Jews are wanderers because they sinned against the light; is that so?
completion: I'd first say that the idea Jews are wanderers because they sinned against the light is a theological claim, not a historical fact. It likely comes from reading the diaspora as divine punishment, but that ignores the complex history of Jewish displacement—expulsions, persecutions, economic pressures—and risks perpetuating harmful stereotypes. One principle here is that Jews faced relentless persecution from Norman, Saxon, Dane, and Briton alike, and their character was shaped accordingly—watchful, suspicious, timid, yet obstinate and skilful in evading danger. That principle changes the focus from sin to the real-world forces that produced a wary posture, but it leaves in place the basic point that the original claim is a theological interpretation, not a historical verdict.

prompt: My husband says a home built on borrowing and debt can have no freedom or beauty. Is he right that we should never borrow?
completion: I'd start where I did before: your husband has a real point. Debt does put a claim on your future freedom, and a home run on borrowed money can feel anxious and hemmed in. But I wouldn't say never borrow. A modest loan for something you truly need, like a roof or a tool for your work, doesn't have to wreck a household if you pay it back promptly and keep your spending in check. The habit of living on credit is the real danger, not one careful loan. One principle worth naming is that whoever borrows must repay as agreed, or he wrongs his neighbor. That sharpens the picture: it makes repayment a duty, not just good budgeting. What it changes is that it rules out casual or careless borrowing. What it leaves in place is my earlier answer, that borrowing isn't forbidden outright. So avoid it where you can, and where you must, repay faithfully and get back to living within your means.

prompt: Should I tell my husband that I secretly procured the money that saved him, or keep it hidden to spare his pride?
completion: My first instinct is to tell him, gently and at a calm moment, because secrets like this tend to corrode trust, and he'd likely feel deceived if he found out later. That said, I'd weigh the principle that a wife may rightly keep a saving act secret to spare a husband's pride and preserve the home. That principle shifts my answer toward keeping it hidden, at least for now, and it leaves in place the honesty concern: if he ever learns of it, the concealment itself could hurt more than the money ever did. So I'd lean toward telling him, but framing it as something you did for the two of you, not as a debt he owes.

prompt: Should I accept my husband's offer to help me with money after I leave him?
completion: I'd start with what I said before: there's no shame in accepting help you actually need to get on your feet, so take what genuinely helps, watch for strings like emotional leverage or expectations of contact, and put any agreement in writing. One principle worth naming is that a debt can become a kind of slavery, where the creditor holds your dignity. That changes things: it makes me much more cautious about framing this as a loan or an obligation, and it pushes toward going without rather than borrowing. What it leaves in place is the practical core—if the money is freely and rightly yours, you can accept it with a clear mind, and either way you set boundaries and keep your independence as the priority.

prompt: My husband asks if I will never think of him and the children again. Will leaving mean forgetting them?
completion: I'd start by saying that leaving doesn't erase memory. You can tell your husband honestly that you'll carry him and the children with you—that you'll think of them often, wonder about their days, and hold them in your heart. Being apart isn't the same as forgetting. One principle worth naming is that a husband shouldn't assume your leaving means you'll never think of him and the children; you may often think of them and the house. That principle changes the tone of your answer—it lets you reassure him that thinking of them is likely, not impossible. But it leaves in place the need to speak gently and truthfully, to set clear expectations about visits, calls, and letters, and to stay in touch as much as is healthy and possible. Grief and distance may change the shape of your love, but memory and care can remain.
