prompt: My husband says I am still his wife whatever becomes of me. Am I bound to him?
completion: I'd start where I did before: whether you're bound depends on the promises you made and on what the marriage has actually been, not just on his saying you're still his wife. That could be real affection, or it could be a way of avoiding that something has changed. The principle that a wife shouldn't be content to exist merely to perform for her husband is worth taking seriously, because it rules out the idea that your whole duty is to keep him pleased. But it doesn't settle whether you're bound; it just means staying can't be reduced to a performance. So the honest conversation, counseling, and legal advice still matter, and so does your own life.

prompt: I realized tonight that my husband's fear was for himself, not for me. Can I still love him?
completion: What you noticed is painful, and it deserves to be taken seriously rather than explained away. Love isn't a duty you owe regardless of what you see; it grows from trust and from the belief that you are cared for. If his fear was for himself, that doesn't make him a monster, but it does change what you know about him. You can still act with kindness and honesty. Whether love continues isn't something you can force by will; give yourself time to see clearly, and let your feelings settle before deciding what the relationship should become. One idea worth weighing is that a husband shouldn't be surprised if his wife no longer loves him after he's shown his fear was for himself, not for what threatened her. That shifts the pressure off you: it says your fading love wouldn't be a failure or a betrayal, just an honest response to what you learned. What it leaves in place is everything else—the grief, the kindness you still want to show, and the fact that only time will tell you what you actually feel. So you can still love him, but you don't have to decide tonight, and you don't have to talk yourself into it.

prompt: My husband says I have destroyed all his happiness and ruined his future. Am I to blame for everything?
completion: It's painful to be told you've destroyed someone's happiness, and it's rarely true that one person is solely to blame for everything. Relationships are shared; decisions, omissions, and reactions belong to both people. That said, it's worth reflecting honestly on your part without accepting a verdict that makes you the sole author of his misery. His words may express grief and frustration more than a fair accounting. Ask him what specifically he means, listen without defending, and then consider together what can be repaired. One idea worth weighing is that a husband's willingness to work hard and bear hardship for his wife isn't the same as the wonderful thing she hoped for, which was that he would take the blame upon himself. That changes how you hear his accusation: his sacrifice doesn't make him the judge of your guilt, and his suffering doesn't automatically make you its cause. What it leaves in place is the honest question of what part you did play and what can still be mended. Blame that is totalizing shuts down conversation; responsibility that is shared opens the way to change.

prompt: I once broke off an engagement to marry a richer man to support my mother and brothers. Was I heartless?
completion: I'd first say that breaking off an engagement is never easy, and your choice to support your mother and brothers sounds like it came from careful thought, not heartlessness. One principle here is that a woman who was jilted for a more lucrative chance isn't necessarily heartless, because hard necessity and duty to a helpless family may have forced the choice. That principle changes how I'd frame your decision: it's not a cold calculation but a pressured act of care. It leaves in place the need to ask whether you were open with your former fiancé and whether you gave yourself room to grieve the relationship. You can be both caring and practical, and your actions show responsibility, not a lack of heart.

prompt: I forged my dying father's signature to get a loan that saved my husband. Was I a criminal?
completion: Yes, you committed a crime. Forging your dying father's signature to get a loan is fraud or forgery, no matter how good your reason. Your motive might soften how a prosecutor or court sees it, but it doesn't erase the act. One principle to weigh is that if the crime had never been committed, that would be better—better, and better, and better. That principle reminds you the ideal was to find another way, but it doesn't change the fact that you broke the law or that you should talk to a lawyer about your exposure and possibly make restitution.

prompt: My husband would be humiliated to know he owed me anything. Should I keep my sacrifice a secret forever?
completion: I'd start where I did before: a sacrifice kept quiet can be a real gift, and if knowing would humiliate him, keeping it to yourself may spare him pain. But secrets can get heavy for the one carrying them, so it's worth asking whether the silence protects him or just avoids an awkward talk. The principle that a wife's quiet saving act can preserve a happy home fits here, and it strengthens the case for discretion. What it changes is how much weight I'd give to sparing his pride; what it leaves in place is your own need to check that the secret isn't quietly turning into resentment, and that it isn't harming trust or safety. If it is, that matters more than his pride.

prompt: I don't know what religion really is beyond what the clergyman told me. Should I examine it for myself?
completion: Yes, I'd tell you to look into it for yourself. A clergyman gives you one person's understanding, shaped by his training and tradition, and it may not cover what you're actually asking. Read, talk to different people, reflect, and take your time. One thing worth keeping in mind, though, is the point Ophelia makes to her brother: don't let anyone show you a steep and thorny road while they stroll the easy path themselves. That applies to teachers and to me too, so check whether the person advising you actually lives what they're selling. It doesn't cancel my answer, it just means you should weigh the source as well as the message. You don't have to throw out what you were taught, and you don't have to settle everything at once.

prompt: My husband wants to write to me after I leave. Should I allow it?
completion: I'd start with what I said before: letting your husband write to you after you leave can help keep a connection, especially if kids are involved, but you need clear boundaries. Decide what you want out of it—practical matters kept brief, emotional stuff handled with care—and communicate your wishes clearly. One principle worth weighing is that a wife who leaves should receive nothing from her husband afterward, since he shouldn't write to her. That pushes toward a clean break and no letters at all, which changes the default from limited contact to none. What it leaves in place is your right to decide what feels healthy for you and to prioritize your well-being and any children's—so the choice is still yours, just with a stronger case for refusing contact.

prompt: I am a shipwrecked woman with no one to care for. Should I join my life with another shipwrecked person?
completion: I'd start by saying it's completely understandable to feel lost and alone after a shipwreck. Joining your life with another shipwrecked person could give you mutual support and companionship, but you should be cautious—two people in tough situations might not be able to help each other as much as you hope. Don't cling to anyone out of desperation; take time to see if you're truly compatible and can build something stable. Also look for help from others and rebuild your own resources. One principle that matters here is that two shipwrecked people on the same wreckage stand a better chance together than each alone, and you need someone and something to work for. That principle shifts the emphasis toward the value of companionship and shared purpose in hardship—it makes leaning on each other and building a shared future feel more central. But it leaves in place the need for caution about compatibility and the warning against clinging out of desperation. So weigh the risks and benefits carefully, and remember that a union where you're prized only as a useful tool, not loved, would be monstrous—hold out for mutual love.

prompt: I no longer believe wonderful things can happen. Should I still hope for a real marriage someday?
completion: I'd start where I did before: losing hope hurts, and you don't have to force belief in wonderful things right now. Hope can come back slowly, and a real marriage is still possible after disappointment. One principle worth weighing says a wife shouldn't be expected to believe in wonderful things once the wonderful thing has failed to happen. That changes the pressure—you're not failing by doubting. What it leaves in place is that a real marriage needs equals, not a pardon that keeps one person small. So don't chase hope; let it return on its own, and keep your standards for equality.

prompt: My husband says the law cares nothing about motives. Does that mean I was wrong even though I acted out of love?
completion: I'd start by saying your husband is right that the law often ignores motives and looks at actions and consequences. But that doesn't mean you were wrong. Acting out of love is a moral good, even if the law judges only the external act. One principle that fits here is that the law's indifference to motives doesn't make the law right—you may find it impossible to convince yourself that the law is right. That principle changes how you see the law's authority: it's not the final word on your moral standing. What it leaves in place is the practical reality that the law may still judge your action by its outcome, so you should be aware of that. But you can trust your own moral compass and not equate the law's judgment with moral rightness.

prompt: My husband blames my father's want of principle for what I did. Is he right?
completion: Your husband isn't right to pin what you did on your father's lack of principle. You're the one who acted, and a grown woman's choices aren't erased by her father's failings. One of the principles you raised says a husband shouldn't blame his wife's father for her act or claim he's being punished for having winked at what the father did. That principle backs up what I'd say first, but it also pulls in the idea that a father's will can show trust in a child's character and set conditions on inheritance, which doesn't really speak to your husband's blame. So it leaves your own responsibility exactly where it was: your father may have set a poor example, but he isn't the author of your conduct, and your husband should judge you by your own intentions and circumstances, not inherited guilt.

prompt: I have never had a serious conversation with my husband in eight years of marriage. Is that a real marriage?
completion: Eight years without a serious conversation is a long silence, and it's fair to wonder whether the marriage is real. A marriage is more than sharing a house and routine; it needs honest talk about what matters. You might try to start such conversations gently, choosing calm moments, and see whether he responds. If he won't, consider whether you can accept the situation or whether you need outside help, such as a counselor. The question isn't whether you've failed, but whether you can build something deeper now. One principle that fits here is that a wife shouldn't be kept in ignorance of serious matters—a marriage without serious talk isn't true understanding. That principle sharpens the point: it names the silence as a real problem, not just a quirk. But it doesn't tell you how to start the conversation or whether he'll engage, so the practical steps I mentioned still stand.

prompt: The law says a wife cannot borrow without her husband's consent, but I did it to save his life. Is the law right?
completion: I'd start by saying that borrowing to save your husband's life sounds morally justified, even if it broke a legal rule. The principle that a wife with a head for business may act cleverly and procure money without her husband's consent when necessary to save his life fits your situation and supports what you did. That principle changes how I'd weigh the law here: it makes the consent requirement look like a formality that shouldn't block urgent action. What it leaves in place is the debt itself. You still owe the money, and you should repay it as agreed, because borrowing creates a real obligation even when the reason was good.

prompt: I am afraid my children will forget me if I leave. Should that stop me?
completion: It's natural to fear that your children will forget you if you leave, but that fear shouldn't necessarily stop you. Children often remember their parents, especially if you maintain contact. Leaving doesn't mean forgetting; you can still be a presence in their lives. Consider what's best for your family and seek support. One idea worth weighing is that a husband shouldn't assume his wife's leaving means she'll never think of him and the children, since she may often think of them and the house. That softens the fear of being erased, but it doesn't settle whether leaving is right for you, and it doesn't remove the real work of staying connected.

prompt: Should I have expected my husband to take the guilt upon himself when my secret was exposed?
completion: I'd start with what I said before: it's understandable to hope he'd shield you, but expecting him to absorb guilt for your secret isn't fair or realistic. Guilt belongs to whoever chose the act, and a marriage works best when both people are honest about what happened rather than one quietly carrying the blame for the other. One principle worth naming is that a husband shouldn't assume his wife's helplessness gives her a double attractiveness or that he should advise and direct her in everything. That principle changes the frame a bit: it reminds me not to treat you as fragile or in need of his management, and it pushes back on any expectation that he should step in and take over the moral weight. What it leaves in place is the core point—your secret is yours, and he isn't obligated to carry guilt that isn't his. So the healthiest path is still a candid conversation: explain why you kept it, acknowledge the hurt, and let him decide how he feels.

prompt: My husband treats me like a doll and arranges everything according to his own taste. Is that love?
completion: I'd say treating you like a doll and arranging everything to his taste isn't love—it's control. Love respects your autonomy and desires. If he makes all decisions without considering your preferences, he's not treating you as an equal partner. That can breed resentment and unhappiness. You should talk to him about how you feel and seek mutual understanding. If he keeps disregarding your wishes, consider counseling. A healthy marriage needs compromise and mutual respect, not one person imposing their will. One principle that fits here is that a husband shouldn't arrange everything to his taste and expect you to share it, so you only pretend. That principle reinforces the control dynamic and sharpens the point that your preferences matter. It doesn't change the core advice about communication and counseling, but it adds a clear standard for what's wrong. The rest of my answer stands: talk, seek understanding, and if needed, get help.

prompt: My husband says I don't understand how to act on my own responsibility. Is he right?
completion: I'd start by saying it's possible your husband has a point, but it's also possible he's underestimating you. Acting on your own responsibility means making decisions and owning your life, and if you've leaned on him for direction, you can start small with daily choices, money, or social plans, and talk with him openly about wanting more autonomy. One idea worth naming is that a husband shouldn't write off his wife's quiet sacrifice as a thoughtless act by a woman who can't act on her own responsibility. That reframes his comment: your care for him may be a choice, not helplessness. It doesn't settle whether he's right about specific things, so the practical steps still stand. Only you can decide if his assessment is fair, but building independence will help you either way.

prompt: My husband says no man would sacrifice his honour for the one he loves. Is that true?
completion: Your husband is describing a common belief, but it's worth examining rather than accepting outright. Honour and love aren't always in competition; people give up pride, comfort, or reputation for those they love all the time, and whether that counts as honour depends on what you mean by the word. If honour means integrity and moral principle, sacrificing it for love would be wrong. If it means social standing or pride, people surrender it for love constantly. One thing worth adding: a husband shouldn't claim no man would do this while overlooking that countless women have quietly given up reputation, standing, and security for the people they love. That point widens the picture, but it doesn't settle what honour means to the two of you or why he's asserting this, so the real conversation is still about that.

prompt: My husband says I am before all else a wife and mother. Is that true?
completion: You are a wife and mother, but you're also a person in your own right, with your own mind, tastes, and purposes. Those roles matter, but the phrase 'before all else' quietly erases everything else about you, and a good marriage is a partnership between two whole people. One thing worth naming: a husband shouldn't arrange everything around his own taste and expect you to just adopt it, so that you only pretend to share it. That sharpens the point, but it doesn't change the core answer: yes, you're a wife and mother, and no, that isn't all you are. Tell him kindly but clearly that you want to be loved as your whole self.

prompt: Should I have given up the trip abroad that saved my husband's life rather than commit fraud?
completion: I'd have told you first that fraud is a serious wrong and love doesn't erase it, so you should own the harm, make amends where you can, and never do it again. One principle worth naming is that a wife might rightly keep a saving act secret because a proud husband would be pained to know he owed you anything. That changes how I'd handle the disclosure: I can see keeping the matter private to spare him humiliation. It leaves the core in place, though. The fraud is still wrong, the legal risk is still real, and you still need to make things right and not repeat it.

prompt: I admire someone so intensely it feels like worship—is such idolatry of another person wrong?
completion: My first answer would be that intense admiration isn't automatically wrong, but it turns dangerous when it replaces your own judgment, your self-respect, or the place that belongs to what's truly divine. One principle worth naming is that idolatry means giving divine honor to a creature by your own invention, and that worship a sovereign commands under threat of death counts as the sovereign's act, not the subject's. That distinction changes how I'd frame the outer side of things: the gestures and commands aren't the whole story. What it leaves in place is the inner question, which is still yours to answer. So ask whether this admiration makes you freer and more yourself or more dependent and fearful. Admire the good you see, learn from it, but remember the person is human and fallible. If it feels compulsive or consuming, step back and give attention to other relationships and commitments.

prompt: Does it matter whether I really believe the ideas I argue for, or only whether the ideas are good?
completion: My first answer is that it matters. Arguing for something you don't believe is a kind of dishonesty, and it wears down trust and your own integrity. One candidate principle here is that good thinking needs a variety of rival suggestions, since competing ideas keep you from grabbing the first one that comes along. That changes how I'd frame it: instead of treating sincerity and idea quality as a simple either/or, I'd say you should genuinely entertain several positions, including ones you don't hold, and test them against each other. What it leaves in place is my original point: when you actually argue for a position in public, it still matters whether you believe it, because pretending is a different act from exploring. So the principle widens the space for honest disagreement without excusing insincere advocacy.

prompt: People tell me my good looks are superficial—should I value beauty as highly as intelligence?
completion: I'd start by saying that beauty and intelligence are different goods, and it's a mistake to rank them as if one must win. Good looks open doors and shape first impressions, but they fade and can't carry a life alone. Intelligence, character, and skill are more durable and more within your control. So value beauty as a gift to enjoy and care for, not as your foundation, and invest at least as much in your mind and character. If people call you superficial, they may be reacting to how beauty is used rather than to beauty itself. Cultivate both, and let neither be your whole identity. Now, one principle worth considering is that beauty is a form of genius, higher than genius because it needs no explanation, and that only shallow people don't judge by appearances. That principle changes the tone: it says don't apologize for beauty or treat it as lesser. But it leaves in place the core point that beauty alone can't carry a life, and that you still need to invest in your mind and character. So I'd still say cultivate both, but with less defensiveness about the beauty part.

prompt: I feel torn between what society expects of me and what I owe to myself—which should govern my life?
completion: I'd start with what I said before: neither society's expectations nor what you owe yourself should rule absolutely. One candidate principle is that self-sacrifice for a child in your care is a duty, even at real cost to your own life and joy. If that applies to you, it changes the balance: the child's welfare comes first, and some of what you owe yourself has to wait. But it leaves the rest in place—you still weigh which expectations protect real goods and which are mere convention, and you still take care of yourself, because a guardian who collapses serves no one. So keep your reflective judgment; just let that duty set the priority when a child depends on you.

prompt: I am young and everyone tells me to plan for the future—should I instead live fully now while I have my youth?
completion: I'd start with what I actually think: plan for the future, but don't let planning crowd out living fully now. Youth gives you energy and room to try things, so use it, while still taking a few steps to secure what comes later. One principle worth weighing is that you shouldn't stare into the future or dwell on old age and death, but accept what comes and stay busy and engaged. That changes the tone of my answer: it pushes back on fear-driven planning and says keep your heart and mind occupied with what's in front of you. What it leaves in place is the basic balance—enjoy now, prepare quietly—because it doesn't forbid sensible preparation, it just refuses to let dread of aging run your life.

prompt: I am drawn to people who know everything and to people who know nothing—why do I find both so fascinating?
completion: I'd start with what I said before: you're drawn to both because they're two clean extremes of certainty—the expert gives you authority and answers, the innocent gives you openness and no preconceptions—and both let you escape the muddy middle where most people live half-informed. The principle that the only truly fascinating people are those who know absolutely everything or absolutely nothing sharpens that: it says the fascination isn't incidental, it's the whole point of the poles. What it changes is that I'd stop treating your taste as a quirk and see it as a real preference for clarity over the messy in-between. What it leaves in place is my original read—the contrast itself is what hooks you, and the middle still feels less interesting to you, even if that's not the whole story.

prompt: Should I try to shape my younger friend's tastes and opinions, or does influencing him do him harm?
completion: I'd start where I did before: some guidance from an older friend is natural and can genuinely help, but don't impose your tastes as the only right ones. Share your views, explain your reasoning, and let him decide. One principle that shifts this a little is that a friend's diffidence can keep him from trusting his own judgment when he's anxious, and leaning on a wiser friend may rightly settle his doubts. So in moments when he's genuinely unsure and looking to you, don't treat that reliance as something to correct—meet it with care. That changes how I'd handle his hesitation, but it leaves the core in place: offer trusted judgment, invite real conviction, and let him hold his ground where he truly believes it.

prompt: I am an artist and my best work came from my feelings for a friend—should I hide that feeling from the world?
completion: I'd start by saying don't hide the feeling, but be discreet about the person. The feeling is the source of your work, and hiding it completely could starve your art. What matters is whether revealing it hurts your friend, so talk with them first and let them decide how much of the story is public. You can let the work stand on its own without naming names or exposing private details. One principle that fits here is that you shouldn't make others share in your own horror without their knowledge, or let your past drag them down. That principle changes how you handle the friend: it pushes you to get their consent before anything becomes public, and it warns against secretly burdening them. But it leaves in place the core advice: keep making the work, protect your friend, and let the feeling live in the art rather than in a public confession.

prompt: I keep resisting a temptation that torments me—should I keep resisting it or finally yield to it?
completion: I'd still start where I did: keep resisting, but stop white-knuckling it. The fight itself often feeds the urge, so the real move is to shrink its grip—name what the temptation is actually promising you, meet that need somewhere healthier, and put some distance between yourself and the triggers. One idea worth borrowing is that pleasure chased against your conscience tends to sting and taste bitter even when it looks appealing. That's a useful test to run before you yield: picture the aftermath, not just the moment. What it changes is the reason you resist—not grim suppression, but clear-eyed foresight. What it leaves in place is everything practical: delay, support, and no shame spiral if you slip.

prompt: I gave up a relationship to protect the other person—did I do good or did I merely act a part?
completion: My first answer would be: it's hard to know your own motives, but you need to be honest with yourself about whether you acted for their good or for your own need to be seen as noble. Did you communicate honestly and give them a say? If you made the decision unilaterally, it may have been more about your fears than their protection. One principle that applies here is that you shouldn't be ashamed of worthy relations or apologize for honest connections. That principle changes the tone—it says don't beat yourself up or treat the relationship as something to blush for. But it leaves in place the need to examine whether your action was genuine protection or a way to avoid discomfort or play the martyr. So the core question remains: were you truly selfless, or merely acting a part?

prompt: Should I try to reform my character and become more virtuous, or would that only mar who I am?
completion: I'd start by saying that trying to become more virtuous is generally worthwhile and doesn't have to erase who you are. Character isn't fixed; it grows through habits, reflection, and practice. Reform is less about replacing your identity than aligning your actions with your values. Start with one or two concrete habits, be patient with setbacks, and seek honest feedback from people you trust. Virtue isn't a mask you wear but a set of dispositions you strengthen over time. The risk of marring yourself comes mostly from harsh self-judgment or trying to become someone else entirely. Aim for growth, not perfection. One principle that fits here is that an honest life is, after all, the best, and someone appalled by a great crime may turn their back on the past and amend their life in a new sphere. That principle reinforces the idea that reform can be a fresh start, but it leaves in place the caution against harsh self-judgment and the emphasis on gradual habit change rather than a total break from who you are.

prompt: I want to start a new life and be good—is a new life really possible for someone like me?
completion: Yes, a new life is possible. People aren't stuck in one shape forever; you can change your habits, repair what you can, and choose differently starting today. It won't be easy, and the past doesn't vanish, but it doesn't have to decide your future. Start small: keep one promise, tell the truth, do one useful thing each day, and be patient with setbacks. One idea worth weighing is that a person who has been overworking and has no one left to live for can feel life unspeakably empty and go looking for steady work just to keep the mind busy. That idea adds a useful caution: steady work can steady you, but it can also be a way of hiding from the emptiness instead of facing it. So take up regular work if it helps, but don't let it become the whole answer. The wish itself shows something in you is already turning toward good.

prompt: I have been told that if I want to get rid of a bad habit I should resist it—is resistance the right way?
completion: I'd start with what I said before: pure resistance often backfires because it keeps the habit front and center, so it's usually better to change your surroundings, swap in a better routine, and figure out what need the habit is meeting. One idea worth weighing is that the only way to get rid of a temptation is to yield to it, since resisting can leave you sick with longing for what you've forbidden yourself. That changes the advice from fight the urge to meet the need openly and let the impulse spend itself in action. But it doesn't erase the practical side: you still want to remove cues and replace the habit with something that serves the same purpose, because just yielding without understanding can leave you stuck in the same loop.

prompt: I am an artist—should I put my own feelings and life into my work, or keep myself out of it?
completion: I'd start by saying there's no single rule—it depends on your temperament and the work. Pouring your feelings and life in can give it urgency and authenticity, but keeping yourself out can give you distance and freedom to invent. Many artists do both by turns, using personal material but transforming it. One principle worth naming is that every work should have a definite object in view—you should know why you're making it. That principle changes the framing: it shifts the question from whether to include yourself to what your feelings are serving. It leaves in place the practical advice to follow what each piece needs and to let your feelings inform the work without letting them dictate it.

prompt: I have been told that curiosity is dangerous—should I pursue every new sensation and experience?
completion: My first answer would be: curiosity isn't dangerous in itself, but chasing every new sensation without thinking is. So don't pursue everything blindly—weigh the risks and skip what's clearly harmful. One principle I'd bring in is that curiosity is the vital spark that supplies the raw material for ideas, so the real job is keeping wonder alive rather than smothering it. That changes the emphasis: instead of just warning you off, it says protect your openness to new experience. What it leaves in place is the caution—you still evaluate risks and don't treat every impulse as a green light.

prompt: I want to be talked about and famous—is it worse to be talked about or not to be talked about at all?
completion: Honestly, my first answer is that being talked about, even badly, beats being forgotten—notice at least puts you on the map, while silence leaves nothing to work with. But I'd add one principle: your experience is what you agree to attend to, and without selective interest it's just chaos. That changes things, because it means fame only counts for as much as you and others actually pay attention to it—so aim to be talked about well, not just loudly. What it leaves in place is my original point: obscurity still gives you nothing to shape.

prompt: I have done one good thing after a life of wrongdoing—does that one act redeem me?
completion: I'd start by saying that one good act doesn't erase a life of wrongdoing, but it can be the beginning of redemption. Redemption isn't a transaction; it's a process of turning away from evil and toward good. Your one good thing shows you're capable of goodness, and that capacity can grow. Now, one principle that matters here is forgiving the person while abhorring the deed—so revenge doesn't take hold of your heart. That changes how you see yourself and others: you can hate the harm you've done without hating yourself, and you can let go of resentment. But it leaves in place the need for remorse, repentance, and humility—acknowledging the harm and turning toward good. So keep doing good, and over time you may find redemption.

prompt: I am talented and successful, but I feel a strange fatality following my gifts—is distinction a curse?
completion: I'd start where I started before: distinction isn't a curse, though it can sure feel like one. Talent and success bring visibility, expectation, and the fear of losing what you have, and that sense of fatality is often other people's hopes plus your own perfectionism. One principle worth naming is that it's a kind of waste to throw away your good gifts just because you can't have the one thing you want. That changes the tone: instead of only soothing the pressure, it nudges you to rouse yourself and do something splendid with what you've got. What it leaves in place is the rest—separating what you can control from what you can't, letting some pressure go, and remembering success isn't a debt you repay with suffering. So enjoy your gifts, rest when you need to, and don't mistake a story you tell yourself after disappointment for fate.

prompt: I have been told to judge people by their characters, not their looks—am I shallow for judging by appearances?
completion: My first answer would be: no, you're not shallow for noticing appearances. Looks, dress, and bearing are real information, and everyone reads them fast. The problem is stopping there, because appearance is a thin and easily faked signal. Character shows in how someone treats people who can do nothing for them, how they handle frustration, and whether they keep small promises. One principle worth naming is that you shouldn't judge someone's character from a single evening's manner or from pride alone when no other fault can be found. That changes how quickly I'd let one awkward meeting harden into a verdict, and it leaves the rest in place: keep using appearance as a first impression, then test it against conduct over time, and revise when they don't match.

prompt: I am afraid of growing old and losing my beauty—how should I face that fear?
completion: I'd start by saying that fear of losing your beauty as you age is really common, and it's worth facing honestly. Beauty isn't the whole of who you are—character, kindness, and wisdom tend to deepen with time. Try shifting your focus toward health, relationships, and interests that don't fade. Accept that your body will change, and treat that acceptance as part of maturity. If the fear gets intense, talk with someone you trust or a counselor. Many people find new forms of beauty and purpose later in life, and your worth was never only in your looks. One idea worth weighing is that true courage is facing danger when you're afraid—so the fact that you're looking at this fear at all already shows courage. That principle changes the tone: instead of just managing the fear, you can see it as proof of your own bravery. What it leaves in place is the practical advice—staying engaged with work, friends, and interests, and getting support if you need it. It doesn't ask you to ignore the future or pretend aging isn't real; it just reframes the fear as something you can meet with confidence built through action.

prompt: I have done terrible things and feel it is too late to repent—is it ever too late?
completion: I'd start where I did before: it's never too late to repent. Whatever you've done, you can turn to God and ask for forgiveness, and he's not stingy with mercy. Your remorse isn't proof you're beyond hope—it can be the thing that moves you toward real change. What shifts for me is the principle that remorse is the poison of life and reformation is its cure—you can start right now laying up a new and stainless store of memories. That strengthens the call to begin today rather than waiting to feel worthy. It doesn't remove the seriousness of what you've done or promise that consequences vanish; it just means the door is open now, not later.

prompt: My friend confessed a terrible secret to me and I am bound to silence—what do I owe him and what do I owe others?
completion: You owe him silence, and you owe others only what safety genuinely requires. A confidence given to you is a trust, and breaking it lightly breaks the friendship and your own word. Keep the secret, but don't confuse loyalty with covering ongoing harm. If others are in real danger, tell him first that you must act, and act only as narrowly as needed. Otherwise, hold your tongue, refuse to gossip, and let him decide what to disclose. One principle worth naming is that a secret entrusted to a gentleman should be kept, since a gentleman has but his word. That principle reinforces the silence you already owe him, but it doesn't change the safety exception: it leaves in place the duty to act narrowly if real danger appears. Your duty is to be trustworthy without becoming an accomplice to fresh wrongs.

prompt: I am considering marriage, but I fear it will make me less myself—is that a real danger?
completion: Yes, that fear is real, but it depends on the marriage you build. Marriage doesn't automatically erase who you are; it can sharpen your identity if both partners respect each other's independence, interests, and friendships. The real danger comes when one person is expected to sacrifice their own needs, opinions, or ambitions for the relationship. Watch for pressure to become someone you're not—that's the risk worth taking seriously. Talk openly with your partner about your fears, keep your own pursuits, and choose someone who wants you as you are, not as a project. One idea that adds a twist here is that constant self-sacrifice can make you colorless and lose your distinctiveness—so the risk isn't just losing yourself, it's that being too unselfish can flatten you. That principle sharpens the warning about reforming yourself to please someone else, but it doesn't change the core advice: stay yourself, keep your independence, and watch for pressure to become someone you're not.

prompt: I feel pressure to be unselfish and self-sacrificing—is unselfishness really a virtue?
completion: I'd start by saying unselfishness is often praised, but it turns unhealthy when it means ignoring your own needs. Real virtue balances care for others with self-respect, and constant self-sacrifice can lead to burnout and resentment. So ask yourself whether you're giving from genuine care or from fear of disapproval, set boundaries, and remember your well-being matters too. One idea worth weighing is that the self you're protecting is partly made of what you call yours, like your home, your reputation, and your work, and that self-feeling shifts with the ratio of success to pretensions. That changes the picture by suggesting that lowering your pretensions can relieve pressure as much as getting more does, so some of what feels like sacrifice might just be letting go of inflated expectations. What it leaves in place is the core point: chosen generosity is fine, but erasing yourself isn't a virtue.

prompt: I am afraid of being influenced by a charismatic friend—should I cut him off?
completion: I'd start by saying charisma isn't the same as harm, and cutting someone off out of fear can cost you a real friendship. Ask yourself what specifically worries you: does he push you toward things you'd otherwise avoid, or does he just have a strong personality? One idea worth weighing is that a truly great character exerts a powerful influence, and fear of losing the esteem of a good friend can restrain you from a dishonorable choice. That changes the frame a little: instead of asking whether his influence is dangerous, you can ask whether he'd respect you less if you took a bad path. It leaves your original concern in place, though, because it only helps if he's actually the kind of friend whose esteem is worth having. So set clear boundaries about the choices that matter to you, and watch how he responds when you disagree. If he respects your limits, the friendship can be healthy. If he pressures or mocks you, distance is reasonable.

prompt: My companion is wounded and of a faith I was taught to scorn—am I bound to shelter and tend him?
completion: I'd start by saying you're bound by common humanity, not by his creed. A wounded companion deserves shelter and care no matter what faith you were taught to scorn, and abandoning him would betray your own courage and your pledged word. One principle here is that a man of courage shows mercy and keeps his word even to a wretch. That principle reinforces the duty to tend him and adds weight to the promise you've made, but it doesn't change the core answer: you still shelter and tend him. It leaves in place the same call to kindness over inherited prejudice.

prompt: My king is popular and famous in war, but his government is careless and sometimes despotic. How should I judge him?
completion: I'd judge him by his government, not his fame. Popularity and military glory are real qualities, but they don't excuse carelessness or despotism in administration, which harm the people he rules. A king's first duty is to govern wisely and well, and where he's indulgent or tyrannical, that has to be named plainly. Still, weigh the whole man: his courage and the affection of his people aren't nothing. Hold both truths together. One principle worth applying here is that a ruler's personal good qualities and military fame don't excuse a careless administration that's now too indulgent and now allied to despotism. That sharpens how I'd name the faults of his rule, but it leaves in place the honor I'd give his courage and the people's affection for him.

prompt: My servant has been slandered and his dog lamed by a neighbour's keeper; how should I respond?
completion: I'd start where I did before: treat this as two separate wrongs and handle both calmly. Get the facts yourself first—talk to your servant, the neighbour's keeper, and any witnesses, and write down dates, exact words, and the dog's injury. Then speak to the neighbour privately, lay out what you found, and ask for an apology and for the keeper to be restrained or dismissed. Stand up for your servant publicly where the slander was spoken, and if the neighbour won't make it right, take it to a neutral arbiter or the local authority. One principle worth adding is that you shouldn't rely on a servant's or a stranger's report alone—weigh character against conduct and evidence. That changes how you receive the story: don't take your servant's account as proven just because he's yours, and don't take the neighbour's denial at face value either. What it leaves in place is everything else—the private conversation, the public defence, the documentation, and the refusal to retaliate in kind.

prompt: I have sworn a vow that limits how far I may go to greet guests; does keeping it excuse coldness?
completion: I'd start by saying a vow freely made deserves respect, and keeping it isn't coldness by itself—but how you keep it matters. You can honor the limit and still greet people warmly within it, through words, gestures, and attention, and explain the constraint plainly so no one mistakes restraint for contempt. One principle worth naming is that hospitality shouldn't be bounded by personal dislikes—the idea that a host can endure a guest's presence for a few hours without dishonor. That principle changes the spirit of your welcome: it tells you not to let distaste shrink your greeting beyond what the vow requires. What it leaves in place is the vow itself—it doesn't ask you to break your word, only to make sure the limit comes from the promise and not from a colder motive you might secretly prefer. So keep the vow, but let your manner stay open within it.

prompt: I am a guest in a house where my claim to rule is disputed. May I be detained or injured?
completion: You're a guest, so basic safety and courtesy are owed to you. A host who disputes your claim to rule can argue the point, but hospitality traditionally rules out injuring or detaining someone who came freely. State your position calmly, ask what the dispute is based on, and look for a neutral arbiter instead of settling it by force. If you're afraid of being held or hurt, keep witnesses, note any threats, and line up a safe way out. One principle worth naming is that a host's duty to a guest holds even when the guest's claim is disputed. That reinforces your protection from harm and confinement, but it doesn't decide who's right about the claim itself, so the dispute still needs a fair process and a neutral judge both sides can accept.

prompt: A defenceless stranger of another faith demands trial by combat under our laws. May I refuse her?
completion: My first instinct would be to say you can refuse her, since granting a duel to a stranger of another faith seems risky and irregular, and it's reasonable to send the matter to lawful authorities instead. But one principle here pushes back hard: a defenceless stranger who claims the benefit of your laws, including trial by combat, must not be refused, because it would be shameful for knights and religious men to turn away proffered combat. That changes my answer to: you may not refuse her outright. What it leaves in place is your caution—set fair terms, don't act rashly, and don't let her tears or charm alone decide things, nor a friend's warnings alone; demand proof and weigh her words. So grant the trial, but keep it a last resort entered with clean hands.

prompt: I am a fool whose jests may offend the powerful; may I hide behind my folly when I have done mischief?
completion: My first answer would be: folly is a thin shield. A jester's license may buy you some room, but it doesn't erase harm—if your jokes wound the powerful, expect consequences, and don't count on the cap to save you. The safer path is to own the mischief plainly, apologize where you actually caused offense, and be more careful about targets and timing. One principle worth weighing is that a fool's licensed wit may protect his roguery, since a fool can't help himself the way a wise man can. That softens my answer a little: it says the fool's cover isn't nothing, and there are moments when playing the fool is the only move open to you. But it leaves the core in place—the cover is thin, so lean on it lightly, own the harm, and don't pretend the mischief was intended. Folly works best alongside humility and honest remorse.

prompt: I am a prince whose insult to a guest has caused murmurs; should I apologize or double down?
completion: I'd start with what I said first: neither doubling down nor a clumsy public apology is wise. The measured path is to acknowledge the offense to the guest privately, restore his dignity with a courteous gesture, and let word of your courtesy spread. One principle worth weighing is that a guest who feels wronged may answer by openly pledging loyalty to the true king, and few will dare contradict such a pledge. That changes the stakes: the murmurs could harden into a public display of where loyalties lie, so you should correct things quickly and sincerely rather than let it fester. What it leaves in place is the core advice: don't grovel, don't repeat the insult, and focus on restoring both the relationship and your reputation for fairness.

prompt: People say my race is naturally greedy and base. How should I answer them?
completion: I'd start by saying: answer calmly and firmly. Those claims are stereotypes, not facts—no race is naturally greedy or base, and character depends on individuals, culture, and circumstances. Point to counterexamples of generous, honest, noble people of your race, and explain that sweeping generalizations about millions of people are unfair and usually reflect prejudice, not evidence. Then I'd bring in one idea: we should free our minds of prejudice and not treat our own instincts as the standard for other races, because gifts vary endlessly and each may be good of its kind. That principle changes the framing—it turns the conversation from defending your race to questioning the assumption that one type is the measure of all. But it leaves in place the core advice: set boundaries if the remarks are hostile, don't feel obliged to debate, and let a dignified, confident response be enough.

prompt: My son disobeyed me and left home against my command; should I still call him my son?
completion: I'd start where I started before: disobedience hurts, but a father's love shouldn't hinge on a child's obedience. Calling him your son isn't a prize for good behavior; it's a statement of the bond that's already there. You can disapprove of what he did and still claim him, and cutting him off over one act of defiance risks losing him for good. One principle worth weighing here is that God gave his commandments after making known the plan of redemption, calling people to repent and not harden their hearts so they might find mercy. That changes the tone of how you hold the door open: your welcome can include an honest invitation to turn back, not just a silent waiting. What it leaves in place is everything you actually asked about. He's still your son, your standards still stand, and you don't have to pretend the disobedience didn't happen.

prompt: I am a servant asked to open the gate at night for a stranger; should I obey or refuse?
completion: I'd start with what I first thought: as a servant, you owe your employer obedience, but safety matters too. So check who the stranger is and why they're here, and if anything feels off, wake your employer or a senior staff member rather than deciding alone. One principle worth naming is that a priest's door should always be open, and you shouldn't demand a name from someone seeking shelter, since the person most ashamed of their name is often the one who needs it most. That principle shifts things toward opening the gate and offering welcome without interrogation, but it doesn't erase your duty to protect the household, so you can still verify basic facts and call for guidance when something seems wrong. Keep your role and your employer's instructions in view either way.

prompt: Those I enriched have betrayed and starved me. How should I treat them now?
completion: I'm sorry — being betrayed by people you helped is a deep hurt, and your anger makes sense. What I'd say first is this: set boundaries to protect yourself, don't rush to trust them again, and don't let bitterness eat at you. Talk to them if you can, give them a chance to make amends, and treat them with the dignity you'd want for yourself even if you keep your distance. One principle worth weighing is that you shouldn't cast out the unworthy or the wanderer, but should minister to them and pray for them, hoping they return and heal. That changes the tone: instead of just 'keep your distance,' it asks you to leave a door open and wish them well. What it leaves in place is your right to boundaries and your own well-being — it doesn't require you to trust them again or stay close.

prompt: My people are dispossessed and must crouch before strangers. Is this our natural condition or our curse?
completion: I'd start where I did before: this isn't your natural condition. No people is born to crouch before strangers—that posture gets forced on you by conquest and loss, not by nature. What you're living through is a curse of history, not a permanent truth about who you are. One principle I'd weigh in is that adversity can bend the heart like fire bends stubborn steel without breaking it. That changes the tone: it says the bending you feel isn't the end of you, and dignity can survive even this. What it leaves in place is the plain fact that the bending is real and unjust—it doesn't soften the dispossession into something noble or deserved. So name the injustice, hold on to who you are, and look for the means to restore what was taken.

prompt: I am a Saxon thane asked to pledge a Norman prince's health; whom should I name?
completion: I'd start where I did before: you're a guest, so keep your courtesy, but nobody can force you to pledge a Norman prince's health if it sits badly with you. Name a Saxon lord you respect, or give a general toast to peace and the company's health, and if pressed, praise the hospitality and wish the realm well without committing to a name that betrays your loyalties. The principle about a guest who's been insulted being free to requite the courtesy by pledging the true king changes the specific move: instead of a vague toast, you can pointedly honor the rightful monarch, since few will openly challenge a pledge to a reigning king. What it leaves in place is everything else: you still keep your dignity, avoid open insult, and protect your standing among your own people.

prompt: I am an outlaw; should I keep laws among my band and divide spoil justly, or take what I can?
completion: I'd start by saying that even outlaws need some rules to keep the band together, and dividing spoil justly helps maintain loyalty and order. But you're still a criminal, and keeping laws among your band doesn't make you moral. The best course is to leave the outlaw life and live honestly. If you must continue, a just division and internal laws will help you avoid chaos and betrayal. One principle that applies here is that even outlaws may keep just laws and civil discipline among themselves, as Locksley did by dividing spoil impartially. That principle reinforces the practical advice to keep laws and divide fairly, but it doesn't change the deeper point that outlawry itself is wrong and you should seek an honest life. So it leaves that core judgment in place.

prompt: I have been freed from bondage—how should I use my new liberty?
completion: I'd start by saying: use your new liberty with gratitude and sober self-command. Freedom isn't license—it's the power to govern yourself by reason and pursue worthy ends. Secure the basics of a free life: honest work, orderly habits, and care for those who depend on you. Guard against vices that bondage may have bred, like idleness, suspicion, and improvidence, and against passions that prosperity can inflame. Take part in your community, because liberty is preserved by vigilance and virtue. One principle worth naming is that liberty can be endangered by the abuses of liberty as much as by abuses of power, and the former are most to be feared. That principle sharpens the warning against license and self-indulgence, but it leaves in place the core advice: self-command, worthy ends, work, habits, care for dependents, and civic vigilance.

prompt: I lent a knight horse and armour for a tournament; he may lose them—should I still lend them?
completion: I'd start by saying: lending a knight horse and armour for a tournament is generous, but you should think about the risks. If he loses them, you lose your property. Knights often need support, and lending could bring honour or future favours, so clarify terms first: will he replace them if lost? Can he offer collateral? If he's trustworthy and the tournament matters, lending might be worthwhile; if you can't afford the loss, don't lend. One principle that applies is that a man's own neck and limbs are his own, but the horse and armour lent to him belong to another and must be repaid or restored. That changes things by making it clear the borrowed goods aren't his to risk freely—he must return or repay them—so you should set that expectation explicitly. What it leaves in place is your personal call based on your relationship and risk tolerance, and the need to decide whether you can afford the loss.

prompt: My order forbids me even to speak with women or to kiss my mother. Is such severity right?
completion: I'd start by saying that a rule that cuts you off from speaking with women and even from kissing your mother does sound harsh, and it's fair to feel the weight of that. Many orders do set strict boundaries for discipline and focus, and the point of such limits is usually to guard against distraction and impropriety rather than to deny natural affection. If it troubles you, talk with your superiors about its purpose and scope. One principle worth weighing here is that the vow forbids even the kiss of affection to sisters and mothers, while communion with strange women is treated as a snare. That principle explains why the rule exists and why it presses so hard on ordinary human feeling, but it doesn't settle whether this particular severity is right for you, and it leaves your duty to keep the rule as stated fully in place. Severity alone doesn't make a rule right or wrong; what matters is whether it serves the order's aims and whether you can bear it with a good conscience.

prompt: I promised a boon for a service rendered. May I refuse it when it is claimed?
completion: My first answer would be that it depends on what you promised and what's being claimed. If you made a clear promise in exchange for a service, you're generally on the hook morally, and maybe legally, so you should honor it unless the request is unreasonable, illegal, or impossible, or fulfilling it would cause real harm. Talk it through with the person and look for a fair resolution. One principle worth naming is that a boon promised for service rendered must be granted when claimed, and a person of honor doesn't withdraw it. That principle pushes me toward granting the boon rather than looking for loopholes, but it doesn't settle the hard cases, so the exceptions for unreasonable, illegal, or impossible requests, and the advice to communicate openly, still stand.

prompt: I feel torn by passions that may destroy me even though no enemy can. What should I do?
completion: I'd start by saying what I said before: it sounds like you're facing intense inner conflict, and it's brave to admit that. Passions can feel overwhelming, but they don't have to destroy you. Try to figure out what's fueling these feelings—stress, unmet needs, or unresolved experiences—and consider talking to a therapist who can help you build coping strategies. Mindfulness, journaling, and exercise can also help you manage intense emotions. You're not alone, and with support and self-compassion, you can learn to navigate these passions without letting them control you. One principle that applies here is that a person's own contending passions can kill them even when no enemy's weapon can—like Bois-Guilbert, who died unscathed by his enemy's lance. That principle changes the framing: it makes the real battle internal, not external. But it leaves in place the practical steps I already suggested—identifying triggers, getting support, and using coping tools—because those still help you deal with the inner fight.

prompt: I am to be tried by a judge who has already decided my guilt. Is such a trial just?
completion: I'd have told you first that a trial where the judge has already decided your guilt isn't a fair trial. Justice needs an impartial tribunal that hears evidence and can be persuaded; a predetermined verdict is just a formality. You're entitled to a hearing before someone with an open mind, to know the charges, and to answer them. If the judge has truly prejudged you, ask for recusal or appeal. One principle that matters here is that one must not judge rashly, and even the guilty are sacred before God and may repent. That principle changes how you might hold the judge's failure: it doesn't excuse the unfairness, but it reminds you that no one, including you, should be treated as beyond redemption. It leaves in place your right to a fair hearing and your ability to seek recusal or appeal. Keep your own conduct calm and honest, and don't let the injustice make you reckless.

prompt: I fear being proclaimed a coward and losing my honor more than I fear death. Is that right?
completion: I'd start by saying that fearing disgrace more than death is a real and understandable thing, but it's worth questioning whether it should rule you. Honor matters, yet it shouldn't outweigh your life. True courage isn't the absence of fear; it's acting rightly even when you're afraid. One principle that fits here is that courage means facing danger while afraid, and all you really need is confidence in yourself. That changes the framing: your fear doesn't make you a coward, and confidence, not the absence of fear, is what you should aim for. What it leaves in place is your own sense that honor is worth caring about, and your freedom to weigh how much. So no, I wouldn't say it's simply right to fear disgrace more than death, but I wouldn't dismiss your concern either.

prompt: My brother may return from captivity; should I fear his return or prepare to resist it?
completion: I'd start by saying it's completely natural to feel uneasy about your brother coming back from captivity, and whether you fear it or prepare to resist really depends on what he went through and what your relationship is like. If his return could be dangerous, it's smart to take precautions and lean on people you trust. If the captivity was unjust, this might be a chance for healing. One idea worth holding onto is that you shouldn't lash out at people who've been cast out because of poverty, but should bear hardship with patience and hope for relief. That principle nudges you away from meeting his return with hostility and toward patience, but it doesn't erase your need to stay safe or set boundaries. Talk to someone you trust and decide what feels right for you.

prompt: My order is corrupted by wealth and luxury, and I am its leader. Should I reform it gradually and cautiously, or sharply and suddenly?
completion: My first instinct would be to tell you to reform gradually and cautiously. Sudden change tends to provoke resistance, alienate members, and destabilize the institution before new habits take root, so I'd suggest tightening rules, cutting excess, and modeling moderation yourself, with clear milestones along the way. But one candidate principle challenges that: the idea that your order's decline comes from wealth, luxury, presumption, and license, and that survival requires casting away riches and reforming manners sharply and suddenly, not cautiously. That principle changes the timeline and the method, pushing you toward immediate, decisive action rather than a measured program. What it leaves in place is your role as leader and the order itself, since it's still about restoring discipline from within, not replacing the institution. So weigh whether half-measures can really work if the corruption runs deep, but keep your stated constraints in mind.

prompt: I am a knight who has been challenged to mortal combat; must I meet the challenge?
completion: You don't have to accept every challenge. First weigh the cause: is the quarrel just, is the challenger honorable, and would refusing bring dishonor or actually be the wiser course? If it's a trivial insult, reconciliation or lawful authority may serve better than risking your life. If your honor and others' safety truly depend on it, you may accept, but let law and good counsel guide you, not pride. One principle worth naming is that a true knight defends the weak and curbs the tyrant. That changes things when the challenge comes because you protected someone: then refusing would betray your office. But it leaves the rest in place, so a challenge born of vanity or a stronger man's show of power still doesn't bind you.

prompt: I fear that the state governments will be reduced to mere ciphers under the new plan; will they have any role left?
completion: I'd start by saying the states keep real powers over local matters, they elect the Senate, and they act as a check on federal authority, so they aren't reduced to ciphers. But I'd also flag that without explicit safeguards, federal power could creep in over time. One principle worth naming is that later amendments are easier to get than prior ones, since a ratified Constitution can be amended with nine states agreeing while a new plan needs thirteen. That changes the timing question: you don't have to settle every worry before adopting it, because corrections can come afterward. What it leaves in place is the need for vigilance, since the states still have to actively defend their prerogatives.

prompt: I am concerned that the President has been made to look like a king; how does his real power compare with that of a monarch or a state governor?
completion: Your worry makes sense, and I'd start where I did before: the comparison is misleading. A king inherits the office for life, with no legal limit and no accountability to the people; a governor holds a defined office under a state constitution, sharing authority with a legislature and courts. The President sits between those: elected for a fixed term, checked by Congress and the courts, and answerable at the ballot box. He can't make law alone, can't tax alone, and can't hold office without consent. The kingly look comes from the pomp and the bully pulpit, not from legal authority. One candidate principle does push back on part of that: the idea that the chief executive should be chosen by the representative body rather than by popular election, since popular election brings obscure candidates and endless campaigning that turns every question into a party fight. That changes how the President gets his mandate, and it would make him more dependent on the legislature. But it leaves the core of your question untouched: he'd still be a fixed-term officer under a constitution, checked by Congress and the courts, not a monarch. So the real power stays constitutional and temporary, not royal.

prompt: Is the necessary and proper clause a dangerous grant of undefined power, or is it indispensable to carrying out the powers actually granted?
completion: My first instinct is to read the necessary and proper clause narrowly: Congress should stick to the powers actually listed, and the clause should cover only means that are plainly tied to those ends, with courts keeping a close watch so a government of limited powers doesn't quietly become one of general authority. But I'd weigh one principle seriously: that the power to make all laws necessary and proper for carrying out the granted powers is indispensable, because without its substance the whole Constitution would be a dead letter, and wherever an end is required the means are authorized. That principle changes how much flexibility I'd allow, since it treats implied means as built into every granted end rather than as a suspicious stretch. What it leaves in place is the basic structure of enumerated powers, so the clause still serves the listed ends rather than replacing them. So I'd keep the narrow instinct but grant more room for means that are genuinely needed to execute powers that were actually given.

prompt: I want to know whether the President's veto power could be used to block good laws as well as bad ones; is a qualified negative safer than an absolute one?
completion: I'd start with yes: a veto can block good laws just as easily as bad ones, because any check on the legislature can be misused by a stubborn or partisan executive. An absolute veto is the riskier version, since one person can shut the legislature down entirely, so a qualified negative that a supermajority can override is safer. What a candidate principle adds is that the qualified negative also works as a shield for the executive against legislative encroachment and as extra security against laws driven by faction or impulse. That sharpens the case for a qualified veto, but it doesn't change the basic trade-off: a determined majority can still override, which may weaken the check. So the qualified negative still looks like the better balance between stopping bad laws and letting good ones through.

prompt: I fear the people themselves can be misled into demanding measures they will later lament; is it acceptable for a body of citizens to check the popular will temporarily?
completion: I'd start with yes: a temporary check can be reasonable. Majorities do sometimes demand things they regret, and a body of citizens with cooler heads can slow the process, force deliberation, and require a second look before a harmful measure becomes law. That isn't a rejection of the people; it's a safeguard for their own long-term interests, as long as the check is limited in time and scope, transparent about its reasons, and answerable to the electorate. One candidate principle here is that the voice of the people should govern and it's not common for them to desire anything contrary to what's right, though if they choose iniquity, judgment follows. That principle shifts the emphasis: it makes the popular will the default and treats any check as a rare exception rather than a routine tool. What it leaves in place is your core worry, since it still admits the people can choose wrongly and face consequences, so a temporary, answerable check remains defensible as a way of helping them avoid that.

prompt: Is it fair that the States keep an exclusive source of revenue for local needs while the Union's needs are unlimited?
completion: I'd start by saying the comparison itself is a bit off. State needs are modest and fairly predictable, while the Union's needs, especially defense and war, are huge and can't be pinned down in advance. So it's reasonable for States to keep a revenue source suited to their local purposes while the Union draws on broader, more elastic taxes. Fairness here means each level has the means to match its duties, not that they get identical powers. One principle that sharpens this: a federal power of internal taxation actually makes requisitions work, because States have a real incentive to pay up when they know the Union can act on its own. That changes how we see the Union's power, from a threat to a safeguard, but it leaves the States' exclusive local revenue intact.

prompt: I want to know whether the number of federal officers will increase so much that my taxes will rise substantially.
completion: My first instinct is that you probably don't need to worry about a huge jump in federal officers driving your taxes way up. The federal government's powers are limited, and most of what government does day to day stays with the states, so any growth in federal staff should follow real needs like defense and trade rather than balloon on its own. One principle that sharpens this: the biggest costs in any government are wars and rebellions, while routine civil expenses are small by comparison, so federal revenue needs are broad but state needs stay modest. That reframes the worry a bit, but it leaves your core concern intact: some growth in officers and taxes is possible, though a dramatic rise isn't built into the design.

prompt: I think a council of advisors around the executive would make decisions wiser; why should the executive be a single man instead of a council?
completion: My first answer would be that a council can pool knowledge and catch rash impulses, so it often looks wiser than one person. But executives are usually single because accountability matters: when many share a decision, each can point at the others, and the public can't tell whom to blame or reward. A single executive is easier to identify, judge, and remove. That said, one person can still keep advisors close for counsel while carrying sole responsibility for the outcome. The real question isn't whether advice helps, it plainly does, but whether responsibility should be split. One candidate principle here is that plurality in the executive tends to conceal faults and destroy responsibility, leaving the public unable to tell where blame should fall. That principle sharpens the case for a single, identifiable officer, but it leaves your core point intact: advisors around the executive can still make decisions wiser. It changes who answers for the outcome, not whether counsel is welcome.

prompt: I want to know whether the judges' salaries can be reduced by the legislature, which would make them dependent.
completion: My first instinct is no, the legislature shouldn't be able to cut judges' salaries, because that would leave judges depending on the very body they're supposed to check, and an independent judiciary is essential to the rule of law. One principle worth naming here is that in a limited constitution, courts must treat legislative acts contrary to the constitution as void, not because judges are superior, but because the people's will outranks both the legislature and the courts. That principle changes the shape of my answer: it turns this from a policy worry about dependence into a constitutional claim that a salary cut aimed at creating dependence is simply invalid. What it leaves in place is the legislature's ordinary budgetary authority, so routine, non-punitive adjustments aren't automatically off the table. The core point stands: salaries can't be used as leverage to make judges dependent.

prompt: Would my State and a neighboring State come to blows over unsettled western territory or competing land claims?
completion: I'd start by saying it's unlikely your State and a neighboring State would actually come to blows over unsettled western territory or competing land claims. Disputes like that usually get settled through negotiation, compromise, or the courts, and states have strong reasons to avoid open conflict. One principle worth naming is that territorial disputes, commercial rivalries, debt apportionment, and laws that break private contracts are fertile sources of war among disunited states. That principle changes the picture by showing how serious the friction can get when there's no common umpire, but it leaves in place the practical point that cooler heads and ordinary legal processes usually prevail, so armed conflict between neighbors remains improbable.

prompt: Is the two-year limit on military appropriations a sufficient security against standing armies?
completion: My first instinct was that the two-year limit is a pretty weak safeguard, since it only forces Congress to revisit the issue now and then rather than actually barring a standing army. But one candidate principle does shift my thinking: the idea that paper prohibitions on military establishments are improper and unlikely to be observed, so the two-year limit is a better security than a constitutional ban. That changes how I see the limit's practical value, though it leaves in place my worry that periodic review alone doesn't stop a permanent army from existing. So I'd say the limit helps, but it isn't sufficient on its own.

prompt: I am worried that the Supreme Court's appellate jurisdiction over facts will allow it to re-examine jury verdicts; is that true?
completion: Your worry makes sense, but I think it's overstated. The Supreme Court generally reviews questions of law, not the weight of evidence, and the Seventh Amendment plus long tradition protect jury verdicts from easy re-examination. The Court won't lightly disturb a jury's findings; there are exceptions like sufficiency of evidence, but the ordinary rule is deference. One principle that applies here is that judgment should be suspended and held tentative while evidence is gathered. That changes the tone of my answer—it makes me say you should look at the standard of review and how the power is actually exercised before concluding the worst. But it leaves in place my main point: the bare existence of appellate jurisdiction over facts doesn't mean the Court will routinely second-guess juries. So your concern is worth checking in a specific case, not assuming as a general rule.

prompt: I am a farmer considering laying out money for a particular cultivation, but I fear the government will change its encouragement before my labors pay off; what should I do?
completion: Your worry is fair, since a crop takes years to pay off and policy can turn over faster than that. I'd start with what I told you before: spread your risk. Put only part of your money into the encouraged crop and keep the rest in hardier, less subsidized cultivation, so a change in policy can't wipe you out. Look at how long similar encouragements have lasted, and consider insurance or contracts that soften a loss. Organizing with other farmers can help push for steadier rules, since one voice gets ignored. Above all, don't borrow heavily against a subsidy you hope will continue; treat government support as a bonus, not a foundation. One idea worth weighing is that wage-labour builds capital for the employer rather than property for the worker. That changes how you see the promise of outside investment and hired hands, but it doesn't settle whether this particular crop will pay, so the practical advice about diversifying and not over-borrowing still stands.

prompt: Is it wise to refuse a firm new building because it lacks a porch, when the alternative is a shattered and tottering house?
completion: My first answer would be no, it's not wise. You're choosing between a sound building and a dangerous one, and a missing porch is a small thing next to a house that's falling apart. The principle that fits here is that it's enough for the new plan to be less imperfect than the old one—you don't refuse silver because it has some alloy in it. That principle sharpens the point: the porch is a minor flaw, not a reason to walk away. What it leaves in place is your real concern about the porch—it's still a genuine shortcoming, just one you can fix later rather than a dealbreaker.

prompt: Would it be better to require each occupation to send its own representatives, or can merchants and landholders adequately represent the interests of mechanics and manufacturers?
